evidence_text:
Cracks in the Foundation: How Data-Hungry and Sensitive to Domain Shift are Vision Foundation Models for Computational Pathology?

Background

Vision Foundation Models (VFM) have emerged as a promising approach for computational pathology, offering scalable feature representations that may reduce labelled-data requirements and improve robustness to variation in tissue preparation and digitisation. However, VFM decoder and dataset size requirements as well as the performance under real-world domain shifts remain unclear.

Methods

We evaluated six contemporary VFMs on a protocol-variant Prostate Cancer (PCa) dataset comprising 37 683 tissue microarray spot images from 10 412 patients. The dataset includes six controlled domain shifts arising from differences in staining duration, section thickness, scanner type, and sampling location. Two clinically relevant downstream tasks were examined: ISUP grading and 5-year relapse prediction. We compared two decoder architectures, quantified dataset-size requirements using a saturation analysis (45–5727 samples), and assessed cross-domain robustness using out-of-domain test sets.

Findings

Larger VFMs consistently outperformed smaller models in peak accuracy and robustness metrics. Contrary to expectations of data efficiency, all models showed strong dependence on training-set size, requiring at least 1000 samples to approach stable results. All VFMs showed notable degradation under protocol-level domain shifts, with performance reductions of 4 to 13 percentage points in both cancer grading and relapse prediction, although larger models exhibited somewhat greater robustness. Furthermore, KNN-based probing performed substantially worse than a decoder-based approach across all architectures.

Interpretations

Despite their strong representational capacity, current VFMs do not yet provide reliable domain generalisation or data-efficient performance in computational pathology. Decoder design remains essential, and substantial amounts of labelled data are still required to achieve clinically meaningful accuracy. Further advances in pre-training strategies, decoder architectures, and domain adaptation methods will be crucial for translating VFMs into robust clinical tools.

Research in context

Evidence before this study

This study focuses on pathology foundation models, which offer promising improvements in performance, data requirements, and robustness to domain shifts for computational pathology. To identify relevant studies, we searched in Google Scholar for research published before 1 April 2025. We searched for studies introducing novel foundation models trained on pathology images, or reviews comparing those models in terms of performance or robustness. The search terms used were ‘computational pathology’, ‘benchmarking’, ‘review’ and ‘foundation model’, as well combinations of these terms. We found that many studies focus on increasing the complexity of pathology foundation models while using increasingly extensive and heterogeneous pre-training datasets. Various benchmarking studies demonstrate the superior performance and robustness of more recent and larger foundation models. However, these studies have limitations in their evaluation datasets. Either they cover only a domain shift due to a different scanner device, or they have small sample sizes. We also identified a research gap regarding the requirement for large datasets to train a decoder based on a pathology foundation model for a specific downstream task.

Added value of this study

The goal of this study was to evaluate the necessity of large downstream task datasets and the domain shift robustness of multiple pathology foundation models. For this purpose, we used our internal protocol-variant prostate cancer dataset, which provides a controlled evaluation setup as multiple domain shift types have been intentionally and separately introduced for different sub-datasets. Our saturation analysis revealed that at least 1000 samples were necessary to achieve good performance. Furthermore, our findings show that none of the evaluated foundation models are robust against all of our domain shifts, though larger models generally perform better.

Implications of all the available evidence

This study reveals that increasing the capacity of pathology foundation models improves performance and robustness. However, we demonstrated that all models exhibit some degree of performance degradation for certain domain shifts and require substantial datasets for training on downstream tasks. These limitations demonstrate that pathology foundation models do not fully address the issues of robustness and data requirements.

The digital scores generated by dPathHRD were significantly correlated with established HRD-related genomic and transcriptomic features. Furthermore, dPathHRD demonstrated the ability to predict therapeutic response to platinum chemotherapy, with the HRD-like group showing higher complete response rates and longer progression-free and recurrence-free survival compared to the homologous recombination proficiency (HRP)-like group across all three cohorts. Interpretation analysis via attention mapping confirmed the model's reliance on biologically relevant histopathological features in tumor and stromal regions. In conclusion, dPathHRD offers a promising, cost-effective alternative to molecular testing, leveraging widely available digital pathology images to inform personalized treatment strategies. Further prospective validation is warranted to confirm its clinical applicability and predictive power.

title: Robust integration of weakly anchored spatial multi-omics

evidence_text: Robust integration of weakly anchored spatial multi-omics Spatial multi-omics holds great promise for dissecting complex biological processes, though inherent technical constraints continue to limit its widespread adoption. Currently, most studies therefore measure distinct omics features on separate tissue sections, necessitating spatial diagonal integration. An emerging practical solution is to leverage hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images as an integration anchor, given their ubiquity, low cost, and compatibility across tissue preparations. However, this anchor is frequently compromised in real-world settings by variations in H&E staining style, absence of reliable histological landmarks, and mismatches in spatial resolutions across omics modalities. To address this, we introduce SpaWeaver, a computational framework that couples a pathology foundation model with a graph Transformer and a latent feature aligner module, providing a highly robust solution for weakly anchored spatial omics data diagonal integration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpaWeaver exhibits superior robustness against isolated or synergistic weak-anchoring factors. The spatial multi-omics profiles generated by SpaWeaver link molecular features originally separated on two sections, unlocking diverse downstream analyses once exclusive to co-assayed spatial multi-omics data, including niche-aware cell–cell communication inference and multi-omics resolved cell state. In this study, it unveils tumor-distance-dependent fibroblast–CD4□T-cell signaling in human colon adenocarcinoma and identifies a hypoxic glycolytic tumor state with pyknotic nuclei in human ovarian cancer. Overall, our approach bridges readily accessible single-omics measurements across weakly anchored tissue sections, enabling unified spatial multi-omics characterization and system-level tissue analysis.

title: ToPoFM: Topology-Guided Pathology Foundation Model for High-Resolution Pathology Image Synthesis With Cellular-Level Control.

evidence_text: ToPoFM: Topology-Guided Pathology Foundation Model for High-Resolution Pathology Image Synthesis With Cellular-Level Control. Synthetic data generation emerges as a strategy to mitigate data scarcity in digital pathology, where complicated tissue and cellular features are correlated with cancer diagnosis. The synthesis of such visuals, however, suffers from limited inter class diversity and scarcity of cellular annotations. Current methodologies struggle with capturing the broad spectrum of pathology features, causing unpredictable objects and defected fidelity. Moreover, discrepancies in image resolution across developmental and operational phases can amplify the distribution shifts, undermining the precision of diagnosis. To address these challenges, we introduce TOpology guided PathOlogy Foundation Model (ToPoFM), a visual foundation model designed for the synthesis of high-resolution pathology images with cellular-level control. Our approach integrates a topology-informed cell arrangement generator to steer large language models for crafting synthetic cell arrangements. We correlate cell arrangement guidance with diffusion model for pathology content generation, then further implement a random sliding inference strategy, merging discrete low-resolution samplings into single high-resolution representation. Our model requires only small patches for training. The efficacy of ToPoFM is demonstrated through extensive experiments, complemented by expert validations, showing high fidelity on data synthesis. Additionally, we underscore the utility of our generated imagery as an augmentation tool, enhancing the performance of downstream tasks, including cancer subtype classification and segmentation.

evidence_text: Associations between spatial distribution of immune cell subsets and clinical outcomes in patients with advanced melanoma treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors: results from the PUMA challenge. Patients with advanced melanoma are treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), yet <50% of patients achieve a durable response while all patients are exposed to the risk of severe side effects. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in pathology images are associated with ICI outcomes, but manual assessment is subjective. In addition, the predictive value of other immune cell subsets, including plasma cells, neutrophils, histiocytes, and melanophages, remains unclear. We organized the Panoptic segmentation of nUclei and tissue in advanced MelanomA (PUMA) challenge to evaluate whether the spatial localization of TILs and other immune cell subsets on melanoma H&E slides collected before start of treatment was associated with treatment outcomes. Algorithm performance was evaluated on a hidden test set, after which top-ranked algorithms were applied to pre-treatment metastatic whole-slide images from a large, multicenter cohort of patients with advanced melanoma treated with first-line ICIs (n = 1102). Automatically quantified tissue features and immune cell subsets were then associated with clinical outcomes. Top-performing algorithms improved detection of immune cell subsets through pathology foundation model features, multi-stage tissue-context learning, and class-specific architectures, although accuracy for rare classes remained limited. Across challenge participants, TIL density showed the most consistent association with treatment response and survival. Associations for stromal TILs were weaker, while plasma cells, histiocytes, melanophages, neutrophils, necrosis and blood vessels did not show independent associations with outcomes. Overall, the PUMA challenge advanced immune cell detection in melanoma histopathology and showed that intratumoral lymphocytes are most consistently associated with treatment response and survival.

title: DiffBulk: Enhancing Spatial Transcriptomic Prediction With Diffusion-Based Training.
xenium_reason: Xenium is mentioned without evidence of dataset generation or reuse
evidence_text: DiffBulk: Enhancing Spatial Transcriptomic Prediction With Diffusion-Based Training. Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) technology detects gene expression from tissue biopsies, playing an emerging role in cancer diagnosis and precision medicine. However, the high cost of ST technology limits its broader application. Recently, deep learning approaches have provided insight into predicting gene expression based on H&E-stained histopathology images. Nevertheless, the relationship between morphological features and gene expression is highly complex. To address these challenges, we propose DiffBulk, a novel two-stage framework that leverages conditional diffusion models to learn expressive image representations enriched with gene expression information. In the first stage, we introduce a gene-to-image conditional diffusion model equipped with a permutation-invariant open-embedding gene encoder, which enables unified training across diverse gene panels. In the second stage, diffusion-derived features are fused with representations from a pathology foundation model, effectively bridging the domain gap and improving downstream gene expression prediction. We evaluate DiffBulk on high-quality Xenium ST data curated from the HEST dataset and the CrunchDAO challenge, constructing tile-level pseudo-bulk datasets for training and evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiffBulk consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all metrics for gene expression prediction. These findings highlight the potential of diffusion-based gene-image representation learning and suggest promising directions for future research.

evidence_text: MetAssist 2.0: A Generalizable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Lymph Node Metastasis Detection Across Multiple Cancer Types. Lymph node metastasis assessment is critical for cancer staging, yet the process is labor intensive and prone to variability, particularly when evaluating micrometastases or isolated tumor cells that can directly alter treatment decisions. We present MetAssist 2.0, a modular artificial intelligence system that combines a pathology foundation model with transformer-based segmentation to automate metastasis detection across cancer types. Trained on colorectal and upper gastrointestinal cancers, it was validated on 8144 slides spanning 7 cancer types and 14 multi-institutional cohorts. MetAssist 2.0 achieved at least 90% sensitivity in 13 cohorts and 91% specificity in 11 cohorts, including challenging subtypes such as mucinous adenocarcinoma and tumor deposits. With only 10 annotated slides, the system adapted to unseen cancer types via few-shot fine-tuning. As a triage tool for colorectal cancer, it could reduce pathologist workload by up to 72% with 98% sensitivity and revealed metastases missed in routine reporting. These results demonstrate broad generalizability and near-clinical-grade performance, positioning MetAssist 2.0 for integration into the pathology workflows.

evidence_text:
Detection of basal cell carcinoma on whole-slide images from Mohs micrographic surgery using weakly supervised learning.

Background

Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) is the gold standard for treating aggressive basal cell carcinoma, but its success depends on expertise in intraoperative interpretation of frozen sections.

Objective

To develop weakly supervised, multiple instance learning framework using a pathology foundation model for automated basal cell carcinoma detection in MMS frozen sections.

Methods

An internal data set of 995 frozen MMS whole-slide images was slide-level labeled as tumor (512) or no tumor (483). Furthermore, tumor regions in the test set were annotated. Whole-slide images were tiled and encoded with Prov-Gigapath features for a weakly supervised multiple instance learning framework. The performance was evaluated as binary slide-level classification and in attention maps showing the localization of the tumor regions prior to validation on 2 external data sets.

Results

The model showed near-perfect diagnostic performance, achieving 97.0% accuracy, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.998 on the internal data set. Furthermore, attention maps visualized diagnostically relevant regions, enhancing model interpretability (Intersection-over-Union = 0.41 ± 0.046 [Dice 0.58 ± 0.046]). External validation confirmed robust performance (90% to 92% accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 0.92-0.95).

Limitations

The absence of tumor region annotations on external data sets.

Conclusion

These findings support the feasibility of artificial intelligence-assisted analysis of MMS frozen sections and justify prospective studies evaluating its integration into clinical workflows.

evidence_text:
High-sensitivity pan-cancer AI assessment of lymph node metastasis via uncertainty quantification. The histological heterogeneity of primary tumors across the pan-cancer spectrum poses a formidable barrier to accurate lymph node metastasis assessment, often causing AI systems to make "overconfident errors" on rare variants that lead to missed diagnoses. To address this, we present UPATHLN, a unified diagnostic platform that synergizes a pathology foundation model-based encoder with a decoupled uncertainty estimation mechanism. We developed and validated the system using a large-scale multicentre dataset of 26,229 lymph nodes from 14 distinct primary origins. In internal validation, UPATHLN achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.986. Crucially, the uncertainty module functioned as a decisive fail-safe: by flagging potential false-negative predictions for mandatory pathologist review, it intercepted all missed diagnoses, securing 100% conditional sensitivity across both the development and independent test cohorts-even for tumors from seven unseen primary origins. Concurrently, this mechanism reduced the review burden on negative lymph nodes by 73.2%. Ultimately, UPATHLN sets a new benchmark for safety-critical AI, demonstrating that explicitly modeling uncertainty is key to unlocking reliable, workload-efficient diagnostics at the pan-cancer scale. Introduction  Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide  1  , primarily driven by metastasis  2 , 3  . Lymph nodes (LNs) are critical anatomical checkpoints in cancer progression  4  , serving as initial metastatic sites and immune regulatory hubs orchestrating host-tumor interactions  5  . Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) status is therefore paramount for prognostic assessment and therapeutic decision-making across diverse cancer types  6  . However, current clinical management relies primarily on crude quantitative approaches—predominantly pN staging  6  —which fail to capture crucial biological features such as lymph node ratio (LNR), metastatic tumor burden, and diverse spatial growth patterns of metastatic cells within LNs. Recent evidence explicitly links elevated LNR to decreased survival rates and shortened recurrence-free intervals  7  , while highlighting how spatial distributions of metastatic cells can modulate the immune microenvironment, potentially facilitating immune escape  8  . Despite these insights, pathologists now face an unprecedented surge in LN specimens due to rising cancer incidence  9  , rendering such detailed, multi-dimensional analysis practically unfeasible in routine workflows.  Deep learning has rapidly advanced pathological diagnosis, with numerous artificial intelligence (AI) systems gaining regulatory approval. However, existing AI approaches for LNM detection  10 – 15   typically follow cancer-specific paradigms. This fragmentation hinders widespread clinical adoption by necessitating multiple, disparate systems  16 , 17  , conflicting with the need for operational efficiency and unified diagnostic standards. Moreover, tumor heterogeneity manifests as a “long-tail distribution”  18 , 19  , where common metastatic patterns coexist with diverse rare variants. Standard deep learning models often struggle with these outliers, prone to “overconfident errors” where the system makes incorrect predictions with high certainty on out-of-distribution data. The reliable detection of these rare but clinically significant variants is crucial for patient safety  20 , 21  , yet remains challenging even with large datasets. While emerging foundation models  22 – 27   offer powerful representational capabilities, their effective application across the pan-cancer spectrum requires substantial annotation resources. Thus, there is an urgent need to transcend these limitations and establish a unified, robust, and safe diagnostic framework capable of not only high sensitivity but also reliable failure awareness across all cancer types.  To address these challenges, we developed UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware AI platform integrating a pathology foundation model with uncertainty-guided active learning and robust uncertainty estimation (Fig.  1 ). Trained and validated on an extensive multi-center, multi-cancer LN dataset, this study demonstrates UPATHLN’s capacity for highly sensitive and safe pan-cancer LNM detection with robust generalization. Ultimately, this study represents a critical step towards establishing a unified, trustworthy diagnostic standard for AI-assisted pathology.    Fig. 1   Development of clinically safe pan-cancer lymph node pathology diagnostic system.   a  Multi-center data composition: clinical samples from three hospitals of varying scales covering lymph nodes (LNs) from 14 primary sites.  b  Surgical case complexity: each case typically involves >10 LNs, increasing diagnostic workload compared to primary tumor assessment.  c  Representative HE examples of lymph node metastases illustrating morphological heterogeneity. Insets highlight thyroid-type colloid-like material and other non-specific patterns that may be prominent in metastases from the indicated primary sites, including mucin pools, stromal fibrosis/desmoplasia, and keratin pearls.  d  Uncertainty-guided active learning framework: system leverages clinical pathology database with iterative refinement where pathologists review high uncertainty (HU) predictions, verify challenging cases through IHC staining (CAM5.2, AE1/3), and exclude poor-quality samples. In clinical practice, uncertainty estimates guide pathologists' review to prevent rare subtype misdiagnosis and enable continuous system improvement.                     Results   Establishment of the UPATHLN platform and active learning optimization  To establish the UPATHLN platform, we curated a large-scale, multi-center pan-cancer dataset comprising 26,229 lymph nodes (LNs) from 8294 whole-slide images (WSIs) across 2738 patients, spanning tumors from 14 distinct primary organs. The dataset was rigorously partitioned into a development cohort and an independent test cohort, with seven rare primary origins strictly held out as unseen primary-origin holdouts to evaluate generalization to previously unseen origins (SFig.  1 ). To ensure high-quality input to the platform, our automated LN extraction pipeline achieved robust performance, with YOLOv8-s demonstrating a recall of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection and nnUNet achieving a Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for tissue segmentation, effectively excluding non-target tissues (Fig.  2a  and SFig.  2 ).    Fig. 2   Deep learning framework for lymph node metastasis detection with iterative refinement.   a  System architecture overview. The pipeline sequentially employs a detection model to localize lymph node regions and a segmentation model to delineate their contours. The core classification framework features a Multiscale Cross-Attention architecture that utilizes the UNI pathology foundation model as a feature encoder. By synthesizing features from multi-scale tissue patches, the model simultaneously outputs tumor confidence via the Classification Module and prediction uncertainty via the Uncertainty Estimation Module.  b – e  Performance metrics comparing original and high uncertainty (HU)-filtered predictions across training iterations: tile-level AUC ( b ), PPV ( c ), NPV ( d ), and lymph node-level sensitivity ( e ).  f ,  g  Lymph node-level metrics: average false positives (FPavg) and average high uncertainty regions (HUavg). At the lymph-node level, each LN was counted once regardless of the number of false-positive or high-uncertainty subregions within it. In bar charts ( b – g ), 95% confidence intervals were derived from bootstrapping (1000 iterations).                   Rather than relying on static training, we optimized the platform using an uncertainty-driven active learning strategy. Misclassified tiles were enriched in the high-uncertainty (HU) tail of the tile-level uncertainty-score distribution (SFig.  4a ). Accordingly, we summarized tile uncertainties into a slide-level ambiguity score and ranked candidate WSIs for expert review (SFig.  3 , “Methods”). Through five rounds of human-in-the-loop iterations, this active optimization substantially improved discriminative performance on the internal validation set, increasing the tile-level AUC from a baseline of 0.953 (95% CI: 0.932–0.974) to 0.986 (95% CI: 0.976–0.996), with consistent gains in both PPV and NPV (Fig.  2b–d ).  To rigorously attribute this high performance to architectural design rather than data accumulation alone, we benchmarked the final model against alternative architectures trained on the identical dataset generated from the final iteration. The multiscale architecture significantly outperformed both the single-scale UNI baseline (AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.910–0.946; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001) and the ImageNet-pretrained feature extractor (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.901–0.935; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001; SFig.  4b ).    Uncertainty-aware classification achieves high-sensitivity LNM detection  Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a clinical fail-safe. While the optimized multiscale classifier achieved a robust intrinsic sensitivity of 0.996 (95% CI: 0.985–1.000; Fig.  2e ), it erroneously classified three metastatic cases as negative when relying exclusively on diagnostic probability scores (false negatives, FNs). In the uncertainty-annotated confusion matrix (SFig.  5a ; HU-flag counts are shown in parentheses), all three FNs were flagged as high uncertainty and therefore routed for mandatory pathologist confirmation. This capability to “rescue” potential false negatives effectively neutralized the risk of missed diagnosis, underpinning the system’s 100% conditional sensitivity and ensuring that ambiguous but critical lesions were correctly routed for pathologist confirmation.  To evaluate clinical workload, we quantified the review burden at the LN level. Here, each LN was counted at most once, regardless of how many false-positive or high-uncertainty subregions it contained. Across iterations, both the LN-level false-positive (FP) rate and HU rate steadily declined (Fig.  2f, g ), reaching final values of 0.112 (95% CI: 0.070–0.155) and 0.156 (95% CI: 0.110–0.202), respectively. The model’s progressive refinement was visually corroborated by prediction heatmaps (Fig.  3a  and SFig.  6 ), and it precisely identified diverse metastatic burdens, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cell clusters (Fig.  3b ). Final validation by pathologists on the remaining development cohort confirmed a 100% positive detection rate with minimal review overhead (1% FP rate and 0.16% HU rate at the LN level).    Fig. 3   Visualization of iterative refinement and representative challenging cases.   a  Representative lymph node whole-slide images (WSIs) with prediction heatmaps from the first iteration and the final (fifth) iteration, showing progressive refinement across active-learning cycles. Right, a magnified example tile from the high-uncertainty (HU) regions identified in the first iteration.  b  Representative isolated LNM detection cases with immunohistochemical (IHC) validation. For each case, the HE slide, the registered IHC section, and the corresponding prediction heatmap are shown, with magnified tumor tiles from the boxed regions. In the magnified panels, orange arrowheads on HE indicate tumor cell foci, and the corresponding IHC images highlight tumor cells by brown chromogenic staining. In the heatmaps, yellow denotes HU regions, red denotes regions with high tumor confidence, and blue denotes lymph node tissue. Scale bars as indicated.                     Validation of pan-cancer robustness and safety  Performance evaluation on the independent test cohort confirmed the system’s robust discriminative power (Fig.  4  and SFig.  7 – 10 ). To establish a baseline, we first evaluated the standalone classification module without uncertainty intervention. Operating strictly on diagnostic probability scores, the module achieved a robust sensitivity of 98.7% and a specificity of 88.0% (SFig.  5b ). Although this represents a high level of diagnostic accuracy, relying solely on this conventional probability thresholding still resulted in 60 FN predictions (missed LNMs). Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a decisive fail-safe mechanism to address this residual risk. It successfully intercepted all 60 initially missed instances by classifying them as HU. This “rescue effect” secured a 100% conditional sensitivity across the entire test cohort, effectively neutralizing the clinical risk of missed diagnoses.    Fig. 4   Pan-cancer generalization performance across 14 primary origins.  The multi-center multi-cancer independent test cohort is stratified into common and rare origins. Primary sites are sorted by WSI count and color-coded: purple (Trained) and mint green (Unseen). Rows display: (1) Total WSI counts; (2) Metastatic status distribution (red: metastatic; blue: non-metastatic); (3) LN-level conditional sensitivity (maintaining 100% via uncertainty referral); (4) False Positive (FP) rate; and (5) High Uncertainty (HU) rate. Color intensity reflects numerical magnitude.                   The operational cost of this safety profile was quantified using the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N). Accounting for the union of FP and HU predictions, the effective RBR-N was 26.8% (3180/11,873). This indicates that 73.2% of negative LNs were safely excluded from manual review.  Subgroup analysis revealed remarkable consistency across organ origins, with a weighted average FP rate of 7.5% (SD: 2.1%) (Fig.  4 ). For the seven cancer types included in training, performance remained stable regardless of sample size. Notably, although Stomach cancer LNs were overrepresented in the training data (35.6%), their performance (HU rate: 5.2%; FP rate: 6.6%) closely mirrored the cohort average, indicating that the model maintained balanced discriminative power despite the non-uniform training distribution. While robust to sample size variations, the model exhibited sensitivity to specific non-neoplastic histological features. LNs from the lung and cervix exhibited higher HU rates (32.6% and 26.0%, respectively). Pathological audit confirmed that in lung cancer, these flags were predominantly triggered by anthracitic pigment, indicating that the model correctly identified non-malignant confounders as HU regions (SFig.  11 ).  Most notably, the system demonstrated exceptional adaptability to the seven cancer types entirely unseen during training. The fail-safe mechanism remained fully effective even in these out-of-distribution domains, with zero missed diagnoses recorded. Regarding efficiency, the model maintained consistently low LN-level FP rates for the majority of these unseen origins (6/7), ranging from 2.4% (kidney) to 10.8% (thyroid) without fine-tuning. The sole exception was penile cancer (SFig.  8 ), a rare type with complex morphology, where the system exhibited an adaptive increase in review rates (HU: 30.2%; FP: 20.0%). This reflects a cautious inference strategy that prioritizes diagnostic safety when encountering highly atypical histological patterns.    Interpretability and pathological characterization of uncertainty  To elucidate the interpretability underlying this robust performance, we deconstructed the uncertainty landscape. Multiscale feature fusion dimensionality reduction analysis (Fig.  5a, b ) clearly delineated tumor and normal regions, with HU areas concentrated at the boundaries in feature space. We were able to effectively extract these areas through uncertainty quantification.    Fig. 5   Visualization and interpretation of uncertainty estimation.   a ,  b  t-SNE visualization of tile-level feature embeddings from the internal validation dataset.  a  Binary prediction distribution (red: tumor; blue: normal), with triangles indicating misclassified samples.  b  Uncertainty level distribution (yellow: High Uncertainty [HU]; blue: Low Uncertainty [LU]), showing HU samples concentrating at the tumor-normal decision boundary.  c  Pathological categorization of HU clusters identifying four non-neoplastic confounders: dense connective tissue (orange), loose connective tissue (teal), bleeding (green), and low-quality regions (blue).  d  Representative heatmaps displaying spatial distributions of HU regions (yellow) alongside tumor (red) and normal (blue) predictions.  e  Clinical workflow illustration: HU predictions trigger pathologist re-review, with IHC confirmation reserved for challenging cases.                   Further analysis allowed categorization of HU regions into types such as dense connective tissue, loose connective tissue, low-quality image areas, and bleeding areas (Fig.  5c ). As shown in Fig.  5d , the model assigned high HU scores to two patients with distinct atypical cytomorphology: one with lymphocyte-like tumor cells featuring scant cytoplasm and naked nuclei, and another exhibiting plasmacytoid/histiocytoid features with moderate cytoplasm. This assessment mechanism enables pathologists to selectively focus on these challenging cases, thereby ensuring diagnostic accuracy and clinical safety while improving efficiency. As the system continues to be applied, manual review of uncertain regions will facilitate ongoing model optimization (Fig.  5e ).     Discussion  This study addresses the limitations of current organ-specific AI paradigms by presenting UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware framework for pan-cancer LNM diagnosis. While previous deep learning approaches have validated LNM detection in organ-specific cohorts, they often operate as “black boxes,” lacking the safety mechanisms required for broad clinical adoption  20  . By devising a specialized Multiscale cross-attention framework to effectively contextualize features from the pathology foundation model, UPATHLN establishes a robust clinical safety net. Notably, this architectural design demonstrated a definitive “fail-safe” capability in a large-scale independent cohort: the uncertainty mechanism successfully intercepted all initially missed metastases, securing 100% conditional sensitivity. This achievement marks a significant advancement: moving from algorithms that prioritize raw accuracy to safety-critical systems that effectively mitigate the risk of FNs in metastatic screening.  The parallel uncertainty estimation branch underpins the technical integrity of this safety profile. Classical uncertainty estimation methods—such as uncertainty-prediction model co-training  28 , 29  , multiple model ensembles  30  , or repeated dropout strategies  28 , 31  —increase computational burden and often flag large unnecessary regions for manual reassessment. By contrast, our independent bypass architecture provides precise localization of diagnostically uncertain regions without compromising inference speed. This decoupled mechanism acts as a reliable diagnostic filter, specifically designed to handle the inherent biological heterogeneity of metastatic disease. It respects the ambiguity of “long-tail” rare variants and non-neoplastic confounders (e.g., anthracotic pigment), routing these cases strictly within the system’s competence boundaries. This “rescue effect” ensures that algorithmic limitations do not translate into diagnostic errors, maintaining high reliability even when encountering complex morphologies that typically confound conventional models.  Furthermore, we successfully navigated the data annotation bottleneck that typically constrains the scalability of foundation models. By coupling high-level feature representations with an uncertainty-guided active learning framework, we efficiently captured a comprehensive spectrum of metastatic morphologies across 14 cancer types without necessitating exhaustive annotation. This strategy proved vital for addressing the diverse patterns of metastatic pathology. Consequently, the system maintained robust performance even on LNM samples from primary sites entirely unseen during training. This demonstrates that uncertainty-driven learning provides a practical, scalable pathway to generalize pathology AI, enabling adaptability to domain shifts and rare cancer types lacking large-scale training data.  UPATHLN reconciles the critical tension between rising diagnostic volumes and the demand for granular prognostic assessment. By safely automating the exclusion of 73.2% of negative LNs, the system liberates pathologists to focus on complex cases. Crucially, this efficiency renders detailed “multi-dimensional analysis”—specifically the precise quantification of tumor-to-lymph node area ratio  12   and spatial distribution patterns—feasible in routine practice. Moving beyond crude pN staging, UPATHLN provides the quantitative depth required for modern precision oncology that is practically impossible to achieve manually.  Despite these advances, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study is retrospective, and all training/validation data were sourced from hospitals in China; therefore, real-world deployment requires prospective multi-center evaluation and external validation across diverse populations, institutions, and scanning protocols. Second, although many artifacts are appropriately flagged as high uncertainty, future work could incorporate dedicated artifact-suppression or quality-control modules to further reduce review burden without compromising safety. Third, while the pipeline is designed to be compatible with different pathology foundation models, we only evaluated UNI and did not empirically compare performance against alternative encoders.  Collectively, UPATHLN advances pan-cancer LNM screening by introducing a risk-aware architecture that balances automation with expert oversight. The synergy between its decoupled uncertainty “fail-safe” and active learning framework ensures robust performance and scalability under heterogeneous clinical conditions. This approach not only streamlines routine triage but also provides a quantitative basis for assessing metastatic burden, potentially informing prognostic insights beyond standard pathological staging.    Methods   Dataset collection and cohort definition  We established a large-scale, pan-cancer dataset combining clinical data from three independent medical centers, with heterogeneous clinical workloads and patient populations, enabling evaluation across varied real-world settings. The primary clinical cohort included 2738 patients (8294 WSIs, 26,229 LNs) covering 14 distinct solid tumor types (SFig.  1a ). We applied specific exclusion criteria to ensure data quality: WSIs exhibiting severe artefacts—such as tissue folding covering >20% of the area, significant out-of-focus blurring, or extreme staining inconsistencies—were removed prior to analysis. In addition to the clinical cohort, we utilized an annotated gastric cancer dataset from our previous work  12   (GLN21) and the publicly available breast cancer dataset from the CAMELYON16 challenge  11   (BLN16) for model initialization.  Crucially, to prevent data leakage, we employed a strict patient-level splitting strategy, where all WSIs and LN sections from the same patient were assigned exclusively to a single cohort. As illustrated in the study design flow (SFig.  3 ), the clinical data were stratified into two independent cohorts. The development cohort consisted of 683 patients (2547 WSIs, 9729 LNs) from 7 common cancer types and was further subdivided to support the active learning workflow (SFig.  1b ). The multi-center multi-cancer test cohort comprised an independent set of 2055 patients (5747 WSIs, 16,500 LNs), serving as the held-out standard for final performance evaluation (SFig.  1c ). To rigorously assess the model’s generalization capabilities, the test cohort was stratified into two groups: the 7 cancer types encountered during training and a distinct set of 7 cancer types (thyroid, pancreas, bile duct, kidney, prostate, penis, and anus). Crucially, samples from these rare origins were strictly excluded from the training pipeline, ensuring that their evaluation represents a true test of the model’s ability to generalize to completely unseen primary origins. For LN counting, pathologists manually reviewed the slides to identify spatially distinct LNs; serial sections of the same node, if present, were identified based on morphological continuity and excluded from the total count to ensure each observation represented a unique LN.  This retrospective, multi-center study was conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Changhai Hospital (CHEC2024-276), the Ethics Committee of the Second People’s Hospital of Wuxi (2024Y-125), and the Ethics Committee of the 960th Hospital of the People’s Liberation Army (2024-087). The requirement for informed consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the use of anonymized data.    Lymph node contour recognition  To increase the training accuracy of LN metastasis detection models, we first developed an LN contour recognition model. The WSIs of LN tissue include not only LNs but also muscle, extraneous fat, and cancer nodules. The presence of these nontarget tissues can adversely affect the accuracy of metastasis detection.  Our model comprises two stages: initially, the YOLOv8-s model is employed for LN detection due to its high efficiency and rapid localization capabilities. The detected regions are subsequently input into the nnUNet  32   model for segmentation to remove impurities from the LN periphery.  We processed images using 1024 × 1024 pixel tiles at 1× magnification and utilized a 256-pixel sliding window for segmentation. The YOLOv8-s model was trained with default parameters, using the annotated contour coordinates as ground truth labels. The nnUNet model was similarly trained with default settings, using the bounding box of annotated regions to cut tiles at 0.25× magnification and employing annotated contours as masks.  During inference, a staged strategy was employed: YOLOv8-s model-predicted coordinates were used to cut local tiles, which were then input into the nnUNet model to obtain precise contour masks. These masks were mapped back to the full 0.25x thumbnail based on relative coordinates. For overlapping sliding windows, an averaging method was used to smooth boundaries.  We annotated 200 WSIs with 721 LNs from various tumor types for the YOLOv8-s model and nnUNet model training. After initial training, predictions of unannotated WSIs in the development cohort were manually reviewed. We reviewed 918 WSIs (comprising 3528 LNs) and reannotated 132 WSIs with incorrect predictions. Then, the YOLOv8-s model was retrained on a combined dataset of the initial 200 annotated WSIs and the 918 manually reviewed WSIs (total 1118 WSIs; randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing). Ultimately, the YOLOv8-s model achieved a recall rate of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection.  Since nnUNet requires contour-level annotations, we used the initial 200 WSIs along with the 132 fully corrected WSIs (comprising 1245 LNs) for retraining. Finally, the nnUNet model achieved a mean Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for LN contour segmentation. A manual review of inference results from the development cohort confirmed the ability of the two-stage model to accurately delineate LN contours and exclude non-LN tissues. This process provides high-quality input data for subsequent metastasis detection. As illustrated in SFig.  2a , we effectively identified and extracted LN contours from complex pathological images, facilitating high-quality input for further metastasis detection. Some missed LN diagnoses are due to atypical morphology (e.g., indistinct capsules) or small nodal size (SFig.  2b ). In clinical applications, missed LN identification is rare, so it does not increase the workload. Pathologists can easily add annotations during the review process. As missed diagnosis cases continue to be collected, this situation will become increasingly rare. The annotation and review process was conducted by two senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience: Y.C. and C.Q.    Data preprocessing for the classification model  Following the extraction of LN contour regions from WSIs, we tiled tumor metastasis areas on the basis of annotations to train the classification model. Given that accurate diagnosis of some LN metastases requires multiscale observations, we applied multiscale tiling to the annotated dataset. This process involved extracting image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both 10x and 4× magnification, as shown in Fig.  2a . The center coordinates of tiles at both scales were aligned to ensure consistent observation of the same region at different resolutions.  By integrating the LN contour mask with the tumor mask, we cropped regions of interest into tumor and nontumor areas. At 10× magnification, a sliding window of 64 pixels was used to divide the region into extractable tiles, with each grid classified on the basis of the proportion of the tumor area annotated by doctors. Specifically, if more than 25% of a grid area was annotated as a tumor, the tile was labeled positive; otherwise, it was labeled negative. To ensure category balance, if the number of tiles in any category exceeded 100 within a WSI, we randomly selected 100 tiles. This sampling strategy maintained balanced categories at the tile level.    Feature extractor  In this study, we utilized UNI  23  , a Vision Transformer (ViT-Large  33  ) foundation model pre-trained on over 100,000 HE-stained WSIs, as a frozen feature extractor. UNI was selected as it represented a leading solution for pan-cancer feature representation at the time of study implementation. Importantly, our proposed multiscale architecture is designed to be foundation-model agnostic. While UNI was employed here as a representative high-performance encoder to validate our framework, the system is compatible with and can readily incorporate other emerging pathology foundation models  22 , 24 – 27  . For feature extraction, we processed image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both the 10× and the 4× magnification levels and randomly cropped them to 224 × 224 pixels. The resulting feature matrix for each tile maintains a shape of (196 + 1, 1024), where 196 represents the length of the patch-tokens, and 1 represents the class token.    Multiscale feature fusion and classification module  By extracting features from the same local region at different magnification levels and then fusing them, the model can capture both global and local pathological morphological features, better locating and identifying tumor areas. Specifically, we adopted the cross-attention module proposed by Zhou et al.  34   to multiscale image feature fusion. As shown in Fig.  2a , the entire cross-attention module consists of two cross-attention blocks and two self-attention blocks. The cross-attention blocks learn the intrinsic connections of multiscale image features by dynamically weighting features from different spatial scales.  In the cross-attention block, the process of generating Q, K, and V for each scale image feature is as follows:   1      Q    4  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x    =  LP     Norm       X    4  x              2      Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    =  LP     Norm       X    10  x             where     LP     ⋅        denotes linear projection and     Norm     ⋅        denotes layer normalization. The forwards pass in the cross-attention block can be summarized as:   3      P    4  x    =  Attn  (    Q    4  x  ′      K    4  x  ,      V    4  x    )  +  Attn  (    Q    4  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )      4      P    10  x    =  Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )  +  Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x    )     where     Attn  (    Q    4  x    ,    K    4  x    ,    V    4  x      ) and     Attn  (    Q    10  x    ,    K    10  x    ,    V    10  x    )     capture the intra-scale feature relationships. The intermediate expression  P  represents the potential connections obtained through interaction between the 4x and 10× magnification images. The attention mechanism     Attn     Q  ,  K  ,  V        includes two matrices multiplication operations, a scaling operation, and a softmax operation:   5    Attn  (  Q  ,  K  ,  V  )  =  softmax         QK    T          d    k           V     where    T    denotes the matrix transpose operator and     d  k     is the scaling hyperparameter set to 64. Next, the residual learning approach incorporates the resulting  P   4x   and  P   10x   into the normalization layer and multiple layer perceptron (MLP):   6      X    4  x    ′  =  MLP  (  Norm  (    P    4  x    )  )  +    X    4  x        7      X    10  x    ′  =  MLP     Norm     P  10  x        +    X    10  x       where     X   4    x   ′       and     X   10    x   ′       represent the inputs fed into the next cross-attention block.  Subsequently, we merged the cross-attention features by concatenating the tokens directly, resulting in a new feature embedding with a shape of (197 + 197,1024).  Finally, we input the new feature embedding into two self-attention modules, followed by LayerNorm normalization. The class token from the feature embedding is then used as the overall feature  F , which is fed into a fully connected layer to predict the tumor probability of the 10x tile.  During training, the parameters of the UNI pretrained ViT-Large feature extractor were fixed, and no backpropagation optimization was performed. We used ColorJitter from Torchvision for transformation with the following parameters: maximum increments of 0.1 for brightness, 0.2 for contrast, 0.2 for saturation, and 0.15 for hue. The tiles were also randomly flipped and rotated by 15°. To address the imbalance between positive and negative samples, we perform balanced sampling of positive and negative samples at the initialization of each epoch. We calculated the loss via cross-entropy between the predicted probabilities and the true labels and optimized it via adaptive moment estimation with weight decay (AdamW) during training, with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate was managed via a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and ending at 1e-6 over 40 epochs. All training and testing were performed on six NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.    Uncertainty estimation module  Deploying deep learning models across multi-center pan-cancer cohorts inevitably introduces challenges related to histological heterogeneity, variable data quality, and out-of-distribution inputs that essentially differ from the training distribution. In such scenarios, enforcing deterministic predictions often leads to high-confidence errors. To address this, we incorporated a parallel uncertainty estimation module into our diagnostic framework. The primary objective of this module is to quantify the reliability of region-level predictions, serving a dual purpose: guiding model optimization through active learning during development and acting as a trigger for pathologist review during clinical inference.  Diverging from conventional approaches that rely on computationally expensive ensembles or require joint training with classification objectives (which may destabilize the primary task)  28 – 31  , we implemented a sequential optimization strategy. Specifically, the uncertainty branch is trained as an independent architectural bypass only after the multiscale classifier parameters are frozen. This design ensures that the uncertainty mechanism is specifically calibrated to the fixed decision boundary of the main model. Consequently, this approach enables precise confidence estimation without compromising the original diagnostic performance, while incurring negligible computational overhead.  Specifically, we implemented this module by adapting the uncertainty estimation algorithm for pretrained models proposed by Kirchhof et al .   35  . As shown in Fig.  2a , using the same feature  F  as the classification model input, we passed it through the uncertainty estimation module comprising three fully connected layers with 512 hidden units and LeakyReLU intermediate activations, outputting a single value normalized by the Softplus function to ensure positivity. We used mean squared error (MSE) loss, comparing the uncertainty module’s predictions with labels derived from the classification model’s forward propagation loss, computed at runtime with backpropagation disabled. Crucially, this design provides an intuitive measure of reliability: a high predicted loss indicates that the model anticipates a likely error on the input, thereby flagging it as a “High Uncertainty” (HU) region for pathologist review.  The loss function is defined as:   8     L  uncertainty   =   1  N    ∑   i  =  1   N        u  i   −   L   pred  i       2      where    u    is the uncertainty module’s predicted value and      L    pred      is the loss from the classification model’s forwards propagation.  The training process employed the same data and sampling strategy as those of the classification module. We used the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate followed a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and decreasing to 1e-6 over 10 epochs.    Uncertainty-driven active learning strategy  To address tumor heterogeneity and optimize annotation efficiency, we implemented a human-in-the-loop, uncertainty-driven active learning framework structured into five distinct iterations (Fig.  1d  and SFig.  3 ). To facilitate this process, the clinically derived development cohort (683 patients) was partitioned into two functional subsets via random patient-level sampling: a large unlabeled candidate pool of 594 patients (2245 WSIs, 8832 LNs) available for selection, and a strictly held-out internal validation set of 89 patients (302 WSIs, 897 LNs). Notably, the internal validation set was comprehensively annotated at the lesion level prior to the active learning process. This set remained fixed throughout the study and served as a reliable ground truth to monitor model convergence and determine hyperparameters without biasing the training process.  The training workflow commenced with an initialization phase (Iteration 1), where the baseline model was trained solely on the fully annotated initialization datasets (GLN21 and BLN16) to establish foundational detection capabilities. Subsequently, we conducted four consecutive rounds of uncertainty-driven refinement (Iterations 2–5). In each round, the model performed inference on the unlabeled candidate pool to compute tile-level uncertainty scores      u    i      (derived from the uncertainty module). WSIs were then prioritized for expert review according to a slide-level diagnostic ambiguity score. Specifically, for a given WSI with N tiles, we defined ambiguity as the mean uncertainty of the top K most uncertain tiles:   9    A   (   W  S  I   )   =    1    K      ∑    i  ϵ  T  o  p  −  K      u    i    ,  K  =   ⌈   0.05  ⋅  N   ⌉      Here,     Top  −  K     denotes the set of tiles with the largest uncertainty scores within that WSI, and ┌.┐ is the ceiling operator. WSIs were ranked by     A     WSI        in descending order and selected for pathologist review.  Specifically, the top 200 WSIs were selected in iterations 2 and 3, while the top 100 WSIs were selected in iterations 4 and 5. Senior pathologists reviewed these flagged samples to correct FPs and verify missed metastases. After each review phase, the corrected samples were incorporated into the expanded training set.    Data annotation and establishment of ground truth  To satisfy the distinct requirements of model development and independent validation, we implemented a two-tier annotation strategy conducted by senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience (Y.C., C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.).  For the development cohort, pathologists performed exhaustive region-level annotations on WSIs selected for the expanded training set and the internal validation set. This involved delineating precise boundaries for all LNs and contouring all internal metastatic foci. This process ensured that the model received high-granularity supervision for distinct metastatic morphologies, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cells (ITCs). During active learning iterations, regions flagged as HU were specifically reviewed and corrected (C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.) to provide high-quality supervision for challenging examples.  For the independent test cohort, we established a rigorous diagnostic standard to evaluate clinical safety. Instead of pixel-level contours, we focused on the definitive metastatic status of each LN. Two senior pathologists (Y.C. and C.Q.) independently reviewed all WSIs. Discrepant cases were adjudicated by a consensus panel. To resolve diagnostic ambiguity in morphologically challenging cases, we performed confirmatory immunohistochemical (IHC) staining (CAM5.2 and AE1/AE3) on 52 challenging cases to determine the final ground truth (SFig.  12 ). This process ensured a non-ambiguous “Positive/Negative” label for every LN in the test set.    Statistical analysis  The detection (YOLOv8-s) and segmentation (nnUNet) models were implemented with probability thresholds of 0.25 and 0.50, respectively. For the classification model, the binary decision threshold was set at 0.50. The uncertainty threshold for each iteration was determined empirically using the Internal Validation Set. To balance the trade-off between the volume of regions flagged for review and FP predictions, we selected the threshold at the intersection point where the average High Uncertainty area per slide (HUavg) equalled the average False Positive area per slide (FPavg) (SFig.  13 ). Isolated positive predictions approximately the size of one tile (3600 μm²) were excluded from analysis owing to resolution constraints.  To comprehensively evaluate the system, we defined detection and classification targets at three distinct levels. Tile-level performance measures the fundamental classification accuracy of individual 256 × 256 pixel image patches, where a tile is labeled positive if tumor tissue comprises >25% of its area. Lesion-level (Region) performance evaluates the model’s ability to correctly localize and classify contiguous metastatic areas (including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and ITCs) within the LN tissue, distinct from simple tile-level accuracy. LN-level performance serves as the primary clinical unit for N-staging; an LN is considered positive if the model identifies at least one metastatic lesion within the nodal area.  We defined specific metrics to assess the safety and efficiency of the proposed human-AI collaborative workflow. Conditional classification sensitivity evaluates the classification performance specifically on all LNs successfully localized by the detection module. For performance evaluation, regions flagged as HU (highlighted in yellow in the prediction heatmaps) were considered positive for sensitivity calculations, as these areas require pathologist review in clinical practice. To quantify workload, we defined the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N) as the proportion of true-negative LNs that required high-magnification manual review. An LN contributes to this burden if it contains any region predicted as False Positive (FP) or High Uncertainty (HU).  Bootstrap analysis (1000 iterations) was performed to calculate 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all performance metrics. AUCs were compared using DeLong’s test (two-sided). title: FTU-Seek: Foundation Model-Guided Hard-Negative Learning for Sparse Functional Tissue Unit Segmentation.

evidence_text: FTU-Seek: Foundation Model-Guided Hard-Negative Learning for Sparse Functional Tissue Unit Segmentation. Background/Objectives: Functional tissue units (FTUs), including tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs), blood vessels, and glands, encode localized immune, vascular, and epithelial organization in histopathology. Accurate quantification of these structures is important for studying tissue architecture and disease-associated tissue organization. However, FTUs are frequently sparse, heterogeneous, and surrounded by large amounts of morphologically similar background tissue, making automated segmentation in whole-slide images (WSIs) challenging. We therefore developed FTU-Seek, a pathology foundation model-guided framework that treats morphology-aware negative-patch selection as a key component of sparse FTU segmentation. Methods: FTU-Seek uses frozen multi-depth features from the UNI pathology foundation model to train a patch-level classifier that distinguishes FTU-containing from FTU-absent tissue. Target-absent patches are subsequently ranked according to their predicted target-containing probabilities, and the highest-scoring hard negatives are selected through a static TopK strategy to construct compact segmentation training sets. The framework was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and internal test cohorts across TLS, blood-vessel, and gland segmentation tasks, with an additional independent 30-WSI held-out cohort for TLS. Positive-only, all-tissue, random-negative, and matched random TopK sampling strategies served as comparators. Segmentation-derived phenotypes were further explored in external TCGA cohorts. Results: The patch-level classifiers achieved mean validation AUCs of 95.92%, 90.11%, and 98.16% for TLS, blood vessel, and gland classification, respectively. For TLS segmentation, the pre-specified Top1000 configuration retained 27.6% of the all-tissue training workload and achieved a slide-level Dice of 76.69 ± 11.89% on the independent 30-WSI held-out cohort. Compared with matched random Top1000 sampling, it improved Dice by 3.72 percentage points (95% CI, 2.05-5.38). Blood vessel and gland segmentation achieved performance approaching all-tissue training while reducing the retained training workload by approximately one-half and one-third, respectively. Compared with matched random sampling, classifier-guided hard-negative selection produced the greatest improvements for sparse and morphologically ambiguous FTUs. Exploratory TCGA analyses further showed associations of TLS phenotypes with overall survival, vascular phenotypes with overall survival and microvascular invasion, and glandular phenotypes with clinicopathological characteristics. Conclusions: FTU-Seek demonstrates that pathology foundation models can support sparse FTU segmentation not only through feature representation but also through morphology-aware construction of segmentation training sets. By prioritizing informative hard negatives, the framework reduces redundant segmentation-training workload while maintaining competitive segmentation performance and supporting quantitative tissue phenotyping from routine histopathology.

title: A weakly supervised deep learning model for OSCC diagnosis and lesion highlighting in histopathology images.

evidence_text:
A weakly supervised deep learning model for OSCC diagnosis and lesion highlighting in histopathology images.

Background

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the predominant histopathological subtype of oral malignancies, and histopathology-based diagnosis remains central to clinical management. With the rapid development of digital pathology and deep learning, automated analysis of histopathology images has shown considerable potential for improving screening efficiency and reducing inter-observer variability. However, in both public datasets and real-world research settings, only image-level labels are commonly available, whereas region-level annotations are often lacking. This limitation makes weakly supervised modeling necessary and also restricts rigorous validation of spatial interpretability.

Methods

To address these challenges, we developed a weakly supervised deep learning framework based on patch-level representation learning and multiple-instance aggregation for image-level OSCC diagnosis with exploratory heatmap visualization. Specifically, histopathology images were divided into patches and encoded into feature embeddings. UNI 2, a recently developed pathology foundation model with highly competitive performance in contemporary computational pathology benchmarks, was adopted as the primary feature extractor to obtain informative patch representations. ResNet-50 was additionally implemented as a conventional baseline encoder for comparative evaluation. A self-attention-based multiple-instance aggregation module was then introduced to capture dependencies among instances within each patch set and to generate binary OSCC predictions.

Results

In five-fold cross-validation, the UNI-2-based model achieved a mean area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9919, compared with 0.9899 for the ResNet-50 baseline. On the independent external validation cohort, UNI 2 further achieved an AUC of 0.9992, outperforming ResNet-50, which achieved an AUC of 0.9564. As an exploratory interpretability analysis, attention responses were visualized as heatmaps to inspect model focus patterns and support qualitative error review, without assuming verified lesion-level correspondence in the absence of region-level annotations.

Conclusions

This framework demonstrates strong image-level diagnostic performance for OSCC and provides exploratory visualization for qualitative model review without requiring additional fine-grained annotations, offering a reusable technical pathway for weakly supervised OSCC histopathology modeling and future multicenter validation.
