evidence_text: Knowledge-enhanced pretraining for vision-language pathology foundation model on cancer diagnosis. Vision-language foundation models have shown great promise in computational pathology but remain primarily data-driven, lacking explicit integration of medical knowledge. We introduce knowledge-enhanced pathology (KEEP), a foundation model that systematically incorporates disease knowledge into pretraining for cancer diagnosis. KEEP leverages a comprehensive disease knowledge graph encompassing 11,454 diseases and 139,143 attributes to reorganize millions of pathology image-text pairs into 143,000 semantically structured groups aligned with disease ontology hierarchies. This knowledge-enhanced pretraining aligns visual and textual representations within hierarchical semantic spaces, enabling a deeper understanding of disease relationships and morphological patterns. Across 18 public benchmarks (over 14,000 whole-slide images) and 4 institutional rare cancer datasets (926 cases), KEEP consistently outperformed existing foundation models, showing substantial gains for rare subtypes. These results establish knowledge-enhanced vision-language modeling as a powerful paradigm for advancing computational pathology.

title: Geranium: Multimodal Retrieval of Genomics Data Visualizations.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Geranium: Multimodal Retrieval of Genomics Data Visualizations. Effective visualization is essential for interpreting genomics data, yet researchers often face challenges in finding relevant, reusable examples. Existing tools offer limited support for searching the vast landscape of genomics visualizations, making the process of authoring new visualizations time-consuming and inefficient. To address this gap, we introduce Geranium, a data visualization retrieval system for searching and authoring genomics visualizations. Geranium supports multimodal retrieval, enabling users to query with images, text, or grammar-based specifications. Retrieved examples serve as scaffolds for authoring, providing templates that researchers can adapt with their own data, thereby streamlining the mechanics of visualization construction. Geranium integrates three embedding methods to combine specialized and general knowledge: grammar-based embeddings tailored to genomics visualizations, multimodal embeddings from a biomedical vision-language foundation model, and text embeddings from a fine-tuned large language model. For each visualization, we construct a multimodal representation that includes a Gosling specification, a pixel-based rendering, and natural language descriptions. We evaluate embedding strategies to maximize top-$k$k retrieval accuracy and conduct user studies with domain collaborators to gather feedback on usability. Our collection comprises 3,200 visualizations across 50 categories, ranging from single-view to coordinated multi-view designs and supporting applications from single-cell epigenomics to structural variation analysis.

title: A vision-language foundation model for precision oncology.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: A vision-language foundation model for precision oncology. Clinical decision-making is driven by multimodal data, including clinical notes and pathological characteristics. Artificial intelligence approaches that can effectively integrate multimodal data hold significant promise in advancing clinical care<sup>1,2</sup>. However, the scarcity of well-annotated multimodal datasets in clinical settings has hindered the development of useful models. In this study, we developed the Multimodal transformer with Unified maSKed modeling (MUSK), a vision-language foundation model designed to leverage large-scale, unlabelled, unpaired image and text data. MUSK was pretrained on 50 million pathology images from 11,577 patients and one billion pathology-related text tokens using unified masked modelling. It was further pretrained on one million pathology image-text pairs to efficiently align the vision and language features. With minimal or no further training, MUSK was tested in a wide range of applications and demonstrated superior performance across 23 patch-level and slide-level benchmarks, including image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval, visual question answering, image classification and molecular biomarker prediction. Furthermore, MUSK showed strong performance in outcome prediction, including melanoma relapse prediction, pan-cancer prognosis prediction and immunotherapy response prediction in lung and gastro-oesophageal cancers. MUSK effectively combined complementary information from pathology images and clinical reports and could potentially improve diagnosis and precision in cancer therapy.

title: A multimodal whole-slide foundation model for pathology.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: A multimodal whole-slide foundation model for pathology. The field of computational pathology has been transformed with recent advances in foundation models that encode histopathology region-of-interests (ROIs) into versatile and transferable feature representations via self-supervised learning. However, translating these advancements to address complex clinical challenges at the patient and slide level remains constrained by limited clinical data in disease-specific cohorts, especially for rare clinical conditions. We propose Transformer-based pathology Image and Text Alignment Network (TITAN), a multimodal whole-slide foundation model pretrained using 335,645 whole-slide images via visual self-supervised learning and vision-language alignment with corresponding pathology reports and 423,122 synthetic captions generated from a multimodal generative AI copilot for pathology. Without any fine-tuning or requiring clinical labels, TITAN can extract general-purpose slide representations and generate pathology reports that generalize to resource-limited clinical scenarios such as rare disease retrieval and cancer prognosis. We evaluate TITAN on diverse clinical tasks and find that it outperforms both ROI and slide foundation models across machine learning settings, including linear probing, few-shot and zero-shot classification, rare cancer retrieval, cross-modal retrieval and pathology report generation.

title: Deep Learning Image Processing Models in Dermatopathology.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Deep Learning Image Processing Models in Dermatopathology. Dermatopathology has rapidly advanced due to the implementation of deep learning models and artificial intelligence (AI). From convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformer-based foundation models, these systems are now capable of accurate whole-slide analysis and multimodal integration. This review synthesizes the most recent advents of deep-learning architecture and synthesizes its evolution from first-generation CNNs to hybrid CNN-transformer systems to large-scale foundational models such as Paige's PanDerm AI and Virchow. Herein, we examine performance benchmarks from real-world deployments of major dermatopathology deep learning models (DermAI, PathAssist Derm), as well as emerging next-generation models still under research and development. We assess barriers to clinical workflow adoption such as dataset bias, AI interpretability, and government regulation. Further, we discuss potential future research directions and emphasize the need for diverse, prospectively curated datasets, explainability frameworks for trust in AI, and rigorous compliance to Good Machine-Learning-Practice (GMLP) to achieve safe and scalable deep learning dermatopathology models that can fully integrate into clinical workflows.

title: A Unified Information Bottleneck Framework for Multimodal Biomedical Machine Learning.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: A Unified Information Bottleneck Framework for Multimodal Biomedical Machine Learning. Multimodal biomedical machine learning increasingly integrates heterogeneous data sources (including medical imaging, multi-omics profiles, electronic health records, and wearable sensor signals) to support clinical diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response prediction. Despite strong empirical performance, most existing multimodal systems lack a principled theoretical foundation for understanding why fusion improves prediction, how information is distributed across modalities, and when models can be trusted under incomplete or shifting data. This paper develops a unified information-theoretic framework that formalizes multimodal biomedical learning as an information optimization problem. We formulate multimodal representation learning through the information bottleneck principle, deriving a variational objective that balances predictive sufficiency against informational compression in an architecture-agnostic manner. Building on this foundation, we introduce information-theoretic tools for decomposing modality contributions via conditional mutual information, quantifying redundancy and synergy, and diagnosing fusion collapse. We further show that robustness to missing modalities can be cast as an information consistency problem and extend the framework to longitudinal disease modeling through transfer entropy and sequential information bottleneck objectives. Applications to multimodal foundation models, uncertainty quantification, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection are developed. Empirical case studies across three biomedical datasets (TCGA breast cancer multi-omics, TCGA glioma clinical-plus-molecular data, and OASIS-2 longitudinal Alzheimer's data) show that the framework's key quantities are computable and interpretable on real data: MI decomposition identifies modality dominance and redundancy; the VMIB traces a compression-prediction tradeoff in the information plane; entropy-based selective prediction raises accuracy from 0.787 to 0.939 at 50% coverage; transfer entropy reveals stage-dependent modality influence in disease progression; and pretraining/adaptation diagnostics distinguish efficient from wasteful fine-tuning strategies. Together, these results develop entropy and mutual information as organizing principles for the design, analysis, and evaluation of multimodal biomedical AI systems.

title: Leveraging Multimodal Foundation Models in Biliary Tract Cancer Research.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Leveraging Multimodal Foundation Models in Biliary Tract Cancer Research. This review explores how multimodal foundation models (MFMs) are transforming biliary tract cancer (BTC) research. BTCs are aggressive malignancies with poor prognosis, presenting unique challenges due to difficult diagnostic methods, molecular complexity, and rarity. Importantly, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA), and distal bile duct cholangiocarcinoma (dCCA) represent fundamentally distinct clinical entities, with iCCA presenting as mass-forming lesions amenable to biopsy and targeted therapies, while pCCA manifests as infiltrative bile duct lesions with challenging diagnosis and primarily palliative management approaches. MFMs offer potential to advance research by integrating radiological images, histopathology, multi-omics profiles, and clinical data into unified computational frameworks, with applications tailored to these distinct BTC subtypes. Key applications include enhanced biomarker discovery that identifies previously unrecognizable cross-modal patterns, potential for improving currently limited diagnostic accuracy-though validation in BTC-specific cohorts remains essential-accelerated drug repurposing, and advanced patient stratification for personalized treatment. Despite promising results, challenges such as data scarcity, high computational demands, and clinical workflow integration remain to be addressed. Future research should focus on standardized data protocols, architectural innovations, and prospective validation studies. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-based methodologies offers new solutions for these historically challenging malignancies. However, current evidence for BTC-specific applications remains largely theoretical, with most studies limited to proof-of-concept designs or related cancer types. Comprehensive clinical validation studies and prospective trials demonstrating patient benefit are essential prerequisites for clinical implementation. The timeline for evidence-based clinical adoption likely extends 7-10 years, contingent on successful completion of validation studies addressing current evidence gaps.

title: PhenoModel: A multimodal phenotypic drug design foundation model for discovering novel potential inhibitors of multiple cancer cells.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: PhenoModel: A multimodal phenotypic drug design foundation model for discovering novel potential inhibitors of multiple cancer cells. Phenotypic drug discovery (PDD) focuses on the observable traits or phenotype of cells or organisms in response to drug treatment, rather than relying primarily on specific molecular targets. Drugs discovered through this approach may have better therapeutic relevance, as they are tested in conditions that closely mimic human disease. In this study, we present PhenoModel, a multimodal molecular foundation model developed using our unique dual-space contrastive learning framework. This model effectively connects molecular structures with phenotypic information. PhenoModel is applicable to a range of downstream drug discovery tasks, including molecular property prediction and active molecule screening based on targets, phenotypes, and ligands. Our results demonstrate that PhenoModel outperforms baseline methods in these areas. Building from this model, PhenoScreen is developed to successfully identify several phenotypically bioactive compounds against osteosarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines. These findings highlight the versatility of PhenoModel and its potential to accelerate drug discovery by uncovering novel therapeutic pathways and expanding the diversity of viable drug candidates.

title: General artificial intelligence for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer: the rise of foundation models.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: General artificial intelligence for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer: the rise of foundation models. Artificial intelligence (AI) and its computer algorithms, including those of machine learning and deep learning, have been transforming the oncology field. Generative AI (Gen AI) and general AI technologies, which can be adapted to various tasks based on diverse inputs, are being increasingly utilized in healthcare applications. Foundation models, driven by Gen AI and general AI technologies, have enthralled the medical world, representing the next generation of large-scale AI tools in medicine that are trained on massive amounts of data and will make a major impact due to their versatility, high performance, personalization enhancement, and assistance of healthcare workers. That said, it is undeniable that there are multiple obstacles that these algorithms must overcome to be successfully utilized in the field. In this review, we first present a brief background and a history of the recent rise of Gen AI and foundation models. Next, we explore their applications in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, specifically in radiology, pathology, precision medicine, personalization of care, and surgical oncology. Then, we discuss some of the limitations that could hinder general and Gen AI's clinical translation.

evidence_text: Impact of tissue staining and scanner variation on the performance of pathology foundation models: a study of sarcomas and their mimics Histopathological analysis is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis and prognostication of cancer. Recent advances in AI, driven by large-scale digitisation and pan-cancer foundation models, are opening new opportunities for clinical integration. However, it remains unclear how robust these foundation models are to real-world sources of variability, particularly in H&E staining and scanning protocols. In this study, we use soft tissue tumours, a rare and morphologically diverse tumour type, as a challenging test case to systematically investigate the colour-related robustness and generalisability of seven AI models. Controlled staining and scanning experiments were utilised to assess model performance across diverse real-world data sources. Foundation models, particularly UNI-v2, Virchow and TITAN, demonstrated encouraging robustness to staining and scanning variation, particularly when a small number of stain-varied slides were included in the training loop, highlighting their potential as adaptable and data-efficient tools for real-world digital pathology workflows.

title: A generalist biomedical vision-language model via multi-CLIP knowledge distillation.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: A generalist biomedical vision-language model via multi-CLIP knowledge distillation. Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models, which are pretrained on natural images with billions of image-text pairs, exhibit strong zero-shot and cross-modal capabilities. However, their application in biomedicine remains challenging due to limited large-scale image-text data and heterogeneous imaging modalities. Here we show that a generalist biomedical foundation model can be effectively built via multimodal medical knowledge distillation. We introduce MMKD-CLIP, which integrates complementary knowledge from nine biomedical CLIP models. Our two-stage pipeline combines CLIP-style pretraining on 2.9 million biomedical image-text pairs across 26 modalities with large-scale feature-level distillation. We evaluate MMKD-CLIP on 58 datasets spanning nine modalities and six tasks, including classification, retrieval, visual question answering, survival prediction, and cancer diagnosis. MMKD-CLIP performs favorably relative to the teacher models, with results supporting its robustness and cross-domain generalization.

title: Meta-encoder: a unified integration framework for multiple pathological foundation models in cancer detection.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Meta-encoder: a unified integration framework for multiple pathological foundation models in cancer detection. The emergence of diverse pathological foundation models has empowered computational pathology tasks within the field of oncology, including tumor subtyping, cancer prognosis, biomarker prediction, gene expression prediction, and so on. However, variations in model architecture and data sources hinder consistent downstream performance and complicate centralized training. Specifically, the lack of data sharing makes retraining foundation models with pooled data infeasible. Here, we propose the Meta-Encoder, a unified framework that integrates features from multiple pathological foundation models to generate a comprehensive representation, achieving superior performance in downstream cancer detection tasks compared to single foundation models. While single models suffice for low-complexity univariate tasks such as cancer diagnosis and prognosis, the Meta-Encoder consistently rivals the best-performing single model, alleviating concerns over model selection. For high-dimensional tasks such as multiplex protein and gene expression prediction within tumor tissues, the attention-based strategies of our Meta-Encoder framework demonstrate substantial advantages over single models, offering an optimal balance of performance and efficiency. By harnessing the complementary strengths of multiple foundation models, the Meta-Encoder enhance the molecular characterization of pathology images, thereby advancing precision oncology.

evidence_text:
Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Approaches for Histopathology-Based Survival Prediction in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.

Background

Accurate prognostic stratification in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains challenging due to substantial tumor heterogeneity. Deep learning (DL)-based approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been widely applied for prognostic prediction using histopathological images. Recently, pathology foundation models combined with multiple-instance learning (MIL) have emerged as a promising alternative. In this study, we aimed to provide a comparative evaluation of conventional CNN-based and foundation model-based approaches for HCC prognosis prediction, with a focus on tissue selection strategies and cross-dataset generalizability.

Methods

We compared a patch-level CNN approach with a foundation model-based MIL approach for overall survival (OS) prediction from hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. A total of 256 patients from Seoul St. Mary's Hospital (SSMH) and 334 patients from the TCGA dataset were included. Models were trained using either all tissue regions or tumor-only regions under five-fold cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), Kaplan-Meier analysis, and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis. Cross-dataset validation and combined-dataset training assessed generalizability.

Results

In the SSMH dataset, the CNN model performed better with tumor-only regions (C-index 0.8308) than with all tissue regions (0.7498). In contrast, the foundation model-based MIL approach showed stable performance regardless of input regions (C-indices: 0.8701 and 0.8752). Similar stability was observed in the TCGA dataset (0.7744 and 0.7722). Cross-dataset validation showed reduced performance, indicating limited generalizability. Combining datasets did not lead to performance improvement. Subgroup analyses showed prognostic information beyond histologic grade, and feature visualization revealed relevant histopathologic patterns.

Conclusions

A foundation model-based MIL approach provides robust and interpretable prognostic modeling in HCC. DL-based prediction offers complementary information beyond conventional clinicopathological variables. Future efforts integrating multimodal data and improving generalizability will be essential for clinical translation.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Clinical Oncology.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Clinical Oncology. Cancer remains a major global health challenge, and the increasing availability of multimodal biomedical data has created unprecedented opportunities for precision oncology. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), have enabled new approaches for integrating heterogeneous data sources, including electronic health records, medical imaging, pathology, genomics, and clinical text. However, current studies remain fragmented across specific tasks, cancer types, and model architectures, and a comprehensive synthesis of how generative AI can support the entire oncology continuum is still lacking. This review provides an overview of generative AI in clinical oncology, covering LLMs, generative adversarial networks, diffusion models, and multimodal foundation models. We summarize their methodological foundations and discuss applications in cancer diagnosis, prognosis prediction, treatment planning, patient management, and clinical trial optimization. Particular attention is given to multimodal data integration, synthetic data generation, clinical reasoning, and decision support, together with current challenges related to interpretability, reliability, data privacy, regulatory governance, and real-world implementation. By consolidating recent technological advances and clinical evidence, this review highlights future priorities toward safe, trustworthy, and clinically deployable intelligent oncology systems. Emerging agent-based architectures and human-AI collaborative workflows may further expand the clinical utility of generative AI in oncology.

LungGPT: A unified multimodal system for interpretable diagnosis and clinical decision support of respiratory diseases. Respiratory diseases cause significant morbidity, yet diagnosis remains labor intensive and dependent on physician expertise. Here, we present LungGPT, a unified multimodal system trained on 147 million tokens of domain-specific electronic health records from 125,917 participants. LungGPT comprises two modules: LungGPT-Dx for respiratory disease diagnosis and early warning of critical illness, and LungGPT-Ex for interpretable diagnostic reasoning and treatment recommendations. In large-scale evaluations, LungGPT-Dx achieves a macro-average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.852 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.839-0.865) across 22 respiratory diseases, with disease-specific AUCs exceeding 0.900 for lung cancer and pulmonary tuberculosis. Crucially, the model further improves early warning of critical illness by incorporating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning into textual data and integrating computed tomography (CT) imaging features. LungGPT-Ex generates high-quality, interpretable reasoning that outperforms specialized clinical models and matches advanced general-purpose models such as GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 in correctness, completeness, and truthfulness. By bridging precision diagnostics and rapid decision-making, LungGPT provides a standardized framework to enhance clinical workflows and improve patient outcomes in respiratory healthcare. Graphical abstract                     Highlights    •  LungGPT is fine-tuned on 147 million tokens to enhance respiratory disease management    •  LungGPT-Dx accurately diagnoses more than 20 distinct respiratory diseases    •  Multimodal integration improves early-warning performance for critical illness    •  LungGPT-Ex generates interpretable diagnostic reasoning and clinical decision support      Shao et al. present LungGPT, a multimodal artificial intelligence system that fuses clinical features, lab tests and imaging to enhance respiratory healthcare. LungGPT enables accurate diagnoses, early warning of critical illness, and interpretable diagnostic reasoning and decision support, offering a powerful tool to streamline workflows and promote standardization in clinical practice.     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Received 2025 Feb 23; Revised 2026 Feb 1; Accepted 2026 Jun 23; Collection date 2026 Sep 15.       Introduction  Respiratory diseases, mainly including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung cancer, pneumonia, and pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), are characterized by high incidence and mortality rates, imposing a considerable disease burden worldwide.  1   ,   2   ,   3   ,   4   These diseases require rapid diagnosis and symptomatic treatment, and progression to critical illness, particularly severe pneumonia, is associated with mortality approaching 50%.  5   ,   6   However, many respiratory disorders present with similar clinical manifestations, making differential diagnosis inherently difficult. In clinical practice, the diagnostic process demands that physicians employ logical reasoning to discern correlations within medical histories, physical examinations, and auxiliary tests to deduce potential diagnoses.  7   ,   8   Manual review of fragmented clinical records is often labor intensive and time consuming,  9   which could lead to physicians overlooking critical nuances and escalating the risk of misdiagnosis. These challenges highlight the urgent need for intelligent systems that support more accurate and efficient diagnosis.  Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled a series of breakthroughs in biomedical applications.  10   ,   11   ,   12   ,   13   ,   14   The field has evolved substantially from deep learning approaches, which excelled in pattern recognition but often required task-specific architectures and large labeled datasets.  15   This trajectory advanced with the emergence of foundation models, particularly large language models (LLMs), which exhibit broad capabilities in knowledge encoding, text comprehension, and clinical reasoning, thus providing intelligent tools to enhance human productivity.  16   ,   17   ,   18   ,   19   ,   20   ,   21   Several general-purpose LLMs are demonstrating promise in their initial medical applications. A recent randomized controlled trial demonstrated that GPT-4 assistance in managing complex cases raised the management reasoning scores of physicians.  22   Moreover, open-source LLMs such as the DeepSeek model show an enhanced capacity to assist in clinical decision-making for both prevalent and rare diseases.  23   ,   24   ,   25   However, most evaluations have relied on public benchmarks, and their effectiveness in real-world clinical settings remains insufficiently characterized.  26   ,   27    The application of foundation models in healthcare is rapidly expanding and demonstrates remarkable potential across multiple clinical domains.  28   ,   29   ,   30   ,   31   ,   32   The recent text-based generative model Delphi-2M successfully reconstructed longitudinal disease trajectories and predicted the incidence of thousands of diseases, achieving a mean area under the curve (AUC) exceeding 0.70.  33   The foundation model Ark+, trained on a public chest radiography dataset, was pretrained by recycling the knowledge of heterogeneous expert labels.  34   In addition, MUSK, a multimodal foundation model, leveraged vision-language alignment to fully exploit pathological image information. It showed superior predictive performance for lung cancer immunotherapy response with an AUC of 0.768.  35   However, existing models are often applied to isolated clinical tasks and lack the interpretability essential for complex medical decision-making.  36   ,   37   It is necessary to develop integrated decision-support systems that can be embedded into clinical workflows, particularly in specialized fields such as respiratory medicine.  In this study, an intelligent system for lung diseases powered by a Generative Pre-trained Transformer (LungGPT) was constructed by pretraining on 1.8 billion general medical tokens and fine-tuning on 147 million domain-specific tokens from 125,917 inpatients ( Figure 1 ). LungGPT is designed to address four critical clinical tasks: (1) diagnosing multiple respiratory diseases, (2) providing early warning of critical illness by synergizing text records with computed tomography (CT) imaging features, (3) generating interpretable diagnostic reasoning, and (4) recommending evidence-based treatment via structured decision pathways. This end-to-end clinical decision-support system unifies diagnostic intelligence with generative assistance and enhances both the efficiency and interpretability of clinical workflows.    Figure 1   Overview of the LungGPT system  (A) The foundational datasets for the system. It included human dialog data with 5.8 billion tokens that were sourced from large-scale open-source repositories including WanJuan-CC and WuDaoCorpora; a medical corpus with 1.8 billion tokens that was derived from research papers, medical textbooks, and clinical guidelines; and 147 million tokens derived from domain-specific electronic health records (EHRs) from 125,917 participants.  (B) Architecture of the LungGPT system. Based on the above datasets, LungGPT-Dx was optimized for respiratory disease classification, whereas LungGPT-Ex was optimized for evidence-grounded generation of diagnostic reasoning and decision support. RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback.  (C) Network structure of the system. The system included text encoding, a multi-head attention mechanism, root mean square layer normalization (RMSNorm), quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) for efficient parametric fine-tuning, a multilayer perceptron (MLP), and a linear layer for data transformation for medical analysis and decision-making.                     Results   Pre-training corpora and clinical cohort  For model pre-training, this study utilized a substantial corpus of 5.8 billion tokens of human dialog data including the safe and high-quality English webtext dataset WanJuan-CC and the super large-scale Chinese corpora WuDaoCorpora.  38   ,   39   Additionally, a specialized medical corpus of 1.8 billion tokens was assembled, which comprehensively integrated authoritative resources from international databases such as PubMed and MEDLINE, as well as the prominent Chinese academic database China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI).  For model fine-tuning, we further incorporated domain-specific data from 125,917 hospitalized participants totaling 147 million tokens. The electronic health record (EHR) data encompassed multi-source records, including demographics, chief complaints, imaging findings, radiological reports, laboratory test descriptions, and follow-up records. Following International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) standardization, we identified a specific cohort of 29,215 patients whose primary diagnosis was a respiratory disease, encompassing a broad range of ICD-10 codes ( Figure 2 A;  Table S1 ). These were further categorized into 22 major disease types through in-depth discussion and reviewed by senior physicians. Co-occurrence analysis revealed substantial multimorbidity across respiratory disease categories, with notable co-occurrence of pneumonia with COPD, pleural effusion (PE), and bronchiectasis (BRO) ( Figures 2 B and  S1 ). Following cohort partitioning, the training and testing datasets showed comparable gender distributions, with male patients accounting for 63% ( Table S2 ). In addition, the age distribution of patients in both the training and testing datasets was similar and the majority of participants were between 40 and 70 years old ( Figure 2 C).    Figure 2   Characteristics of the respiratory disease cohort  (A) A network graph illustrating the relationships between 22 respiratory diseases and their associated codes. Each node represents a disease, and the size of the node corresponds to the number of patients.  (B) A chord diagram depicting the flow of respiratory comorbidities among participants. The width of each flow line was proportional to the number of participants sharing the corresponding comorbid conditions.  (C) Age distribution of participants by gender in the training and testing datasets.  ASTH, asthma; BRO, bronchiectasis; CB, chronic bronchitis; COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; ILD, interstitial lung disease; LA, lung abscess; LBT, lung benign tumor; LC, lung cancer; LI, lung injury; MD, mediastinal disease; PC, pulmonary cyst; PE, pleural effusion; PEMB, pulmonary embolism; PEMP, pulmonary emphysema; PH, pulmonary hypertension; PNC, pneumoconiosis; PNE, pneumonia; PT, pneumothorax; PTB, pulmonary tuberculosis; RF, rib fracture; SAS, sleep apnea syndrome; URTI, upper respiratory tract infection.                     Diagnostic performance across respiratory diseases  LungGPT-Dx, a pretrained model fine-tuned with EHR data, was used to diagnose respiratory diseases. The system performed well in the evaluation of 22 respiratory diseases with AUC values ranging from 0.754 to 0.967 and a macro-average AUC of 0.852 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.839–0.865) in the testing dataset ( Figure 3 A). The diagnostic performance of the LungGPT-Dx model for most diseases reached AUC values greater than 0.800. Notably, the model demonstrated strong discriminative performance for several major diseases, including pulmonary hypertension (AUC 0.948, 95% CI: 0.921-0.970), lung cancer (AUC: 0.921, 95% CI: 0.912-0.929), PTB (AUC: 0.903, 95% CI: 0.872-0.930), asthma (AUC: 0.902, 95% CI: 0.863-0.939), interstitial lung disease (AUC: 0.883, 95% CI: 0.856-0.910), COPD (AUC: 0.863, 95% CI: 0.847-0.881), and pneumonia (AUC: 0.821, 95% CI: 0.810-0.831) ( Figure 3 B;  Table S3 ). Furthermore, the model demonstrated robust predictive performance across the majority of diseases, achieving high top-1 and top-3 accuracies, alongside a strong F1 score, recall, and precision ( Figure 3 C). Specifically, the macro-averaged metrics reached 0.719, 0.767, and 0.763 for the top-1 accuracy, top-3 accuracy, and precision. Further subgroup analyses revealed performance variations across gender. LungGPT-Dx showed superior diagnostic performance in female patients, with a macro-average AUC of 0.881, compared with 0.836 in male patients ( Figure S2 ).    Figure 3   Diagnostic performance of LungGPT-Dx across respiratory diseases  (A) Confusion matrix of the predicted versus actual categories for 22 respiratory diseases. Each cell represented the ratio of predicted to actual numbers of samples, with the color intensity indicating the level of the ratio.  (B) Bar plot showing the diagnostic area under the curve (AUC) of LungGPT-Dx for each of the 22 respiratory diseases.  (C) Radial bar plot displaying diagnostic metrics of LungGPT-Dx across the 22 diseases: top-1 accuracy (ACC), top-3 ACC, F1 score, recall (REC), and precision (PRE).                   When compared with state-of-the-art baseline LLMs based on a 349-case evaluation subset, LungGPT-Dx demonstrated superior group-wise performance, with an AUC of 0.862, surpassing comparator models including DeepSeek-R1 (0.829), PULSE (0.834), GPT-4o (0.825), HuaTuoGPT (0.715), and Qwen (0.672) ( Figure S3 ;  Table S4 ). It also demonstrated superior top-1 accuracy (0.756), F1 score (0.758), and precision (0.788). These findings underscore LungGPT-Dx’s exceptional diagnostic precision and its significant advantages over existing models, positioning it as a potential AI-based diagnostic tool for respiratory diseases.    Early warning of critical illness  In critical care management, particularly for life-threatening respiratory emergencies, rapid and precise assessment is of utmost importance. To address this, LungGPT implemented a hierarchical diagnostic framework for critical illness ( Figure 4 A). The system initially processed unstructured EHR data for disease detection. Then, it employed prompt engineering with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to convert these textual findings into structured information, which was subsequently fused with CT imaging data through AI models to stratify severe conditions. As illustrated in the CoT schematic for severe pneumonia (SP), the model simulated clinical decision-making by systematically evaluating major and minor criteria derived from both textual and visual modalities ( Figure 4 B).  40   Ultimately, this multimodal paradigm not only enhanced risk stratification but also provided interpretability for its subsequent reasoning and diagnostic decisions.    Figure 4   Workflow and performance evaluation of the LungGPT in diagnosing critical illness  (A) The hierarchical workflow of the LungGPT for identifying critical illness. In Step 1, LungGPT obtained primary diagnostic results and the corresponding explanatory content by analyzing the electronic health record (EHR) text. In Step 2, the system transformed the textual diagnoses into structured database information using prompt engineering with chain-of-thought (CoT) and introduced an artificial intelligence model for computed tomography (CT) images, thereby achieving the stratification of severe and acute conditions such as severe pneumonia (SP) and acute pulmonary embolism (APE). PNE, pneumonia; PEMB, pulmonary embolism.  (B) CoT process for the diagnosis of severe pneumonia. The CoT technique was utilized to transform the EHR text and CT images into structured information, which enabled disease diagnosis based on corresponding clinical criteria.  (C) Performance evaluation metrics for identifying SP, rapidly progressive lung cancer (RPLC), APE, and acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD).                   Quantitative performance evaluations demonstrated that this multimodal integration significantly enhanced diagnostic accuracy ( Figure 4 C). By combining CT imaging data with text-based CoT, the model showed substantial improvements in identifying severe conditions, increasing the AUC for SP from 0.776 to 0.802. It also markedly improved the AUC for rapidly progressive lung cancer (RPLC, volume doubling time <400 days) from 0.595 to 0.899, identifying high-risk patients who warrant expedited clinical assessment to avoid delaying treatment. Furthermore, for acute conditions, this integration increased the AUC for acute pulmonary embolism (APE) from 0.714 to 0.802 and for acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) from 0.816 to 0.869, facilitating timely clinical interventions for high-risk patients. These improvements in identifying critically ill patients may support more timely triage and inform targeted clinical management.    Diagnostic reasoning evaluation  Furthermore, LungGPT-Ex summarized medical texts to generate diagnostic reasoning and treatment planning with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and prompts ( Figure 5 A). Three board-certified clinicians (3–5 years of clinical experience) independently evaluated outputs for 600 diagnostic cases. The clinicians assessed the model outputs in terms of three key metrics including correctness, completeness, and truthfulness on a 3-point Likert scale (1: fair, 2: good, and 3: excellent).    Figure 5   Clinical assessment of the ability of LungGPT to generate text  (A) Study design for clinician evaluation of diagnostic reasoning and decision-generation outputs produced by LungGPT-Ex and five comparator models using correctness, completeness, and truthfulness.  (B) Distributions of reader scores for diagnostic reasoning. The heatmaps denoted reader preferences as measured by a 3-point Likert scale. The box indicates the interquartile range (IQR), whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR (Tukey’s method), dots represent outliers, and + denotes the mean. Statistical significance was determined using Friedman test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. ∗∗∗ p  < 0.001. ns, not significant.  (C) Distribution of reader scores for decision generation. The heatmaps denoted reader preference as measured by a 3-point Likert scale. The box indicates the IQR, whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR (Tukey’s method), dots represent outliers, and + denotes the mean. Statistical significance was determined using Friedman test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. ∗∗ p  < 0.01, ∗∗∗ p  < 0.001. ns, not significant.                   In terms of diagnostic reasoning, LungGPT-Ex outperformed most LLMs ( Figures 5 B and  S4 ;  Table S5 ). For correctness, LungGPT-Ex achieved an average score of 2.84, reflecting its ability to minimize false or misleading information. This performance significantly exceeded that of PULSE (1.34), HuaTuoGPT (1.38), Qwen (2.31), and DeepSeek-R1 (2.33), while closely matching that of GPT-4o (2.89). Regarding completeness, LungGPT-Ex scored 2.71, highlighting its capacity to provide detailed and comprehensive diagnostic explanations. This score surpassed PULSE (1.25), HuaTuoGPT (1.33), Qwen (1.84), and DeepSeek-R1 (2.27). Its truthfulness score (2.90) was comparable to GPT-4o (2.92) and DeepSeek-R1 (2.87) and significantly outperformed PULSE (1.43), HuaTuoGPT (1.54), and Qwen (2.59).    Decision generation evaluation  In the task of treatment planning, LungGPT-Ex continued to demonstrate exceptional performance ( Figures 5 C and  S5 ;  Table S6 ). It achieved a correctness score of 2.63, outperforming PULSE (1.18), HuaTuoGPT (1.27), Qwen (2.44), and DeepSeek-R1 (2.45), and nearly matching GPT-4o (2.72). With respect to completeness, LungGPT-Ex scored 2.65, on par with GPT-4o (2.64) and substantially higher than DeepSeek-R1 (2.32), Qwen (2.27), and HuaTuoGPT (1.30). Its truthfulness score was particularly notable, achieving 2.92 and comparable to GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen, significantly outperforming HuaTuoGPT (1.57) and PULSE (1.35).  Beyond diagnostic explanation, LungGPT-Ex generated patient-specific management suggestions spanning scheduled surveillance and follow-up, pharmacologic therapy, surgical or interventional evaluation when indicated, multidisciplinary team consultation, comprehensive treatment planning, and so on. By organizing diagnostic evidence and potential management options into a structured format, LungGPT-Ex could assist clinicians in interpreting model outputs, thereby improving the efficiency of clinical decision-making.    Clinical application of LungGPT  In practice, LungGPT used unstructured EHR data as input and then produced concise summaries including diagnoses, evidence-based diagnostic reasoning, and tailored decision recommendations ( Figure 6 ). As illustrated in a representative case of a 57-year-old male presenting with recurrent cough, sputum production, dyspnea, and hemoptysis, the model accurately identified severe pneumonia—supported by clinical manifestations such as acute symptom exacerbation, auscultatory findings of wet rales, and chest CT revealing scattered patches, nodules, and consolidations in both lungs. Additionally, LungGPT recognized acute exacerbation of COPD and chronic pulmonary heart disease, integrating longitudinal history and multimodality data into a coherent diagnostic narrative. The system further provided clear therapeutic guidance for severe cases, including prioritized antibiotic treatment, cardiopulmonary function support, and individualized monitoring plans. The clinical application of LungGPT was facilitated by a streamlined interface with several steps ( Figure S6 ). Specifically, it provided tailored recommendations for key disease categories including infectious, neoplastic, airway, and interstitial lung diseases. This example illustrates how LungGPT automatically generates structured diagnostic reasoning and clinical decision-support recommendations from complex patient records.    Figure 6   Application of LungGPT for tailored diagnosis and decision recommendations in respiratory diseases  After inputting the prompt command, the system could analyze admission records to diagnose disease. It also generated text summarized to provide clinicians with diagnostic reasoning and decision recommendations. This example highlighted the identification of severe pneumonia, supported by clinical findings such as recurrent cough and imaging results, and delivered clear therapeutic guidance, notably outlining specific interventions like oxygen therapy and anti-infective regimens for critical cases. All generated outputs were reviewed under clinician supervision, and final diagnostic and treatment decisions remained the responsibility of the treating physician.                      Discussion  In this study, a domain-specific multimodal system named LungGPT was developed for respiratory disease diagnosis and clinical decision support. This system was adept at processing information from multiple sources, including chief complaints, imaging findings, and laboratory tests to classify 22 respiratory diseases. Moreover, LungGPT excelled in the timely identification of critical conditions and provided intervention options. Meanwhile, LungGPT was capable of generating diagnostic reasoning and treatment planning based on specific prompts. Its performance was superior to that of most existing models, positioning it as a powerful auxiliary tool in clinical practice.  The rapid advancement of AI has fundamentally transformed the execution of healthcare tasks.  41   ,   42   ,   43   ,   44   A paradigmatic development in modern AI is the emergence of foundation models.  45   Leveraging large-scale datasets for pretraining and fine-tuning, general-purpose AI systems capably serve a broad spectrum of downstream tasks. LungGPT achieved superior diagnostic performance with a notable enhancement after pretraining and fine-tuning. This advantage was largely attributable to the large-scale, high-quality clinical corpus derived from 125,917 inpatient EHRs. This underscores the significant impact of domain-specific fine-tuning on amplifying the capabilities of LLMs.  46   ,   47   However, the diagnostic performance remains suboptimal for some diseases. On the one hand, overlapping features and hierarchical disease coding relationships often complicate diagnosis given the complex comorbid relationships. To address this, top-3 accuracy was additionally reported to account for clinically plausible alternative diagnoses in the ranked model outputs. On the other hand, the diagnostic accuracy for certain diseases was hindered by limited data volume, suggesting that zero-shot or few-shot learning may offer promising solutions for further improvement.  48    Another paradigm in modern AI focuses on generative models, which integrate high-dimensional data to create content spanning text, images, and molecular designs.  45   However, general-purpose LLMs often lack the rigorous precision required for medical applications. Leveraging real-world cases as prompts, LungGPT generated diagnostic reasoning and decision-making schemes whose format and phrasing closely mirror those of authentic inpatient records. The model was comparable to GPT-4o in terms of correctness, completeness, and truthfulness, providing powerful technical support to assist physicians in improving their productivity. Meanwhile, through RAG that draws on authoritative sources including guidelines, expert consensus, and professional textbooks, LungGPT-Ex generated clinical summaries that remain fully aligned with contemporary practice. This ability to update and standardize prompts in a timely manner endowed this model with higher accuracy in the text generation for respiratory diseases.  49   Future developments could incorporate real-time dialog functionality, enabling more natural and efficient interactions between physicians and the model.  50   ,   51    LLMs leverage encoded medical knowledge to aid clinicians toward precision diagnostic efficiency. Google introduced Med-PaLM, which integrated clinical knowledge with instruction-tuned learning and achieved expert-level performance on the MultiMedQA benchmark.  52   Its successor, Med-PaLM 2, further incorporated retrieval and verification strategies, attaining an accuracy of 86.5% on the MedQA dataset, which represented a 19% improvement over the Med-PaLM.  53   In respiratory medicine, foundation models cover a wide range of aspects such as disease screening, diagnosis, and treatment. For example, GPT-4o has been used to evaluate malignancy progression of pulmonary nodules to support lung cancer screening by dynamically monitoring the size and morphology.  54   While models like text-based Delphi-2M and imaging-based Ark+ can predict respiratory diseases, they lack the capability for treatment recommendation.  33   ,   34   In this study, LungGPT unified diagnostic inference and decision support, positioning itself for seamless integration into routine practice.  Guided by the clinical demands of respiratory medicine, LungGPT has preliminarily explored the integration of data from various sources and has achieved promising results in the decision support of various diseases. Currently, multimodal generative models have advanced rapidly.  55   ,   56   ,   57   The integration of multimodal data enables clinicians to gain a comprehensive understanding of diseases to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis, alleviating the limitations imposed by single-modality data.  58   ,   59   ,   60   For instance, BiomedGPT, as a vision-language generalist model, utilizes joint learning of imaging and textual features to achieve cross-modal alignment, which enables it to perform a wide range of biomedical tasks.  61   Nevertheless, real-world deployment confronts formidable challenges. Datasets must be watermarked for full traceability,  62   while hallucinations, biases, and equity concerns that are inherent to LLMs continue to impede adoption.  63   Consequently, clinicians, researchers, health-policy experts, and patient representatives must be integrated from the earliest design and development stages to safeguard fairness and ethical alignment.  64    In summary, LungGPT, as a domain-specific LLM trained on large-scale data, excelled in predicting 22 respiratory diseases and risk stratification for critical illness. It furthermore generated interpretable and traceable diagnostic reasoning and decision recommendations. The multimodal system provides an end-to-end framework spanning diagnosis, early warning of critical illness, and decision support. This system was expected to substantially enhance the quality of healthcare services.   Limitations of the study  The clinical translation of LungGPT confronts several challenges. First, the generalizability and robustness of LungGPT require further external validation across diverse demographic and regional settings. Second, the integration of multimodal and dynamic clinical data is needed to evolve LungGPT into a generalist medical AI agent, thereby operationalizing cross-scale precision medicine and enabling comprehensive exploitation of molecular-to-patient information within an AI framework to deliver truly individualized therapeutic decisions.  65   In addition, progression from an experimental architecture to a regulated decision-support tool demands rigorous regulatory scrutiny. To address these issues, prospective and multi-center studies are necessary to iteratively refine the model.    Experimental model and study participant details  The data used in this study consist of both general medical corpora and domain-specific electronic health record (EHR) data. Specifically, the general medical corpus was employed during pretraining to enable the large language model (LLM) to acquire representations relevant to clinical reasoning. Moreover, we ensured that this pretraining did not compromise the model’s instruction-following and interactive capabilities. To achieve this goal, we incorporated both an online human dialogue corpus and a general medical corpus sourced from research papers, textbooks, and clinical guidelines. Domain-specific EHR data from 125,917 participants were derived from West China Hospital of Sichuan University for the period from 2009 to 2021 and were utilized in the fine-tuning phase. These records included comprehensive information about patient conditions, such as demographic details, chief complaints, imaging findings, radiological reports, laboratory test descriptions, pathological reports, pulmonary function tests, and follow-up records. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee in the West China Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu, China (No. 2024.1762). Informed consent was waived because of the retrospective nature of the study.    Method details   Multimodal data processing   Data curation  To enhance the capabilities of models in both general communication and specialized domains, the pre-training data incorporated 5.8 billion tokens of open-source human dialogue from WanJuan-CC (English) and WuDaoCorpora (Chinese). Furthermore, to ground the model in robust medical knowledge, a dedicated corpus of 1.8 billion tokens was constructed from peer-reviewed research and clinical guidelines indexed in PubMed, MEDLINE, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). This general medical corpus comprised the latest clinical studies, specialized textbooks, and practice guidelines related to respiratory disease management.  Domain-specific EHR data were derived from 125,917 hospitalized patients with at least one respiratory disease diagnosis. Eligible patients were those with a confirmed respiratory disease and complete inpatient EHRs. Patients with unclear diagnoses or suspected misdiagnosis, as well as those who could not be clearly matched to a specific respiratory disease, were excluded. Cases deemed unsuitable for inclusion by the researchers were also excluded. A total of 29,215 patients with a primary diagnosis of respiratory disease were included in this study, and the dataset was partitioned into a training set and a testing set at an 8:2 ratio.    ICD-10 label encoding  To ensure data consistency and comparability, we standardized all patients’ diagnostic information by ICD-10 coding, which was manually annotated ( Table S1 ). Initially, we implemented a fuzzy matching algorithm that compared the disease names written by physicians with the ICD-10 code list to find the most similar matches. This step aimed to reduce the annotation workload. Despite the assistance from fuzzy matching, all the coding was manually verified and annotated by our team of experienced clinical coders. This manual process ensured that each diagnosis was accurately matched to the correct ICD-10 code. By relying on manual annotation, supported by fuzzy matching for efficiency, we maintained a high level of accuracy and consistency in the ICD-10 coding process for our dataset.    Chest CT image acquisition  Chest computed tomography (CT) images were retrieved in DICOM format from the Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS). Eligibility criteria included volumetric CT acquisition within 48 hours before or after the index admission, axial slice thickness ≤ 2.5 mm, and complete lung coverage from the lung apices to the costophrenic angles. Patients who met these CT criteria and had complete EHR data were included in the multimodal cohort for critical illness prediction. Severe pneumonia, rapidly progressive lung cancer, AECOPD, and acute pulmonary embolism were selected as the critical illness subtypes for investigation. The role of multimodal information fusion in enabling precise differential diagnosis was assessed across these conditions.     LungGPT architecture and workflow   Task-specific large language models  We developed two distinct LLMs for the tasks of disease diagnosis and decision explanation, named LungGPT-Dx (7B) and LungGPT-Ex (110B), respectively. Both models were based on the Qwen architecture  68   and trained using quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA).  70   The LungGPT-Dx was fine-tuned for ICD-10 annotated disease diagnosis, which significantly enhanced its performance in classification tasks. However, fully fine-tuning an LLM often compromises its conversational and logical reasoning abilities.  71   Therefore, LungGPT-Ex underwent supervised fine-tuning (SFT) separately and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)  72   based on Qwen-110B, enabling it to have a nuanced understanding of diagnostic criteria while maintaining robust conversational capabilities.    Retrieval-augmented generation  The general medical corpus underwent data preprocessing to construct a textual knowledge base, which was then embedded into vectors to form a vectorized knowledge database. The knowledge database was designed for continuous real-time updates. In situations where updating the base model with pretraining was not feasible, the real-time augmentation of medical knowledge through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) effectively mitigated the model’s limitations in handling medical knowledge. In implementation, retrieved clinically relevant passages from the knowledge base. This could provide reference information for LungGPT-Ex in terms of diagnostic criteria and maintain reliable answers.    Integrated pipeline  The workflow of our proposed framework included LungGPT-Dx, LungGPT-Ex, and the structured database. In practical applications, the patient’s EHR was first input into LungGPT-Dx, which generated a textual diagnosis of potential respiratory diseases. Next, the patient’s EHR was concatenated with the diagnostic output from LungGPT-Dx to create a query, which was then processed via LangChain  73   to retrieve relevant knowledge from a structured database. This integration of EHR data and diagnostic results formed a knowledge-enhanced input. This enhanced input was subsequently fed into LungGPT-Ex, which was responsible for providing a comprehensive explanation of the diagnosis. LungGPT-Ex then delivered a detailed diagnostic explanation and generated treatment planning.  To achieve precise identification of critical respiratory conditions, we developed a hierarchical framework that integrated textual clinical data with radiological features. First, a chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting strategy  74   was employed to identify key physiological indicators and symptomatic abnormalities within the EHR, mapping these findings to predefined clinical semantic categories. Simultaneously, a deep learning model was utilized to extract high-dimensional features from chest CT images.  75   Through this integrated reasoning process, the system generated evidence-based syntheses aligned with established clinical guidelines, enabling the high-fidelity identification of critically ill patients.     Model benchmarking and evaluation   Comparator models  To ensure fair benchmarking between LungGPT and the baseline LLM models, we implemented strict evaluation protocols. All the comparator models were used in their original public releases without domain adaptation in our study. Specifically, PULSE was implemented using the Bloomz architecture; the publicly available LLaMA-based 7B medical version of HuaTuoGPT was utilized, the Qwen-7B general-purpose implementation of Qwen was employed, GPT-4o was accessed via an official API without customization, and the publicly available DeepSeek-R1 was used for DeepSeek. The complete model configurations were detailed in  Table S7 .    Respiratory disease diagnosis  For the performance evaluation of LungGPT-Dx, we employed several key metrics including area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC), the top-1/3 accuracy (ACC), precision (PRE), recall (REC), and the F1 score (F1). These metrics were critical for assessing the effectiveness of our classification approach. The AUC quantified the model’s ability to discriminate between positive and negative cases across all classification thresholds, with higher values indicating better overall diagnostic performance. Top-1/3 ACC measured the frequency with which the correct diagnosis appears within the top 1 or 3 predictions made by the model. They provide a clear picture of the model’s ranking ability, with top-1 accuracy being the strictest measure and top-3 accuracy offering a broader view of the model’s capabilities. PRE was the ratio of the number of correctly predicted positive observations to the total number of predicted positive observations. It is a measure of the model’s accuracy in identifying relevant instances among the retrieved instances. REC or sensitivity, was the ratio of the number of correctly predicted positive observations to the total number of observations in the actual class. It assesses the model’s ability to identify all relevant instances. The F1 score was the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and it provided a single metric that balanced concerns regarding both false positives and false negatives. It is particularly useful when dealing with imbalanced datasets.    Diagnostic reasoning and decision support  Considering the evaluation of the diagnostic criteria provided by the LungGPT-Ex, we adopted the Likert Scale Scoring system. The Likert scale was a widely recognized psychometric tool used to gauge subjective assessments, where respondents specify their level of agreement or disagreement with a statement.  Correctness, completeness, and truthfulness were the key evaluation indicators for the responses of LLMs. Correctness was used to evaluate whether the diagnostic criteria can support the diagnostic result accurately to ensure alignment with established medical knowledge. Completeness measured whether the diagnostic criteria cover all necessary aspects needed to reach a proper diagnosis and was used to assess the thoroughness of the LLM’s output. Truthfulness was used to assess whether the diagnostic criteria are based on real and verifiable information to ensure the reliability and trustworthiness of the information provided by the LLM. Each criterion was assessed on a 3-point scale, where 3 represents the best score and 1 represents the worst score.  By combining these quantitative and qualitative evaluation methods, we aimed to thoroughly assess the performance and reliability of this proposed method for respiratory disease diagnosis and to ensure that it meets the high standards required for clinical application.     Implementation details  LungGPT integrated with hospital information systems (HIS) via a secure application programming interface (API), compliant with data privacy regulations. Clinicians could access a web-based dashboard, input a patient’s identifier to retrieve structured (demographics, medical history) and unstructured (radiology reports, progress notes) data, with support for manual upload of additional lab results or imaging findings. Then LungGPT-Dx generated a ranked list of respiratory diseases, and LungGPT-Ex produced diagnostic rationales and treatment recommendations using a vectorized knowledge base of clinical guidelines. Outputs were reviewed by clinicians, who retained final decision-making authority, with options to adjust suggestions based on bedside observations. The interface underwent iterative usability testing by participating clinicians. Feedback from participating clinicians, including observations on usability and diagnostic alignment, informed iterative refinements to the interface and model outputs.     Quantification and statistical analysis  To evaluate the diagnostic performance of LungGPT, metrics such as AUC, the top-1/3 ACC, PRE, REC, and the F1 score were adopted. 95% confidence intervals for AUCs were estimated using the DeLong method. To evaluate the quality of the diagnostic explanations and treatment planning generated by LungGPT, three clinicians independently assessed outputs by using a 3-point Likert scale across three distinct dimensions (correctness, completeness, and truthfulness). To compare the clinical scores quantitatively, statistical analyses were performed using the Friedman test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. All the statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 26.0), where ∗ indicating  p  < 0.05, ∗∗ indicating  p  < 0.01, and ∗∗∗ indicating  p  < 0.001. evidence_text:
Predictive value of <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT PyRadiomics features using a tabular deep learning model for cancer-related cognitive impairment in patients with DLBCL without CNS involvement.

Objective

To evaluate the predictive value of tabular deep learning models trained on handcrafted 18F-FDG PET/CT PyRadiomics features and clinical data for cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) among patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma without central nervous system involvement (non-CNS DLBCL).

Material and methods

We retrospectively analyzed 112 non-CNS DLBCL patients who underwent brain 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG)PET/CT. Based on Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Cognitive Function (FACT-Cog) scores, patients were classified into the CRCI group (n = 73) and the non-CRCI group (n = 39) and randomly partitioned into training (n=89) and test (n=23) sets at an 8:2 ratio. Five-fold cross-validation was performed within the training set for model development, and bootstrap resampling was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals for AUC. Radiomic features were extracted with PyRadiomics from automatically segmented brain regions using MOOSE120 software. These handcrafted PET/CT radiomic features and clinical variables were organized as structured tabular datasets; raw PET/CT images were not used as direct model inputs. Feature selection was performed using correlation coefficients. The performance of seven tabular deep learning models was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and decision curve analysis (DCA), and different input modalities (clinical, PET, CT, and combined) were compared. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were applied to interpret feature contributions.

Results

The AutoInt and Neural Oblivious Decision Ensembles (NODE) models showed the best predictive performance, achieving training areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.905 and 0.904, and test AUCs of 0.858 and 0.808, respectively. DCA suggested potential clinical utility. In the modality-specific analysis, the AutoInt model integrating CT, PET, and clinical features achieved a training AUC of 0.905 and a test AUC of 0.858, representing the most favorable test-set performance among the evaluated AutoInt input modalities. A CT texture feature from the left occipital lobe emerged as the highest-ranked model contributor in SHAP analysis, with a mean absolute attribution score of approximately 0.0078.

Conclusions

Tabular deep learning models based on handcrafted PET/CT PyRadiomics features showed preliminary potential for predicting CRCI in patients with non-CNS DLBCL. Among the evaluated models, AutoInt achieved the most favorable performance in the exploratory internal test set. Multimodal integration of PET, CT, and clinical tabular features may provide complementary information for CRCI prediction. SHAP analysis identified a left occipital CT texture feature as the top-ranked model contributor; however, this finding should be regarded as exploratory rather than a validated biomarker. Introduction Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and represents an aggressive but potentially curable hematological malignancy ( 1 , 2 ). The R-CHOP regimen has significantly improved survival outcomes in DLBCL patients; however, approximately 20%–50% of cases still develop refractory disease or experience relapse. Recent years have witnessed substantial therapeutic advances, including novel cytotoxic agents, optimized stem cell transplantation techniques, and targeted immunotherapies such as BCL-2 and PD-1 inhibitors. These developments have greatly expanded treatment options for patients with refractory DLBCL, thus improving clinical outcomes ( 1 ). With improvements in lymphoma treatment and prolonged survival, long-term complications affecting quality of life have become increasingly important. Among these complications, cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) has emerged as a growing clinical concern in cancer survivors, including patients with lymphoma ( 3 – 5 ). CRCI manifests as declines in attention, executive function, memory, and information processing speed, significantly impairing patients’ quality of life. CRCI is a multifactorial condition and may be associated with treatment-related neurotoxicity, systemic inflammation, fatigue, emotional distress, aging, and reduced cognitive reserve ( 5 – 8 ). In patients with non-CNS DLBCL, the absence of direct CNS lesions makes early identification of CRCI particularly challenging, because cognitive symptoms may be subtle and conventional structural imaging may fail to detect early functional or metabolic alterations.Our preliminary study found that the baseline non-CNS DLBCL group exhibited glucose hypometabolism in multiple brain regions compared to the healthy control group. Neuropsychological scales, including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Cognitive Function (FACT-Cog), currently serve as practical tools for CRCI identification ( 5 – 9 ). However, scale-based assessment may be influenced by education, mood, fatigue, and patient-reported perception, and may not fully reflect underlying brain metabolic or structural changes. Recent neuroimaging studies using fMRI, DTI, and FDG-PET have provided objective approaches for detecting functional, structural, and metabolic brain alterations associated with cognitive impairment ( 10 – 14 ).Among these modalities, 18 F-FDG PET is particularly relevant because it quantifies regional cerebral glucose metabolism, which is closely related to neuronal activity and neurovascular coupling. Therefore, FDG-PET may provide objective metabolic information complementary to scale-based cognitive assessment ( 3 , 8 , 15 ). However, most studies use single- or dual-modality approaches, which lead to suboptimal detection efficiency. Advances in medical data integration and computational power have made artificial intelligence (AI)-based medical image analysis an active area of research ( 16 ). In radiomics-based workflows, quantitative features are first extracted from predefined regions of interest and then combined with clinical variables as structured tabular inputs for prediction models. Tabular deep learning models are capable of capturing nonlinear interactions and high-order feature relationships among these handcrafted imaging features and clinical variables. Importantly, this strategy differs from end-to-end image-based deep learning because raw PET/CT images are not directly input into the network ( 16 – 19 ). This PyRadiomics feature-based tabular modeling approach has not yet been explored in CRCI research involving DLBCL. Therefore, the contribution of the present study should be interpreted in a specific methodological and clinical context: the focus on non-CNS DLBCL, the integration of PET-derived, CT-derived, and clinical tabular features, the comparison of multiple tabular deep learning architectures, and the use of a SHAP-based interpretability framework ( 3 , 20 – 23 ). Accordingly, this study leveraged 18 F-FDG PET/CT images to extract PyRadiomics features from automatically segmented brain regions and integrated these imaging-derived features with clinical variables to construct structured PET/CT tabular datasets. We developed and compared tabular deep learning models to identify patients with non-CNS DLBCL who are at risk of CRCI at an early stage, thereby providing a foundation for improving their quality of life. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study participants This retrospective study enrolled non-CNS DLBCL patients (baseline or post-chemotherapy) who underwent cerebral 18 F-FDG PET imaging at our institution between October 2020 and January 2025. Patients were further categorized according to treatment status at the time of PET/CT and cognitive assessment as either baseline/pre-treatment or post-chemotherapy. For post-chemotherapy patients, treatment regimen, and the interval from the last chemotherapy cycle to cognitive assessment were extracted from medical records when available. All cognitive assessments were completed within 48 hours before PET/CT examination. Demographic data (sex, age, years of education) were collected. Treatment-related information, including treatment status, chemotherapy regimen, and the interval from the last chemotherapy cycle to cognitive assessment, was extracted from medical records when available. The treatment-related characteristics are summarized in the Results section. All participants provided written informed consent, and the study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of our institution (Ethics Approval No: KYLL-2023-0035). Inclusion criteria: (1) Age ≥18 years; (2) DLBCL group: Pathologically confirmed DLBCL without evidence of brain metastasis or other intracranial abnormalities on imaging, and completion of cerebral 18 F-FDG PET examination. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) history of other malignancies; (2) pre-existing neurological or psychiatric disorders, psychological conditions, alcohol or drug abuse, severe cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, diabetes mellitus, or other metabolic diseases; (3) incomplete clinical data or inability to undergo long-term follow-up; and (4) PET images with significant artifacts or defects. These exclusion criteria were applied to reduce potential CRCI mimics, including neurological, psychiatric, vascular, endocrine, metabolic, or substance-related conditions that could independently affect cognitive performance or brain FDG uptake.
