Because the kidney is composed of diverse and highly specialized cell populations, disease mechanisms may manifest through cell type-specific transcriptional alterations. Recent advances in single-cell and snRNA-seq have enabled high-resolution characterization of kidney cell populations and injury-associated transcriptional states. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 These approaches have provided important insights into kidney biology and disease mechanisms, including the identification of rare glomerular cell types such as podocytes that are often underrepresented in conventional transcriptomic studies. 14 However, most single-cell studies of kidney disease have focused on individual disease entities or tissues obtained from nephrectomy specimens, limiting the ability to compare transcriptional alterations across multiple glomerular diseases using diagnostic human biopsy tissues. To address this gap, we performed snRNA-seq on snap-frozen kidney biopsy tissues obtained from patients with 4 major glomerular diseases—MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD—together with control kidney samples. By integrating transcriptomic profiles across disease groups and controls, we aimed to identify both shared and disease-specific transcriptional programs across kidney cell types and to characterize disease-associated cellular states within the human glomerulus. Methods Ethical Considerations and Patient Consent The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of Seoul National University Hospital (IRB Nos. H-2203-053-1303 and H-1404-117-575). The study samples were collected from the KORNERSTONE project, a multicenter, prospective cohort study and biobank for glomerular diseases, run under the National Biobank Project of the Republic of Korea. 15 Patients provided informed consent for the collection of the biospecimens, their use in this study, and their use in a public database. The study was conducted under the National Research Project Single Cell Atlas of Immune Disease ( http://www.scaid.org/ ). Kidney Tissue Collection The study subjects were enrolled in the KORNERSTONE project before their first diagnostic kidney biopsy. At our institution, three biopsy cores were typically obtained per patient and first evaluated by an attending nephropathologist for routine clinical diagnostics (light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy). Intact biopsy tissue not required for diagnostic evaluation was immediately snap-frozen at the bedside for biobanking. For snRNA-seq, the remaining cores were used in their entirety; because standard biopsy cores traverse the cortex and may variably extend toward the corticomedullary region, the sequenced material represents mixed cortical regions. We selected patients with preserved kidney function (eGFR ≥ 30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ), to minimize disease-nonspecific transcriptomic effects of advanced fibrotic changes. Inclusion required primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without other glomerulonephritis pathologies; patients with urine protein creatinine ratio > 3 g/g (MCD, MN, and DKD) who were immunosuppression-naïve were prioritized to capture active disease. In this study, we included a total of 30 patient kidney samples (from 7 MCD, 6 MN, 13 IgAN, and 4 patients with DKD). Clinical data from the initial visit and treatment initiation were analyzed. For control kidney tissues, we used the normal kidney cortex obtained during radical nephrectomy surgery for kidney cancer. We carefully reviewed the clinical histories to exclude patients with diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease and selected those without proteinuria or obstructive changes in the kidney. To minimize ischemic bias, an intraoperative gun biopsy was obtained from the exposed kidney before renal artery clamping, away from cancerous lesions. Tissues were snap-frozen and delivered to central storage. A total of 7 control patients were included in the study. Results Baseline Characteristics of the Study Subjects We collected data from 37 participants, including individuals with MCD ( n = 7), MN ( n = 6), IgAN ( n = 13), and DKD ( n = 4), as well as a control group ( n = 7). All patient samples were obtained from immunosuppressants-naïve individuals with typical clinical presentations, including primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti- PLA2R antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without another diagnosis. Control kidney tissues were obtained from chemotherapy-naïve patients undergoing nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma, using noncancerous lesions in cortical tissue. The baseline demographics of the study subjects are presented in Supplementary Table S1 . The mean spot urine protein creatinine ratio for each condition was 8.09 ± 4.87 g/g for the MCD group, 7.98 ± 6.49 g/g for the MN group, 1.05 ± 1.36 g/g for the IgAN group, and 3.68 ± 1.78 g/g for the DKD group. The control group had no proteinuria. The baseline eGFR was 89.8 ± 26.8 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 in the study subjects with typical clinical features. We analyzed a total of 333,938 nuclei from biopsy tissues ( Figure 1 a) and identified 12 main cell clusters, annotated based on known canonical markers, including podocytes, PECs, various tubular cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells ( Figure 1 b, c). We next examined the distribution of these subtypes across clinical groups and observed pronounced, disease-specific heterogeneity ( Figure 1 d). To validate these annotations, we compared our data with an external dataset from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project. 9 This comparison revealed a high correlation in marker gene expression profiles ( Supplementary Figure S1 A). Furthermore, upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in our DKD samples showed a similar pattern to those in the Kidney Precision Medicine Project dataset ( Supplementary Figure S1 B). Finally, we performed more detailed subclustering and annotation for each major cell type ( Supplementary Figure S1 C, Supplementary Table S2 ). Disease-Dominant, Cell Type-Common, Cell Type-Dominant, and Disease-Common DEGs in Glomerular Diseases Our analysis of DEGs revealed a dichotomous pattern—upregulated DEGs were largely disease-specific but shared across cell types, whereas downregulated DEGs were cell type-specific but common across diseases ( Supplementary Table S3 ). We identified disease-dominant upregulated gene modules enriched in each condition ( Figure 1 e and f; Supplementary Table S4 ). The MCD-dominant module was enriched for transporter-related genes (e.g., SLC13A1 , SLC36A2 ; Module 5). The MN-dominant module included genes associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (e.g., SPP1, VIM ) and the interferon response (e.g., HIF1A, IFNAR2 ; Module 8). The IgAN-dominant module was associated with previously reported pathways, including aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption (Module 2). In DKD, upregulated modules were associated with differentiation and metabolic processes (Module 15) ( Figure 1 f; Supplementary Table S5 ). Representative genes within each module also showed preferential expression in the corresponding disease group at the sample level ( Supplementary Figure S2 A). Module score analysis confirmed significantly higher in scores in the corresponding disease groups compared with others ( Supplementary Figure S2 B). In contrast, downregulated DEGs exhibited a cell type-restricted pattern shared across diseases ( Figure 1 g and 1h; Supplementary Table S4 ). In podocytes, genes related to the actin cytoskeleton (e.g., IQGAP2 , MICAL2 ) 16 , 17 and cell-cell adhesion were reduced (Module 12). In PECs, genes negatively regulating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling were downregulated (Module 14). 18 Tubular cells showed decreased expression of metabolic pathways, including fatty acid metabolism, in proximal tubule- and thick ascending limb-specific modules (Modules 1 and 3). 19 , 20 In collecting duct principal cells, the downregulated module included the glucocorticoid receptor and NR4A1 . Endothelial cells demonstrated reduced expression of SPRED2 , with gene ontology analysis indicating negative regulation of the MAPK cascade (Module 9; Supplementary Table S6 ). 21 For each cell type, module scores were significantly lower in diseased samples than in controls, without differences in unrelated cell types ( Supplementary Figure S2 C). Disease-Associated Intermediate Epithelial State Between Injured Podocytes and Activated PECs Subclustering of glomerular cells identified a distinct population positioned between podocytes and PECs on uniform manifold approximation and projection ( Figure 2 a). 22 These cells coexpressed canonical markers of both lineages along with a distinct transcriptional profile ( Figure 2 b, Supplementary Figure S3 A). A pseudotime analysis further demonstrated the transcriptional proximity of this population to both podocytes and PECs ( Figure 2 c). This population was enriched for PEC activation and proliferative signaling programs, including MAPK- and epidermal growth factor receptor-related pathways involving ERBB 2, EGF , FGFR , and CD 24, together with cluster-defining genes such as CASR and PRDM 16 ( Supplementary Figure S3 B and C). 18 , 23 This cluster also showed significant upregulation of genes known to be highly expressed in proliferative PECs ( Figure 2 d). 22 Importantly, the proportion of this cluster was significantly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.35, R² = 0.13, P = 0.031) with clinical severity index that we defined ( Figure 2 e). Disease-Specific Gene Expression in Podocytes and Podocytes With Endocytosis Feature We further focused on podocytes, given their crucial role in glomerular pathophysiology. Comparison of downregulated DEGs between controls and disease groups revealed 2 dominant patterns—genes commonly reduced across all glomerular diseases ( n = 101) and genes selectively reduced in DKD ( n = 124; Figure 3 a). The commonly downregulated DEGs were primarily associated with the regulation of cell migration and the negative regulation of the immune system ( Figure 3 b). This latter finding is consistent with the prominent interferon-γ response observed in the disease groups ( Figure 3 c). Upregulated DEGs were enriched in disease-specific gene modules across glomerular diseases, highlighting the strong disease specificity of transcriptional activation programs ( Figure 3 d). Upregulated DEGs in MN showed enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related genes, whereas IgAN was associated with genes involved in cell-substrate junction assembly ( Figure 3 e). Across diseases, slit diaphragm-associated genes including TJP1 and MAGI2 were consistently downregulated, along with VCL , which contributes to maintenance of the glomerular filtration barrier. 26 , 27 , 28 Additional disease-specific patterns were observed, including detachment-associated genes ( NOX4, TCF21 , and SLIT2 ) 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 in MCD and regeneration-related genes ( PROM1 and PAX8 ) 33 , 34 in DKD ( Figure 3 f and Supplementary Figure S4 A and B and Supplementary Table S9 ). The expression of GADD45A , VIM, and CDH6 , 35 , 36 , 37 which are known to be associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition, was found to be specifically elevated in MN. Podocytes were divided into 3 clusters and annotated using marker genes ( Figure 3 g and Supplementary Figure S4 C). One population was characterized by high expression of genes associated with cubilin and amnionless complex, including LRP2 , CUBN , CLCN5 , and PRKCA , and was therefore designated the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure S4 C and D). 38 A similar transcriptional pattern cluster was also observed in podocytes in independent external single-cell datasets, including in patients with chronic kidney disease ( Supplementary Figure S4 E, F, and G). 9 Compared with conventional podocytes, podocyte endocytosis showed increased PAX2 , 39 and reduced expression of CDKN1C , 40 PODXL, and NPHS2, together with higher proliferation module scores ( Supplementary Figure S4 H and I). Importantly, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis cells significantly increased with baseline proteinuria severity (quasibinomial generalized linear model, β = 0.042, P = 0.001, pseudo-R 2 = 0.226), whereas patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment exhibited higher podocyte endocytosis module scores, suggesting an association between this transcriptional state and poor treatment response ( Figure 3 h and i). Accordingly, the gene module score was significantly greater in the MCD and MN groups than in the other glomerular disease groups and the control group ( Figure 3 j). These findings suggest that the activation of endocytosis-related gene programs in podocytes reflects the severity of proteinuria and may also have prognostic implications. We validated the presence of “podocyte endocytosis” at both the transcriptomic and protein levels through the coexpression of LRP2 and NPHS1 in Xenium in situ and megalin (encoded by LRP2 ) and WT1 in immunofluorescence ( Figure 3 k–l and Supplementary Table S7 ). Additionally, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis tended to be higher in glomerular disease in Xenium in situ and IF ( Supplementary Figure S4 J and K). To further characterize the signaling environment associated with podocyte endocytosis, we performed CellChat analysis across glomerular and peri-glomerular populations. Among the inferred pathways, Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling showed preferential communication toward the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure 4 L). Bradykinin signaling originated from multiple glomerular populations, whereas complement and interleukin17 signaling were primarily inferred from juxtaglomerular apparatus cells, PECs, and podocytes. Together, these findings indicate an injury-related signaling microenvironment around podocyte endocytosis cells. Drug2Cell (Wellcome Sanger Institute, Cambridge, UK) 41 identified candidate compounds targeting podocyte endocytosis, including phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitors (Apremilast, Roflumilast, and Crisaborole) and the cyclic guanosine monophosphate-modulating agent isosorbide ( Supplementary Figure S4 M), suggesting that modulation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate and cyclic guanosine monophosphate pathways may offer promising therapeutic avenues for targeting podocyte endocytosis-related injury. Stromal Activation and Myofibroblast Expansion Across Glomerular Diseases Stromal cells (including vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts) were subclustered into 12 clusters ( Figure 4 a, Supplementary Figure S5 A). 9 Across glomerular diseases, stromal cells showed consistent enrichment of TGF-β signaling, with the strongest activation observed in the myofibroblast cluster ( Figure 4 b and c). Trajectory analysis restricted to fibroblast-lineage cells revealed a differentiation continuum from fibroblasts to myofibroblasts present across all disease groups ( Figure 4 d), consistent with the established role of TGF-β signaling in myofibroblast activation. Along this trajectory, gene programs transitioned from mesenchymal differentiation to extracellular matrix organization, reflecting acquisition of myofibroblast functions ( Supplementary Figure S5 B). The expression levels of genes corresponding to the trajectory of the myofibroblast-enriched state and myofibroblast-associated genes, such as SULF1, NOX4, and COL16A1 , were consistently increased in glomerular diseases ( Supplementary Figure S5 C). Correspondingly, the proportion of myofibroblasts was significantly increased in disease samples compared with controls ( Figure 4 e). A heatmap analysis of fibroblast-associated cell types (e.g., fibroblasts, medullary fibroblasts, adaptive fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts) using their DEGs revealed a gene module (Module 4) that was commonly upregulated across all glomerular diseases (module 4, Supplementary Figure S5 D and Supplementary Table S9 ). This module was significantly enriched for markers of myofibroblasts, TGF-β signaling-related genes, and genes of the Wnt pathway. Consistent with this, functional analysis of the module showed enrichment for biological processes related to myofibroblast function, such as extracellular matrix organization ( Supplementary Figure S5 E). The presence of this shared profibrotic pathway indicates that a common fibrotic program is activated across these diverse glomerular diseases. The myofibroblast gene module score was significantly increased across all glomerular diseases ( Supplementary Figure S5 F). Importantly, this module score was inversely correlated with eGFR(linear regression r = -0.47, R 2 = 0.22, P -value = 0.003), directly linking the fibrotic signature to declining kidney function ( Figure 4 f). Consistent with this, the proportion of myofibroblasts itself was also higher in the disease groups and was significantly associated with lower baseline (quasibinomial generalized linear model β = −0.013, P -value < 0.001, pseudo-R 2 = 0.339) and follow-up eGFR (quasibinomial generalized linear model β = −0.009, P -value = 0.012, pseudo-R 2 = 0.171) in regression analyses ( Figure 4 g and h). These associations persisted throughout the follow-up period, supporting a potential relationship between myofibroblast expansion and progressive kidney dysfunction. Cell-cell interaction analysis highlighted Periostin pathway as a disease-specific pathway originating from myofibroblasts ( Figure 4 i). This pathway primarily targeted PECs and, in primary glomerular diseases, also affected podocytes ( Figure 4 j). POSTN signaling is implicated in wound healing and fibrosis, 42 , 43 and POSTN-expressing fibroblasts were enriched within diseased glomeruli ( Figure 4 k). Their abundance was significantly associated with both proteinuria severity (R 2 = 0.29, P -value = 0.016) and the proportion of podocyte endocytosis (R 2 = 0.284, P -value = 0.019; Figure 4 l and m). These results indicate that myofibroblasts are common pathogenic cell types in glomerular disease and are associated with a decline in kidney function. Among them, POSTN-expressing myofibroblasts are additionally associated with proteinuria and appear to represent a key cellular component underlying glomerular disease manifestations. To identify potential therapeutic targets for myofibroblasts, we applied the Drug2Cell framework ( Supplementary Figure S5 G). 41 Among the top-ranked candidate compounds, cetirizine and olaratumab were identified as potential modulators of myofibroblast-associated programs. 44 These findings suggest that targeting myofibroblast activity may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for glomerular disease-associated fibrosis. TGF-β and Interferon Signaling in Endothelial Cells are Key to the Pathogenesis of Glomerular Diseases Endothelial cells were subclustered and annotated into 11 distinct cell types using known canonical markers ( Figure 5 a and b). DEGs revealed disease-associated transcriptional modules linked to vascular and immune signaling pathways (Module 2, Figure 5 c and d and Supplementary Table S9 ). Among these, endothelial cells from primary glomerular diseases showed enrichment of vasculogenesis-related programs, whereas disease-specific DEGs were particularly prominent in the MCD and MN groups ( Figure 5 e). Functional enrichment analysis indicated that these signatures were associated with TGF-β signaling and interferon responses, respectively ( Figure 5 f). Gene module scoring showed that TGF-β signaling was most strongly elevated in MN, followed by MCD and DKD ( Figure 5 g), whereas the interferon-α response score was the highest in the MCD group. Both pathways were consistently increased in disease groups compared with controls. When analyzed at the subcluster level, these signaling programs were enriched in glomerular endothelial-related subclusters, with the interferon-α response showing the highest expression in the degenerative endothelial cluster ( Figure 5 h), with interferon-stimulated genes showing particularly high expression in MCD ( Figure 5 i). Discussion This study presents a single-nucleus transcriptome analysis of human biopsy-confirmed glomerular diseases, comprising 333,938 nuclei obtained from 37 individuals, including 30 treatment-naïve patients with MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD and 7 controls. By profiling diverse kidney cell populations from diagnostic biopsy cores, our dataset provides a comprehensive view of early disease-associated transcriptional changes across glomerular diseases. Another strength of this study is the inclusion of subjects without substantial GFR reduction, which enabled us to compare cell type-specific transcriptomic alterations in relatively early disease states. Our transcriptome data may enhance the understanding of disease-specific pathophysiologic mechanisms of glomerular diseases, which may lead to the discovery of diagnostic or therapeutic biomarkers and common pathological pathways contributing to the progression of chronic kidney disease. This atlas therefore provides a framework for interpreting cell type–specific transcriptional alterations across major glomerular diseases. A notable observation from our analysis was the distinct pattern of transcriptional regulation across diseases and cell types. Upregulated genes tended to form disease-dominant modules, whereas downregulated genes were largely organized by cell type. This pattern suggests that disease-specific signaling programs activate distinct transcriptional responses, whereas functional impairment manifests through loss of cell type-specific gene expression. For example, the MN-dominant transcriptional signature was enriched for epithelial-mesenchymal transition and interferon-γ response pathways, consistent with immune-mediated injury associated with phospholipase A2 receptor autoimmunity 45 , 46 and IgAN modules with MAPK signaling, consistent with MAPK and/or extracellular signal-regulated kinase activation in mesangial injury. 47 Nevertheless, several upregulated modules also exhibited cell type-restricted patterns that complemented the corresponding downregulated programs within the same cell type. For example, proximal tubule modules paired upregulated transport programs with downregulated metabolic programs, suggesting adaptive tubular hypertrophy; endothelial modules paired vasculogenic activation with loss of MAPK negative regulators. We also identified a glomerular epithelial population exhibiting a hybrid transcriptional profile shared between podocytes and PECs. Podocytes are terminally differentiated cells that undergo structural injury and transcriptional remodeling under stress, whereas PECs retain proliferative potential and can respond dynamically to podocyte loss. The hybrid epithelial population was enriched in diseased glomeruli and showed activation of epithelial stress- and proliferation-associated programs, suggesting epithelial plasticity and remodeling within the injured glomerular compartment. This observation is consistent with previous studies showing that pathological activation of PEC signaling pathways can lead to abnormal PEC proliferation and contribute to glomerulosclerosis. Spatial transcriptomic analysis further supported the presence of these cells within diseased glomeruli. Although the lineage relationships of these cells cannot be resolved from cross-sectional human biopsy data alone, their shared transcriptional features and spatial localization support the existence of an injury-associated hybrid epithelial state in glomerular disease. Our study further identified a podocyte subpopulation characterized by expression of genes involved in protein endocytosis, including the cubilin and amnionless complex components LRP2 and CUBN . 38 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 Previous studies have suggested that podocytes may activate endocytic pathways under protein overload to maintain filtration barrier integrity. Consistent with this, the podocyte endocytosis program was associated with increased proteinuria and remained elevated in patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment. Recent work suggesting that antinephrin autoantibodies in podocytopathies induce nephrin internalization and glomerular endocytic activity provides a potential mechanistic framework, and the prominent MCD enrichment may reflect this adaptive or injury-associated response to slit diaphragm dysfunction. 52 The preferential enrichment of Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling toward this population further suggests an injury-associated microenvironment, consistent with podocyte dedifferentiation features. These findings suggest that this transcriptional state may represent an adaptive but injury-associated podocyte response with potential relevance to disease severity and treatment response. In addition to epithelial injury programs, we observed consistent activation of stromal fibrotic pathways across glomerular diseases. Trajectory analysis suggested differentiation from fibroblasts to myofibroblasts, accompanied by enrichment of TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix programs. Notably, the abundance of myofibroblasts correlated with declining kidney function even in patients without severe functional impairment at diagnosis, suggesting that fibrotic remodeling begins early in disease progression. Spatial transcriptomic data further revealed enrichment of POSTN-expressing fibroblasts within diseased glomeruli, supporting the existence of localized fibrotic microenvironments that may promote ongoing glomerular injury. Our data extend previous observations by demonstrating these fibrotic programs at single-cell resolution within human biopsy tissues. Drug2cell analysis further identified candidate compounds targeting disease-associated cellular states, providing a framework for future therapeutic hypothesis generation. The enrichment of distinct pathways in endothelial cells offers potential mechanistic insights into these diseases. For instance, the prominent TGF-β signaling in MN may contribute to the increased glomerular basement membrane thickness characteristic of the disease. 53 Furthermore, the upregulation of major histocompatibility complex molecules in both MCD and MN suggests that endothelial cells may activate antigen-experienced T-cells, implicating T-cell involvement in nephrotic syndrome. 54 , 55 Finally, the elevated interferon signature in MCD could help explain its characteristic steroid sensitivity. 56 There are several limitations in this study. First, glomerular cells comprised a relatively small proportion of total captured nuclei, reflecting the technical challenges of profiling human diagnostic biopsy tissue. Nevertheless, the absolute number of glomerular nuclei ( n = 13,475) was sufficient to identify multiple disease-associated cell states such as podocyte endocytosis. Second, the cohort is heterogeneous with limited samples per disease; however, the use of treatment-naïve diagnostic biopsies allowed us to capture early disease-associated transcriptional programs rarely accessible in human studies and was designed for shared rather than disease-specific classification. Third, our dataset mainly comprises transcriptomic information. Further enhancement by the inclusion of proteomic or epigenetic profiling could expand the insights related to pathophysiologic alterations in glomerular disease. 57 Lastly, control tissues were obtained from histologically normal cortex of nephrectomy specimens rather than healthy donor biopsies; subtle transcriptional alterations from tumor microenvironment effects cannot be fully excluded. To minimize these effects, control samples were collected by intraoperative biopsy-gun before renal artery clamping, mimicking native biopsy acquisition. Future validation with living donor or preimplantation biopsies may further confirm disease-associated programs. In conclusion, we report an extensive snRNA-seq dataset generated from rare and clinically valuable treatment-naïve human kidney biopsy tissues across MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. This dataset uniquely captures disease-relevant transcriptomic states of kidney-resident cells at the time of diagnosis, offering a snapshot that is difficult to obtain in other models or settings. Our findings provide novel insights into disease- and cell type-specific alterations in glomerular diseases. As a resource study, this work constitutes a foundational reference atlas that may support future investigations aiming to discover diagnostic markers, therapeutic targets, and mechanistic pathways in human kidney disease. Importantly, because the KORNERSTONE cohort is primarily composed of Korean patients, this dataset also expands the ethnic diversity of currently available kidney single-cell reference resources, which remain heavily weighted toward Western populations. title: Spatially interpretable artificial intelligence framework to tailored neoadjuvant dual HER2 blockade in HER2-positive breast cancer.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Spatially interpretable artificial intelligence framework to tailored neoadjuvant dual HER2 blockade in HER2-positive breast cancer. Neoadjuvant dual HER2 blockade with trastuzumab and pertuzumab plus chemotherapy represents the current standard-of-care for HER2-positive breast cancer. However, treatment responses remain heterogeneous, underscoring the lack of clinically practical tools for predicting treatment efficacy and informing personalized therapy. Here, we developed HER2-LADDER (Layered AI-based Dual-targeteD anti-HER2 Recommendation), a spatially interpretable and clinically accessible artificial intelligence framework that integrates clinicopathological and spatial topological features from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) slides. Using these spatially derived features, HER2-LADDER accurately predicted response to neoadjuvant TCbHP/PCbHP, achieving AUCs of 0.944 in the model construction cohort (N = 276), 0.917 in the temporal validation cohort (N = 82), and 0.869 in the trial-based validation cohort (N = 85). On the basis of HER2-LADDER scores, patients were stratified into Low (highly responsive), Medium (responsive), and High (resistant) groups, identifying candidates for treatment de-escalation (THP or TCbH/PCbH), standard-of-care (TCbHP/PCbHP), or alternative regimens (e.g., next-generation anti-HER2 antibody-drug conjugates), respectively. Importantly, Xenium in situ profiling further revealed biological correlates underlying model predictions, including HER2-enriched tumor cell aggregation and neutrophil-helper T-cell interactions, thereby highlighting the mechanistic interpretability of the model. Collectively, HER2-LADDER unites digital pathology and high-resolution spatial profiling into a clinically accessible AI framework, offering a robust, transparent, and biologically grounded tool to tailor individualized HER2-targeted therapy optimization.

evidence_text:
Explainable machine learning and multimodal single cell analysis link NR4A2 to CD8<sup>+</sup> T-cell terminal exhaustion and a CD8-adjusted prognostic signature in hepatocellular carcinoma.

Background

Terminal exhaustion of CD8+ tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes constrains the benefit of immune-checkpoint blockade in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The orphan nuclear receptor NR4A2 (Nurr1) belongs to a transcription-factor family implicated in murine T-cell exhaustion, yet its behaviour in the human HCC microenvironment has not been characterised across data modalities. We asked whether NR4A2 is specifically coupled to the terminal-exhaustion programme of human HCC CD8+ T cells, and whether that coupling is reflected in chromatin, tissue topography and bulk-tumour outcome data.

Methods

We reanalysed publicly available human HCC datasets spanning four modalities: single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; GSE149614, GSE98638, GSE151530, GSE125449), single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq; GSE227265), imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (10× Xenium human liver-cancer section) and bulk RNA sequencing with overall-survival annotation (TCGA-LIHC). NR4A2 was profiled across cell compartments and, at higher resolution, across CD8+ T-cell states defined from curated exhaustion, progenitor, effector and naïve gene modules. We tested NR4A2-exhaustion coupling at single-cell and pseudobulk level, examined NR4A2 motif accessibility, traced NR4A2 along a diffusion-pseudotime exhaustion axis, evaluated spatial co-localisation of exhausted CD8+ T cells with tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), benchmarked machine-learning classifiers of the exhausted state, and compared the human NR4A2 co-expression direction with the published NR4A1/2-knockout phenotype. We additionally trained interpretable gradient-boosted-tree models with SHAP attribution to characterise the exhausted and NR4A2-high states, scored a NR4A2 co-expression regulon, related the programme to immunotherapy-relevant signatures, and modelled overall survival using a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score.

Results

NR4A2 was broadly expressed across HCC compartments and was highest in myeloid cells rather than being T-cell restricted; at whole-compartment and bulk-tumour resolution it was not a clean exhaustion marker. At the resolution of CD8+ T-cell states, however, NR4A2 was sharply enriched in terminally exhausted cells (mean 3.62 versus 1.05; Mann-Whitney p ≈ 3.4 × 10-83) and correlated with the exhaustion module (single-cell Spearman ρ = 0.45) but not with the effector module (ρ = 0.06), arguing that NR4A2 is not a generic activation gene. NR4A2 expression increased monotonically along a diffusion-pseudotime axis toward terminal exhaustion (ρ = 0.37). In Xenium tissue, exhausted CD8+ T cells were modestly but significantly enriched in the neighbourhood of TAMs relative to other CD8+ T cells (permutation p = 0.005). The human NR4A2 co-expression direction was 83% concordant with the published NR4A1/2-knockout differential-expression direction. In bulk TCGA-LIHC, NR4A2 was lower in tumour than adjacent liver and only weakly exhaustion-correlated, consistent with hepatocyte-dominated bulk signal and reinforcing the need for compartment-resolved analysis. Interpretable machine learning attributed NR4A2-high status to an immediate-early/AP-1 activation programme, a NR4A2 co-expression regulon was selectively active in exhausted cells, and the programme tracked the T-cell-inflamed phenotype (ρ = 0.87); although raw bulk NR4A2 was non-prognostic, a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score independently predicted shorter overall survival (hazard ratio 1.42 per standard deviation, p < 0.001).

Conclusions

A NR4A2 co-expression regulon was most active in exhausted cells; explainable modelling linked NR4A2-high status to an immediate-early/AP-1 activation programme; the programme marked immune-hot tumours; and although bulk NR4A2 was non-prognostic, a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score was independently associated with worse overall survival (HR 1.42 per SD, p < 0.001). Across four independent data modalities, NR4A2 behaves as a resolution-dependent marker of the terminal-exhaustion programme in HCC CD8+ T cells that is spatially associated with the myeloid niche. The convergence supports NR4A2 as a candidate component of an HCC exhaustion signature and a hypothesis-generating target for functional study, while underscoring that its association is masked in bulk and whole-compartment data.

title: Spatial multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomics uncover senescence-associated cellular programs during colon adenoma to cancer progression
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text:
Spatial multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomics uncover senescence-associated cellular programs during colon adenoma to cancer progression Colorectal cancer develops through a normal-adenoma-carcinoma sequence, yet only 5-10% of adenomas progress to malignancy, and the cellular programs governing that sequence remain poorly defined. Here we generate a spatial multi-omics atlas of human colon adenomas, combining Visium CytAssist and protein co-detection across 24 nonadvanced and advanced tubular adenomas with single-cell resolution Xenium Prime 5K profiling of 101 patient-matched normal, adenoma, and carcinoma cores from 16 patients. Integrating whole-transcriptome and 31-plex protein data identifies nine spatial clusters and two dysplastic epithelial populations that co-express stemness, proliferation, and senescence programs. These programs occupy a shared, spatially confined epithelial niche that expands from adenoma to carcinoma. Spatial analysis revealed GDF15, a senescence-associated secretory factor, mediated the coupling between senescence and stemness in advanced adenomas, and that GDF15-high epithelium locally excludes CD8+ T cells in adenoma and, more broadly, in carcinoma. These findings position senescence as a spatially instructive rather than merely tumor-suppressive program during colorectal carcinogenesis and suggest GDF15 might be a potential candidate target for cancer prevention and interception in the colon.

Statement of Significance

Spatial multi-omics identifies spatially co-localized senescence and stemness programs in dysplastic epithelium during colorectal tumorigenesis and links GDF15-associated niches to CD8-positive T-cell exclusion, nominating GDF15 for colorectal cancer prevention and interception strategies.

title: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer. Cellular senescence, a stress-induced program causing stable cell-cycle arrest, is a hallmark of liver aging, fibrosis, and cancer. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms, spatial organization, and cancer-associated alterations in the liver remain unclear. We profiled 43 normal human livers spanning ages and fibrosis stages using a single-cell multiome, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX, complemented by fibrotic mouse models and 24 colorectal cancer liver metastases. We found CDKN1A+ senescent hepatocytes, fibroblasts, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells associated with age, liver disease, or cancer. Senescence differed between aged and fibrotic livers, with similar patterns in mice. Spatially, CDKN1A+ hepatocytes localized periportally, while SERPINE1+ aging-associated hepatocytes formed spatial clusters, potentially mediated by Claudins and THBS1. Fibrotic regions contained CXCL12+ senescent fibroblasts interacting with CXCR4+ immune cells. Chemotherapy intensified senescence in hepatocytes by 5-fold relative to aging and led to unique CDKN2A+ populations. Across conditions, senescent cells shared AP-1 activation, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and apoptosis resistance, suggesting therapeutic opportunities.

title: Learning Discrete Cell and Niche Codes from Spatial Transcriptomics Using Dual Residual Vector Quantization
xenium_reason: Xenium is mentioned without evidence of dataset generation or reuse
evidence_text: Learning Discrete Cell and Niche Codes from Spatial Transcriptomics Using Dual Residual Vector Quantization Spatially-resolved transcriptomics (SRT) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution while preserving each cell’s spatial location, enabling the joint study of  cell identity and cellular  niche , the recurring microenvironment that organises tissue function. Existing representation-learning methods typically capture only one of these axes at a time. We present SQUINT, a graph vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) that learns  two disjoint codebooks per cell from a shared architecture: a  cell codebook quantising the per-cell embedding before neighbourhood aggregation, biased toward cell-intrinsic identity, and a  niche codebook quantising the embedding after graph neural network (GNN) aggregation, biased toward spatial context. Both use residual vector quantization, giving a coarse-to-fine discrete-token hierarchy. SQUINT is trained with per-branch negative-binomial reconstruction objectives and three domain-motivated components that we show are crucial: a within-section cosine adjacency loss that anchors the niche codes in the spatial graph, a cross-section contrastive loss on the cell latents that aligns transcriptomically matched cells, and a decoder section covariate that absorbs batch effects. Across three datasets spanning four spatial assays (STARmap, MERFISH, CosMx, Xenium) and four tasks – niche identification, cell-type identification, cross-section integration, and spatial gene-expression imputation in held-out regions – SQUINT outperforms or is competitive with strong baselines on identification and achieves the most faithful cross-section integration. The resulting discrete vocabulary makes tissues directly consumable by transformer-style foundation models and enables one-step query-to-reference atlas mapping via code-distribution similarity, which we demonstrate on a CosMx human non-small-cell lung cancer cohort.

title: Deep spatial transcriptomic profiling of ovarian clear cell carcinoma in the real-world setting.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Deep spatial transcriptomic profiling of ovarian clear cell carcinoma in the real-world setting. Ovarian clear cell carcinoma (OCCC) is a rare cancer type of significant relevance to East Asian women harboring critical unmet needs for novel therapeutic options. It is a histological subtype of ovarian cancer with distinct pathological features, molecular profiles, and biological functions. Diverse heterogeneity contributing from histopathological and multiomic molecular features has yet to be translated to guide clinical care. Here, we presented a proof-of-concept study to demonstrate the feasibility of applying deep spatial transcriptomic (ST) profiling of tumor samples from an advanced OCCC patient in the real-world setting, aiming to identify therapeutic options beyond standard-of-care. Matched primary ovarian and metastatic bladder tumor sections were profiled by using GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiling and Xenium In Situ platforms. The spatial architecture and neighborhood niches were identified from GeoMx Cancer Transcriptome Atlas (CTA) and Xenium 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel. An immunosuppressive Wnt-activating tumor microenvironment (TME) was identified by GeoMx while a tripartite spatial relationship between SLC2A1+ hypoxic cancer cells, IFIT2+ inflammatory cancer cells, and MMP12+ dendritic cells linking towards metabolism and immune responses was identified by Xenium. Our deep ST profiling findings provided significant biological insights and demonstrated feasibility to make novel discoveries, one patient at a time.

title: FineST: contrastive learning integrates histology and spatial transcriptomics for nuclei-resolved ligand-receptor analysis.
xenium_reason: Xenium is mentioned without evidence of dataset generation or reuse
evidence_text: FineST: contrastive learning integrates histology and spatial transcriptomics for nuclei-resolved ligand-receptor analysis. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing cell-cell communication (CCC) across various biological processes, ranging from embryonic development to cancer progression. However, its limited resolution and high data sparsity hinder the detailed characterization of CCC patterns within complex tissues. Here, we introduce FineST, a deep contrastive learning model that leverages a histology foundation model to fuse ST and histology images, enabling Fine-grained Spatial Transcriptomics analysis. This approach facilitates precise nuclei segmentation, high-resolution RNA expression imputation, and the identification of intricate ligand-receptor interactions. Using both colorectal cancer VisiumHD and breast cancer Xenium datasets, we demonstrate that FineST significantly outperforms existing methods in high-resolution RNA imputation, cell type prediction, and CCC pattern discovery. With focused application to the Visium platform, FineST reveals novel biological insights into tumor-immune interactions across multiple cancer types, including invasive fronts in breast cancer, tertiary lymphoid structures in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and PD-1 therapy resistance barriers in hepatocellular carcinoma. These findings highlight a new paradigm in ST analysis through the integration of readily available histology images.

title: SpNeigh: spatial neighborhood and differential expression analysis for high-resolution spatial transcriptomics.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: SpNeigh: spatial neighborhood and differential expression analysis for high-resolution spatial transcriptomics. Spatial transcriptomics technologies such as Xenium, MERFISH, and Visium HD enable high-resolution profiling of gene expression while preserving tissue architecture. However, most computational methods for spatial analysis do not explicitly model local tissue context, such as boundaries, neighborhoods, or gradients. Here, we present SpNeigh (https://github.com/jinming-cheng/SpNeigh/), an R package for spatial neighborhood analysis and spatially aware differential expression modeling. SpNeigh includes tools for boundary detection, spatial neighborhood extraction, distance-based weighting, and gradient-based statistical testing. It supports both region-based differential expression and smooth spatial modeling using spline-based regression, along with a spatial enrichment index that identifies genes enriched near defined spatial features. We demonstrate the utility of SpNeigh across multiple platforms and tissues, including mouse brain, human breast cancer, and human liver, revealing intermediate populations at tissue interfaces, immune microenvironment differences, and spatially zonated gene expression patterns. SpNeigh offers a flexible and interpretable framework for dissecting spatial gene expression dynamics in complex tissues.

title: MGCL-ST: multi-view graph contrastive learning for spatial transcriptomics imputation.

evidence_text: MGCL-ST: multi-view graph contrastive learning for spatial transcriptomics imputation. High-resolution, continuous spatial gene expression profiling is critical for dissecting complex tissue microenvironments, yet current spatial transcriptomics (ST) platforms suffer from spatial gaps and insufficient resolution. Here, we present MGCL-ST, a multi-view graph contrastive learning method for super-resolution ST imputation. By jointly modeling local and global spatial graphs with histological features derived from a pathology foundation model, MGCL-ST accurately imputes unmeasured gene expression across the tissue space. Evaluated across three diverse platforms, MGCL-ST outperforms state-of-the-art methods in imputation accuracy and spatial clustering, significantly enhancing biological interpretability and enabling the precise mapping of tumor microenvironments. MGCL-ST is available at https://github.com/guxin2002/MGCL-ST .

evidence_text:
Identification of high-risk cells in single-cell spatially resolved transcriptomics data using Diagnostic Evidence GAuge of Single-cells with spatial smoothing.

Summary

The examination of high-risk cells and regions in tissue samples from spatially resolved transcriptomics platforms offers meaningful insights into specific disease processes. For existing methods, while cell types or clusters can be identified and associated with disease attributes, individual cells are unable to be associated in the same manner.

Method

Diagnostic Evidence Gauge of Single-Cells and Spatial Transcriptomics (DEGAS) solves the above problem by employing latent representations of gene expression data and domain adaptation to transfer disease attributes from patients to individual cells from single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. In this research, we present and evaluate DEGAS's versatility in adapting to data arising from various single-cell spatially resolved transcriptomics (scSRT) platforms. DEGAS successfully identified high-risk cells and regions in liver hepatocellular carcinoma and skin cutaneous melanoma, which were validated through known markers. Additionally, DEGAS was applied to our newly generated Type II Diabetes Xenium dataset, revealing high-risk cells within the tissue samples.

Availability and implementation

The DEGAS software can be accessed at https://github.com/tsteelejohnson91/DEGAS. For the updated smoothing functions and associated codes, visit https://github.com/dchatter04/DEGAS-Spatial-Smoothing, which is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18510221. Sources for the datasets reviewed are detailed in their respective sections. A description of some datasets, along with extra tables and figures, is provided in the Supplementary Materials file. Our newly generated Xenium data for Type II Diabetes can be found at https://doi.org/10.7303/syn68699752.

title: Halo: a pretrained model for whole-cell segmentation from nuclei images in spatial transcriptomics.
xenium_reason: Xenium is mentioned without evidence of dataset generation or reuse
evidence_text: Halo: a pretrained model for whole-cell segmentation from nuclei images in spatial transcriptomics. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables measurement of gene expression while preserving spatial organization within tissues. Accurate reconstruction of single-cell transcriptomes requires precise whole-cell segmentation, yet many ST experiments provide only nuclear staining images, making reliable inference of cell boundaries difficult. Here we introduce Halo, a pretrained segmentation model that reconstructs whole-cell boundaries by integrating nuclear morphology with the spatial distribution of RNA transcripts. Halo converts transcript coordinates into molecular density maps that are processed jointly with DAPI images using a Cellpose-SAM segmentation architecture. Halo is pretrained on multimodal Xenium data from 12 tissue types and can be directly applied to new datasets without additional training, providing a ready-to-use alternative to supervised approaches that require dataset-specific fitting. Across diverse tissues, Halo achieves substantially higher agreement with the 10$\times$ multimodal reference segmentation than existing methods, in terms of both cell boundaries and RNA-to-cell assignments, while requiring only DAPI staining and transcript spatial information. Improved segmentation leads to more reliable cell-type identification and more accurate estimation of cell morphological features. By providing a pretrained, generalizable model for whole-cell reconstruction, Halo enables scalable and reproducible cell segmentation for image-based ST.

title: Evidence of off-target probe binding affecting 10x Genomics Xenium gene panels compromise accuracy of spatial transcriptomic profiling.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Evidence of off-target probe binding affecting 10x Genomics Xenium gene panels compromise accuracy of spatial transcriptomic profiling. The accuracy of spatial gene expression profiles generated by probe-based in situ spatially resolved transcriptomic technologies depends on the specificity with which probes bind to their intended target gene. Off-target binding, defined as a probe binding to something other than the target gene, can distort a gene's true expression profile, making probe specificity essential for reliable transcriptomics. Here, we investigated off-target binding affecting the 10x Genomics Xenium technology. We developed a software tool, Off-target Probe Tracker (OPT), to identify putative off-target binding via alignment of probe target sequences and assessing whether mapped loci corresponded to the intended target gene across multiple reference annotations. Applying OPT to a Xenium human breast gene panel, we identified at least 14 out of the 313 genes in the panel potentially impacted by off-target binding to protein-coding genes. To substantiate our predictions, we leveraged a Xenium breast cancer dataset generated using this gene panel and compared results to orthogonal spatial and single-cell transcriptomic profiles from Visium CytAssist and 3' single-cell RNA-seq derived from the same tumor block. Our findings indicate that for some genes, the expression patterns detected by Xenium demonstrably reflect the aggregate expression of the target and predicted off-target genes based on Visium and single-cell RNA-seq, rather than the target gene alone. We further applied OPT to identify potential off-target binding in custom gene panels and integrate tissue-specific RNA-seq data to assess effects. Overall, this work enhances the biological interpretability of spatial transcriptomics data and improves reproducibility in spatial transcriptomics research.

evidence_text:
Spatial Transcriptomics and Mechanisms of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Associated Interstitial Nephritis.

Introduction

Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated acute interstitial nephritis (ICI-AIN) is the most common finding on histopathology among patients with ICI-associated acute kidney injury (ICI-AKI). Patients with ICI-AIN often have T cell-dominant infiltration of the kidney and high tissue levels of CXCR3 ligands such as CXCL9, 10, and 11; however, the mechanisms of inflammation in ICI-AIN are not well-understood.

Methods

We applied a subcellular spatial transcriptomics platform (Xenium Prime 5K) to compare the cellular composition of kidney biopsy tissue from patients with ICI-AIN with ICI-treated patients with acute tubular necrosis (ICI-ATN).

Results

Across 8 kidney biopsy specimens (4 with ICI-AIN, 4 with ICI-ATN), we analyzed 332,000 cells, comprising kidney parenchymal cells and infiltrating immune cells. Using a spatially aware cellular neighborhood-based classification, we identified cellular niches corresponding to each part of the nephron, in addition to unique fibrotic and inflammatory niches. Gene pathway analysis identified interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and/or signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) signaling as strongly increased in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN. Although all inflammatory niches were overrepresented in ICI-AIN, CD8+ T cell infiltration, and proinflammatory myeloid cells were the dominant immune niches. Spatial niche crosstalk analysis revealed that CD8+ T cell-derived IFN-γ likely induced a proinflammatory program in myeloid cells, with increased production of CXCL9, 10, and 11. Furthermore, IFN-γ signaling in ICI-AIN was associated with reduced oxidative phosphorylation in kidney tubular niches.

Conclusion

Spatial transcriptomics thus revealed novel insights into key differences in the pathophysiology of ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN, with IFN-γ-producing CD8+ T cells as potential drivers of ICI-AIN. These drugs, which are now approved to treat > 20 cancer types, have dramatically improved outcomes for a number of malignancies. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 AKI is common in the setting of ICIs, with real-world studies showing that 15% to 25% of patients treated with ICIs develop AKI. 5 Although AIN is the most common histopathologic lesion seen in ICI-AKI, 6 , 7 AKI can also occur because of non-ICI-related causes, including ATN. Distinguishing ICI-AIN from ICI-ATN is challenging without a kidney biopsy, because there are no clinical features specific to ICI-AIN. 6 Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying ICI-AIN are not well understood. Recent studies have shown that proinflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis factor, IFN-γ, and IFN-γ-induced chemokines such as CXCL 9, 10, and 11 are elevated in ICI-AIN but not in patients treated with ICI with AKI from other causes. 8 , 9 , 10 Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of tissue from patients with ICI-colitis 11 and myocarditis 12 have each identified an immune cell infiltration dominated by T cells and inflammatory myeloid cells, in addition to organ-specific differences, such as interleukin-17A-producing T cells in ICI-colitis. In contrast to ICI-colitis and ICI-myocarditis, our understanding of the immune cell infiltrate, cellular interactions, and damage pathways in ICI-AIN is limited. Given the expanding indications for ICIs, the burden of disease of ICI-AIN is expected to increase. 13 , 14 New insights into underlying mechanisms are urgently needed to improve the identification of at-risk patients, enable noninvasive diagnosis of ICI-AIN, and identify new therapeutic targets without inhibiting the antitumor response. Here, we utilized Xenium Prime 5K (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA), a novel spatial transcriptomics technology, to compare and contrast the cellular composition of kidney biopsy specimens from patients with ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN. Methods Patient Selection and Tissue Collection We identified adult patients (≥ 18 years old) at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and/or Dana-Farber Cancer Institute who had received at least 1 dose of ICI therapy within 180 days before development of AKI (defined as a ≥ 1.5-fold rise in serum creatinine from pre-ICI baseline) 15 and who had a kidney biopsy performed for clinical purposes between 2021 and 2024. A total of 8 archival formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded kidney biopsies were obtained (4 with moderate-to-severe AIN and 4 with ATN, as adjudicated by 2 renal pathologists at Brigham and Women’s Hospital). All patients had consented to blood and urine collection, as well as archival tissue collection. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of archival tissue was conducted under institutional review board approved protocol (#2023P000393). Additionally, all patients had available urine proteomics data (Olink Target 96 Immuno-Oncology Panel and Olink Target 96 inflammation, with 140 unique proteins; Olink Proteomics, Uppsala, Sweden), as previously described. 8 This study was approved by the Brigham and Women’s Hospital and/or Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (21-685) and Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Boards (#2021P00044 and #2023P000393). Xenium Slide Preparation Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks of kidney biopsies were sliced onto Xenium slides according to the “Xenium In Situ for Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded-Tissue Preparation Guide” ( CG000578 Rev C, 10x Genomics) 16 protocol. The Xenium slides were then prepared following the “Xenium In Situ for Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded-Deparaffinization and Decrosslinking” protocol ( CG000580 Rev D, 10x Genomics). In brief, the slides were incubated at 60 °C for 30 minutes and then sequentially immersed in xylene, ethanol, and nuclease-free water to deparaffinize and rehydrate the tissue. The Xenium slides were then immediately incubated in the decrosslinking and permeabilization solution at 80 °C for 30 minutes, followed by a wash with phosphate-buffered saline. The Xenium slides were then processed according to the “Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression” user guide ( CG000760 Rev A, 10x Genomics) for the remaining slide preparation steps. The samples were hybridized with probes from Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue & Pathways Panel (PN-1000671, 10x Genomics) at 50 °C for 18 hours. After hybridization, the slides were washed and incubated with a ligation reaction mix, followed by another wash step and DNA amplification. Cell segmentation staining was then performed, and the slides were treated with an autofluorescence quencher and , 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole before loading into the Xenium instrument. Xenium Analyzer Setup and Data Acquisition Processed Xenium slides were loaded in the Xenium analyzer and imaged, following the guidelines in the “Xenium Analyzer User Guide ( CG000584 Rev F, 10x Genomics).” After scanning, the Xenium slides were removed from the Xenium analyzer and processed with post-run hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining according to the “Xenium In Situ Gene Expression-Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining” protocol ( CG000613 Rev A, 10x Genomics). Xenium Data Analysis We performed both image-based segmentation using CellPose 17 and transcripts-based cell segmentation using Baysor (v0.7.1) 18 with the previous cell labels from the multimodal staining information. Then, we integrated the Xenium data with single cell RNA-seq reference atlas through Harmony and projected the labels using nearest neighbors, which are further curated with licensed nephrologists. Spatial domain clustering analyses were performed using the natural boundaries-based method, Tessera. 19 Niches were further identified using the de novo clustering analysis and manual curation, and further validated with the approximate positions of tissues on the H&E imaging. Downstream data analysis is described in more detail in the Supplementary Methods . Using Olink Data to Refine Transcriptomics Analyses Using Olink data, we focused on proteins that we had previously shown to be differentially abundant in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN. 8 , 20 For proteins that were included in both the Inflammation and Immuno-Oncology panel, we used the results from the Inflammation panel. We performed pseudo-bulk aggregation of the transcripts per kidney biopsy by the AggregateExpression function in Seurat (v5.3.0) 21 and normalized expression levels to the biopsy area. Results Study Design and Cohort Description We analyzed kidney biopsies of 4 patients with ICI-AIN and 4 with ICI-ATN using the Xenium Prime 5K (10x Genomics) spatial transcriptomics assay to measure in situ expression of 5001 genes ( Figure 1 a). Patients with ICI-ATN were chosen as the comparator, because they share potential confounders (malignant disease, cancer treatment, and unspecific kidney tissue changes caused by AKI); in the ICI-ATN cases, treatment with ICIs was not judged to be the cause of the AKI and often an alternative etiology was identified. Baseline demographics and characteristics of the AKI event are shown in Supplementary Table S1 . Additional information on the kidney biopsy characteristics can be found in Supplementary Table S2 . The time between AKI onset and kidney biopsy ranged from 2 to 18 days (median 7.5 days); all biopsies showed mild-moderate signs of irreversible damage and fibrosis (interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy range 10–40%). (b) Marker heatmap for the major cell types in spatial transcriptomic data. Rows show the cell types, columns show top selected markers, the size. (c) UMAP of spatial transcriptomic cells with cell type annotation in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, the size of the circle indicates the proportion of cells expressing the marker, the color indicates the average expression scale. (d) Differential abundance of cellular composition measured by ratio over all cells for both groups. (e) Cell type ratio in all patients of ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, with corresponding color legend below. Immune Cells in ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN After cell segmentation and quality control ( Supplementary Figure S1 ), followed by label transfer and manual curation strategy, we identified a total of 332,341 cells (79% kept cells after quality control of resegmentation) with 21,251 to 66,751 cells per patient sample ( Supplementary Figure S1 ). Using curated cell types from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project atlas as a reference, we took 4875 overlapping high-quality genes between Xenium and Kidney Precision Medicine Project single-cell RNA-sequencing and jointly clustered the cells to define 24 major cell types. These cell types comprised both kidney parenchymal cells and immune cells across all 8 patient samples, expressing known biomarkers. The alignment performed well at the major lineage level ( Figure 1 b–c, Supplementary Figure S1 ), as we observed high correlation of gene expression fold changes between the Kidney Precision Medicine Project atlas and our Xenium datasets ( Supplementary Figure S2–3 ), although the cell segmentation of cell types with complex, nonspheroidal geometries also led to spillover of transcripts into neighboring cells (e.g., in glomerular cell types). Next, we applied covarying neighborhood analysis 22 to identify cell states strongly associated with ICI-AIN and found immune cells to be significantly expanded in ICI-AIN (global P -value 0.02, Figure 1 d). Compared with ICI-ATN, on average, ICI-AIN biopsies contained 27-fold more XBP high plasma cells in ICI-AIN, 8-fold more IL3RA + plasmacytoid dendritic cells, 7.9-fold more proliferating T cells, 7.6-fold more FOXP3 + CTLA4 + regulatory T cells (Tregs), and 3.6-fold more CXCL9 + CIITA + inflammatory myeloid cells ( Figure 1 e, Supplementary Figure S1 , false discovery rate < 0.05 for each). We also identified more kidney parenchymal cells in ICI-ATN, including SCNN1G+ collecting duct cells (2.2-fold higher), PODXL + podocytes (3.4-fold higher), KCNJ10 + distal convoluted tubular cells (2.3-fold higher), and CUBN + proximal tubular cells (2.1-fold higher), likely influenced by the variable sampling of kidney medulla during biopsies ( Supplementary Table S2 ). By mapping the cell types and individual detected marker transcripts in space, we were able to confirm the identified cell types in their spatial context, including high levels of CD19 and CD3E transcripts in a large lymphoid aggregate, PODXL transcripts in glomeruli, and CUBN in proximal tubular cells ( Figure 1 f–g). In summary, we were able to characterize the immune cell infiltrate in ICI-AIN using spatial transcriptomics and identified a high density of plasma cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and T cells, among others. Immune and Fibrosis Niches in ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN To dissect cellular neighborhoods in their spatial context, we identified cellular niches using the Tessera package. 19 Tessera is an automated tissue-agnostic tissue segmentation method that introduces novel concepts of spatial cellular neighborhoods, or “niches,” delineates the tissues by closed multipolygons that aggregate spatially coherent cells, and approaches that infer the tissues’ edge with natural tissue boundaries. Tessera enables reducing the sparsity of spatial transcriptomic data and circumvents potential problems associated with cell segmentation methods by aggregating cells, thereby increasing the number of relevant transcripts per unit and decreasing misattribution errors. Using Tessera to characterize cellular niches in these biopsies, our approach enables us to identify potentially novel cellular niches and biologically meaningful architectural units within the spatial transcriptomic data. In total, we aggregated cells to 22,690 niches. Based on the clustering of these niches based on transcriptional similarities, we defined 9 major spatial niches, including immune, vascular, and fibrotic niches, and 6 kidney tissue-related niches ( Figure 2 a–d). The kidney-related niches included all major parts of the nephron—for example, glomerular niches were marked by high expression of PODXL and WT1 . Similarly, we identified niches corresponding to the proximal tubule (with high expression of CUBN and LRP2 ), loop of Henle (marked by UMOD and CASR expression), distal convoluted tubule (marked by TRPM6 expression), and collecting duct (expressing SCNN1G and HSD11B2 and combining both intercalated and principal cells; Figure 2 d). Additionally, we identified niches associated with pathology; injured proximal tubular regions were marked by the expression of markers like HAVCR1 (encoding kidney injury molecule 1) and SOX9 in addition to the proximal tubule transcriptional signature, as has been extensively studied in the context of AKI. 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 Immune niches contained different immune cell subsets; generally, we identified high levels of IFN-γ-induced transcripts like SLAMF7 , CD38, and CXCL9 . Similarly, areas of fibrosis were marked by high expression of genes like PDGFRA and COL5A1 . The identity of the niches was confirmed by their cellular composition ( Figure 2 c), with the spatial expression of key marker genes following accurate niche distribution ( Figure 2 e–h). We then applied covarying neighborhood analysis to characterize the cellular niches that were significantly expanded in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN (global P -value 0.03). We observed an expansion of immune fibrotic niches, as well as niches containing loop of Henle transcriptional profile in ICI-AIN, whereas the remaining kidney-specific niches were decreased in ICI-AIN ( Figure 2 i). The injured proximal tubule niche was more highly represented in ICI-ATN samples as marked by VCAM1+ niches ( Figure 2 j). Using a niche-based approach, we were thus able to identify all major parts of the nephron in addition to immune cell and fibrotic niches. Immune Niche Subtyping Identifies Key Immunological Processes in ICI-AIN To better understand the immune cell infiltration in ICI-AIN, we performed unbiased subclustering of the immune niches ( Figure 3 a). We confirmed key features of the ICI-ATN and ICI-AIN histopathology in serial sections ( Supplementary Figure S4 ). Some niches corresponded to the microenvironment of specific immune cells, such as plasma cell niches with high levels of transcripts as FCRL5 and TNFRSF17 (encoding B-cell maturation antigen) or plasmacytoid dendritic cells (expressing LIL4RA , and IL3RA [encoding CD123]) ( Figure 3 b). The tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS)-like niches showed high expression of genes that are involved in the interaction of B and T cells, such as CD28 and ICOS , as well as their component cells. Other niches showed stronger transcriptional signals of the infiltrated kidney tissue or fibrotic processes in addition to an immune cell signature (termed “CD8 infiltrated kidney” and “inflammation with fibrosis”). We detected 2 separate types of myeloid cell niches, one with higher expression of proinflammatory genes (like CSF2RB and MMP9 ) that are often associated with monocyte-derived cells, which we termed “myeloid inflammation,” and another myeloid niche type with increased expression of transcripts associated with tissue-resident or regulatory myeloid cells (such as CD163 , MRC1 which encodes CD206, and F13A1 ). Notably, T cell-related transcripts such as CD3E and CD8A were detected in all immune niches to varying degrees, highlighting the role of T-cell infiltration as a general feature of ICI-AIN. Distinct Chemokine Axes Underlie Immune Niche Subtype Heterogeneity To better understand drivers of immune niche heterogeneity, we performed ligand-receptor analysis and observed greater overall ligand-receptor interaction strength across ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN ( Supplementary Figure S5 A and B). In both ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, CXCL12-CXCR4, and CXCL9-CXCR3 interactions were observed in all patients, although the latter pair had higher strengths of association in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN ( Supplementary Figure S5 C–F). CXCL12-CXCR4 was globally present in areas with myeloid inflammation, TLS, and plasma cells in ICI-AIN, whereas it was limited to a few niches in ICI-ATN. Investigating the different immune subniches, expression of CXCR3 ligands CXCL9, 10, and 11 was observed in all subniches, but most prominently in the “myeloid inflammation” niches. This was associated with massive expansion of CXCR3-expressing cells ( Figure 3 e–f, Supplementary Figure S5 G–J). The chemokine axes CCR7 and/or CCL19 and CXCR5 and/or CXCL13, both associated with B-T cell interaction and TLS, were most strongly detected in the TLS-like immune niches. CXCL12 was most strongly increased in plasma cell niches, as has previously been reported in bone marrow plasma cells. 27 Our analyses highlight the role of chemokines in the spatial organization of immune infiltrates in ICI-AIN, with CXCR3-CXCL9 interactions in areas of myeloid inflammation and CXCR5-CXCL13 interactions in TLS. Spatial Transcriptomics Builds on Findings from Urine Proteomics Building upon our previous urine proteomics analysis, 8 we compared paired aggregate gene expression and proteomic abundance of 5 differentially abundant proteins in ICI-AIN (CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, FASLG, GZMA) and 1 in ICI-ATN (epidermal growth factor; Supplementary Figure S6 ). 8 Mean aggregate transcript levels in ICI-AIN for these genes were changed in the same direction as the urinary protein abundance. Gene expression of CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, and GZMA each completely separated the groups, often showing better separation than urine protein levels. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Identifies Interferon-Driven Responses in ICI-AIN We next asked what signaling pathways contribute to the immune cell activation and tissue inflammation in ICI-AIN. Comparing differentially expressed genes within the niche types separately, IFN-γ-induced genes, such as STAT1 and CXCL9, showed the strongest expression in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN in most cellular niches ( Supplementary Figure S7 ). Gene set enrichment analysis of immune-related pathways in the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (RRID:SCR_012773) and Hallmark gene set collections similarly identified an increase in IFN-driven pathways (such as “Interferon gamma response”, “chemokine signaling”, “Janus Kinase-STAT”) in ICI-AIN ( Supplementary Figure S7 ). Especially within the tubular niches, including the injured proximal tubule, collecting duct and loop of Henle, we observed a strong reduction in the expression of genes related to oxidative phosphorylation in ICI-AIN. In summary, the IFN-γ response signature was the dominant transcriptional immune signature in ICI-AIN. Tissue-Resident CD8 + T Cells in ICI-AIN Produce IFN-γ and CXCL13 As we identified IFN-γ and/or STAT1 as the predominant signaling pathway and IFN-γ-induced genes as the top differentially expressed genes in ICI-AIN, we next investigated the cellular source of IFN-γ production. The greatest number of IFNG transcripts (75.1% of all IFNG transcripts identified in immune cells) were identified in CD8 + T cells as compared with other immune cell subsets, including CD4 + T cells ( Figure 4 a). Investigating differentially expressed genes within the CD8 + T cells, we found IFNG to be one of the top upregulated genes in ICI-AIN ( Figure 4 b). CXCL13 was also increased in CD8 + T cells, as were markers of repeated activation, such as PDCD1, LAG3, and CTLA4 in ICI-AIN CD8 + T cells. Although ICI-ATN CD8 + T cells expressed markers of short-lived effector T cells like KLRG1 and CX3CR1 , CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN showed higher levels of residency program markers like ZNF683 (encoding HOBIT), CXCR6, and ITGAE (encoding CD103). Additionally, CD8+ T cells from patients with ICI-AIN were enriched for IFN-induced genes like STAT1 , GBP1, and GBP5.
