As identified by gene set enrichment analysis, gene expression relating to oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in ICI-AIN samples, and tubular epithelial cells rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation because of their high energy demand. 28 Using the spatial niche data, we found this reduction localized mostly to the niches related to parts of the kidney tubule ( Figure 4 c). The gene module score for oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in the injured as compared with the noninjured proximal tubule niches. However, in both injured and healthy proximal tubule niches in AIN samples, there was an additive reduction in oxidative phosphorylation gene signatures in multivariable linear regression models ( Supplementary Figure S8 ). IFN-γ-signaling within the noninjured proximal tubule niches was strongly anticorrelated with a gene signature for oxidative phosphorylation ( Figure 4 d). Another hallmark effect of IFN-γ is the polarization of myeloid cells into a proinflammatory, tissue-aggressive state, as we observed in the “inflammatory myeloid” cluster ( Figure 3 a–b). 29 Within this cluster, we found the expression of genes typical for a proinflammatory myeloid polarization (such as MMP9 , IDO1 ), as well as the highest gene expression signature of an IFN-γ response ( Figure 4 e–f). In summary, CD8 + T cell-derived IFN-γ was associated with reduced oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells and a proinflammatory signature in inflammatory myeloid cells. Tissue-Resident Macrophage Niches Associate With Fibrosis Finally, we investigated which immune cell niches were associated with fibrosis in ICI-AIN. To this end, we calculated the probability of neighboring an area of fibrosis for each subtype of immune niche, normalized for the relative abundance of immune niches. The CD8+ infiltrated and tissue-resident myeloid cell niches in ICI-AIN were most likely to neighbor fibrotic niches compared with the ICI-ATN group ( Figure 4 g). Additionally, we defined a fibrotic niche transcriptional signature as the top 100 differentially expressed genes for the fibrosis niches and calculated a signature score for each immune subniche. Consistent with the neighborhood analysis, the tissue-resident myeloid niches had the highest fibrosis signature score ( Figure 4 h), highlighting their role in a fibrotic tissue response. Discussion Here, we have described the landscape of immune infiltration and fibrosis in the kidneys of patients with ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN. Using high-resolution spatial transcriptomic analysis, we elucidated key features of ICI-AIN, including a strong activation of IFN-γ/STAT1 signaling, a reduction in oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells, and a heterogeneous immune cell infiltration. Based on the Tessera algorithm 19 for the identification of niches with similar transcriptional profiles, we were able to identify biologically meaningful, functional units, thereby circumventing the problems associated with cell segmentation. Some niches corresponded to histoanatomical parts of the kidney, like the glomeruli or specific segments of the tubule, allowing us to compare the gene expression within specific kidney regions. Other niche types corresponded to pathological changes, including immune cell infiltration and fibrosis. Clustering-based analyses enabled us to investigate the heterogeneity of the immune cell infiltrate in detail, highlighting how TLS-like structures, myeloid cell-dominant inflammation, and fibrotic processes happen in parallel within the ICI-AIN-damaged kidney. Analyzing the spatial expression of chemokine and/or receptor pairs enabled us to understand the mechanisms that determine the architecture of these meta-structures. Our analyses found that CD8 + T cells are associated with the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN given the limited control of ICI-ATN ( Figure 5 ). T cell infiltration appeared to play a functional role in all the immune cell niches we identified, and T cell-related genes were among the most abundant in all niches. These T cells, expressing markers of repeated activation like PD1, CTLA4, and LAG3, seemed to coordinate the recruitment and activation of other immune cells by the expression of CXCL13 (attracting B and T cells and forming TLS-like structures) and IFN-γ (inducing an inflammatory myeloid phenotype). These inflammatory myeloid cells, in turn, may have induced tissue damage by producing metalloproteases like MMP9 and by recruiting additional CXCR3-expressing inflammatory cells producing CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11. Figure 5 Schematic of the inferred pathophysiology in ICI-AIN with a focus on the role of CD8 + T cells. CD8 + T cells with transcriptional markers of tissue-residency and repeated stimulation are the main producers of IFN-γ. IFN-γ reduces oxidative phosphorylation in kidney tubules and induces a proinflammatory program in myeloid cells. These proinflammatory myeloid cells lead to tissue damage and also produce the chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11, attracting additional CXCR3 + lymphocytes, including additional CD8 + T cells. CD8 + T cells also produce CXCL13, a chemokine that attracts B cells and induces the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures in the kidney. Notably, CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN recapitulated features associated with T cells of the tumor microenvironment with transcriptional features of exhaustion and instigation of TLS structures by the production of CXCL13. 30 , 31 , 32 Plasma cells also showed increased abundance in the ICI-AIN samples, and we hypothesize that these indicate productive B-T cell interactions in these TLS-like structures. Plasma cells have also been identified in ICI-associated myocarditis; however, no antibodies against myocardial antigens were identified. 12 Although T cells in ICI-ATN samples showed a transcriptional signature typical of short-lived effector cells (expressing KLRG1 and CX3CR1 ), the CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN expressed more HOBIT ( ZNF683 ), CD103 ( ITGAE ), and CXCR6, markers of tissue-resident memory cells. 33 Interestingly, a CD8 + T cell subset with high expression of HOBIT was identified in the peripheral blood of a patient with kidney allograft rejection after ICI treatment. 34 A similar signature of ITGAE + tissue-resident T cells was recently reported in ICI-related colitis. 11 It is therefore plausible that CD8 + tissue-resident memory T cells, disinhibited by ICI treatment, are the primary cell type that initiates the inflammatory cascade observed in ICI-AIN. Our analyses also implicated niches with a high density of a tissue-resident transcription profile in the development of kidney fibrosis. This is consistent with recent reports highlighting the role of a similar population in fibrotic damage in lupus nephritis. 35 , 36 Although we reported the spatial association of these niches with fibrotic area, future research is needed to determine if these cells mediate fibrosis or protect against further damage. The immunological changes we observed may inform the selection of novel treatment targets in ICI-AIN. Currently, ICI-AIN is treated by holding or discontinuing ICIs and administering glucocorticoids, which may compromise anti-tumor immune response. 37 , 38 Drugs targeting IFN-γ and its receptors, and especially drugs such as baricitinib and ruxolitinib—which target the downstream signaling of Janus Kinase and/or STAT—may thus have greater utility in treating ICI-AIN. To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive spatial data of ICI-AKI to date; however, there were limitations. Alignment of kidney structures with spatial transcriptomic areas was poor, and high-resolution images of H&E stainings were performed on serial sections. Furthermore, kidney biopsies from patients with ICI-AIN show great heterogeneity, and the small number of samples analyzed, along with the lack of inclusion of “healthy” controls, may have limited our ability to explore key differences. Notably, medullary cell types and niches were overrepresented in the ICI-AIN samples because of higher representation of kidney medulla in ICI-AIN samples. However, we chose the ICI-ATN group as controls as they share important confounding features with the ICI-AIN group (malignant disease, cancer treatment, and unspecific kidney tissue changes caused by AKI). Additionally, the commercial Xenium 5K panel may have limited utility in providing insight into cell types within the nephron. Methods for cellular segmentation in spatial transcriptomic and proteomic analyses are still an area of active investigation; thus, transcripts of neighboring cells may spill over and dilute marker gene identification, especially in areas with challenging cell morphologies, such as the glomerulus. Current spatial transcriptomic approaches result in relatively sparse data, which can lead to biases. For example, the emphasis on CD8 + T cells in our data could, at least in part, be explained by the higher transcript density of CD8A compared with CD4 . Although we used a niche-based approach to mitigate these limitations, orthogonal approaches like single-cell transcriptomics in ICI-AIN will be needed to phenotype infiltrating immune cells at higher resolution. In summary, we used spatial transcriptomics to show that IFN-γ-producing CD8 + T cells may be implicated in the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN, and that CD8 + T cell-derived IFN-γ likely induces a proinflammatory state in myeloid cells, with increased tissue production of CXCL9, 10, and 11. Future studies with a larger number of samples will be needed to validate our findings and investigate the association of specific immune niche subsets with disease severity and/or refractoriness, treatment response, and likelihood of kidney recovery. evidence_text: Iron-catalyzed oxidative stress reveals an exposome-related ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche in BRCA1-linked renal carcinogenesis. Early cancer initiation under chronic oxidative stress requires the survival of epithelial cells that should otherwise be eliminated by regulated cell death. However, the spatial and morphological identity of such stress-adapted cells remains poorly defined. Here, we integrated Xenium single-cell spatial transcriptomics, quantitative nuclear morphometrics, mitochondrial analyses, and human cancer datasets to investigate iron-driven renal carcinogenesis in Brca1(L63X/+) rats. Ferric nitrilotriacetate exposure induced dynamic remodeling of proximal tubular epithelium, characterized by loss of homeostatic transport and mitochondrial programs, and activation of Myc, Met, Lcn2, Anxa2 and iron-handling genes. BRCA1 haploinsufficiency expanded a karyomegalic proximal tubular state associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, chromatin hyperchromasia, nuclear remodeling, and ferroptosis-resistant transcriptional features. Subclassification of karyomegalic cells identified distinct stress-adaptive populations, including a BRCA1-associated K2 state enriched for Myc/Met/Lcn2 signaling and preferentially embedded within a pro-oncogenic epithelial-stromal microenvironment. Of note, neighboring non-karyomegalic proximal tubular cells acquired related iron-handling and survival-biased programs, indicating that karyomegaly marks a broader pre-neoplastic field rather than an isolated abnormality. Human TCGA renal cancer analyses and morphometric assessment of BRCA1-mutant breast tissue further supported the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated gene modules and nuclear remodeling. These findings define a spatially organized, ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche as an early lesion in iron-driven carcinogenesis and establish quantitative nuclear morphology as a functional readout of exposome-related oxidative stress adaptation in genetically susceptible tissues. mutant) rat     n.s.   not significant     NSD   nuclear substructure density     OA_PT    oxidative stress–adaptive  proximal tubule     OCR   oxygen-consumption rate     PCA   principal component analysis     PFI   progression-free interval     PII   peripheral intensity index     PT   proximal tubule (tubular cell[s])     RCA   rolling circle amplification     RCC   renal cell carcinoma     REF   rat embryonic fibroblast     ROI   region of interest     ssGSEA   single-sample gene set enrichment analysis     ST   stromal cell(s)     STN   solid tissue normal (non-tumorous portion)     TA   tissue array     TCGA   The Cancer Genome Atlas     TEM   transmission electron microscopy     TR_PT    transient regenerative  proximal tubule     UMAP   uniform manifold approximation and projection     WSI   whole slide image (imaging)     WT   wild-type       1  Introduction  Iron is essential for life [ 1 ], yet its redox activity also drives oxidative reactions that promote mutagenesis and malignant transformation [ 2 , 3 ]. Although persistent oxidative stress is increasingly recognized as a trigger of tumor initiation, how damaged epithelial cells survive this hostile redox environment and acquire tumor-initiating potential remains poorly understood. We previously established a ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) model of Fenton reaction–driven carcinogenesis that reproducibly induces metastatic renal adenocarcinomas and enables mechanistic analysis of oxidative stress–mediated tumorigenesis [ [4] ,  [5] ,  [6] ]. However, the spatially organized molecular programs that allow a subset of injured epithelial cells to evade elimination and persist as pre-neoplastic precursors have not been defined.  Hereditary cancers account for 5–10% of human malignancies [ 7 , 8 ]. Among hereditary cancer genes,  BRCA1  and  BRCA2  are best known for their association with breast and ovarian cancers [ 9 ], but growing evidence suggests broader roles in epithelial cancer susceptibility, including renal cell carcinoma [ 10 , 11 ]. We recently established Brca1/2 haploinsufficient rat models that recapitulate key aspects of human disease [ [12] ,  [13] ,  [14] ]. Notably, Fe-NTA–induced carcinogenesis is markedly accelerated in Brca1 haploinsufficient rats and accompanied by recurrent  c-Myc  amplification and mitochondrial abnormalities during early tumorigenesis [ 15 , 16 ]. These findings raise the possibility that BRCA1 deficiency promotes the emergence of stress-adaptive epithelial states that evade ferroptotic elimination during tumor initiation.  Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics enable single-cell–resolution molecular profiling while preserving tissue architecture and histological context [ 17 ]. Here, we integrated Xenium-based spatial transcriptomics with quantitative digital nuclear morphometrics to investigate early carcinogenic processes under iron-driven oxidative stress. This approach identified a previously unrecognized ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic epithelial population associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oncogenic signaling, and iron-handling programs. Integration with human cancer datasets further suggested that related stress-adaptive programs and nuclear abnormalities may be relevant to human epithelial tumorigenesis. Together, our findings establish a spatial and morphological framework for understanding how exposome-related [ 18 ] oxidative stress intersects with hereditary susceptibility during the earliest stages of tumor initiation.    2  Materials and methods   2.1  Renal carcinogenesis model by ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA)  All the animal experiments were approved by the animal experimental committee of Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine.  Sprague-Dawley  strain male rats of wild-type (WT) and  Brca1(L63X/+ ; mutant, MUT) [ 12 ] were bred as described previously [ 15 ]. Representative kidney specimens of 1 and 3 weeks under the carcinogenesis protocol were obtained and fixed either in phosphate-buffered 10% formalin for 48 h for paraffin-embedding, or 2 % glutaraldehyde in 1 mM phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for resin-embedding.    2.2  Tissue array construction  Six formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) rat kidney samples were organized into a tissue array (TA) format to enable simultaneous Xenium processing (three samples per slide; two slides per instrument run). RNA quality was pre-verified by RNAScope in situ on the sections from all the donor blocks. After confirmation, sample area was selected and manually extracted to re-form new TA blocks with samples coring within proper size of area (∼12 mm × 24 mm). From each TA block, 5 μm sections were cut with a rotary microtome (Leica RM2135) and mounted onto  Xenium  adhesive slides (10x Genomics). Sections were dried overnight, then stored in a desiccator until processing. All cutting and mounting steps were performed with precautions to maintain tissue morphology and RNA integrity (sterile, RNase-free tools and surfaces).    2.3  Gene panel design  A custom 50-gene  Xenium In Situ  probe panel (ID:  TCMFHM ) was designed for  Rattus norvegicus  using the 10x Genomics Custom Panel Designer ( Table S1 ). Target genes were selected to represent major renal cell types and key kidney injury pathways, prioritizing established marker genes for nephron segments (proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct principal/intercalated cells), glomerular cell types (podocytes, endothelial), interstitial cells (stromal cells), immune infiltrates (inflammatory cells), and urothelium, alongside transcripts implicated in our previous differential expression array analyses [ 15 , 19 , 20 ]. Gene selection was further guided by a published rat kidney single-cell transcriptomic atlas (E-GEAD-450 [ 21 ]), retaining only genes with robust, cell type-specific expression in the reference dataset. The final panel included renal biomarkers and ferroptosis-, oncogenic/tumor suppressor-, mitochondria-associated genes relevant to renal pathophysiology [ 15 , 22 ]. Probes were tiled across exonic regions with high specificity, minimizing off-target homology and maximizing RNA accessibility; negative control and decoding control probes were included for quality control [ 23 ].    2.4  Xenium in situ workflow  FFPE tissue sections (5 μm) were processed using the Xenium FFPE in situ transcriptomics protocol (10x Genomics, v1.0; Demonstrated Protocol  CG000580 ;  Fig. 1 A). Briefly, sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, subjected to antigen retrieval and RNA exposure, and enzymatically digested under RNase-free conditions to facilitate probe penetration while preserving tissue morphology. Probe hybridization was performed at 50 °C for approximately 18 h. After stringent washes, adjacently hybridized probe pairs were ligated for 2 h at 37 °C and amplified by rolling circle amplification (RCA) for 2 h at 30 °C to generate detectable signals [ 24 ]. Tissue autofluorescence was reduced by chemical quenching, and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for visualization and segmentation. Processed slides were mounted in Xenium imaging buffer, sealed in Xenium cassettes, and stored at 4 °C in the dark until analysis.  Fig. 1   Xenium in situ enables spatially resolved single-cell atlas of the rat kidney with customized gene panel.  A,  Experimental workflow: Wild-type (WT) and  Brca1 -mutant (MUT) rats received ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) treatment and were dissected at the indicated time-points (control, 1 week, 3 weeks) to obtain kidneys. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) sections were processed on the Xenium platform. Following in-situ transcript capture and high-plex imaging, the identical sections were stained with H&E to provide histological context (Scale bars, 10 μm).  B , UMAP embedding of Xenium-profiled cells from the WT control kidney, marked by cell-type annotation derived from canonical marker genes ( Table S1 ).  C,  Dot-plot of the top markers per cell type. Circle size indicates the percentage of nuclei expressing the gene; color denotes mean of normalized expression (z-scored).  D,  WT control renal cortex: H&E image overlaid with Xenium-decoded cells colored by cell-type annotation in B (scale bar, 100 μm).                        2.4.1  Xenium analyzer instrument  Automated imaging and transcript decoding were performed on the 10x Genomics Xenium Analyzer using software v2.0.1.0. The instrument acquired high-resolution images through 15 iterative cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and signal removal. Four fluorescent channels were used per cycle, allowing each gene in the custom panel to be identified by a unique optical barcode. Images were acquired at 200 nm/pixel resolution with a 20× objective, and Z-stack images were collected at 0.75 μm intervals. Adjacent fields of view were tiled and computationally stitched using DAPI nuclear signals as fiducial landmarks to generate a registered whole-tissue image.  Transcripts were decoded by matching fluorescent puncta to the predefined barcode codebook. Only transcripts with a Q-score ≥20, corresponding to approximately 99% decoding accuracy, were retained for downstream analysis [ 23 ]. Detected transcripts were exported with XY coordinates, gene identities, and Q-scores. Negative-control probe signals accounted for <0.03% of total reads, indicating low background noise.    2.4.2  Cell segmentation and transcript assignment  Cell segmentation was performed using the Xenium onboard segmentation pipeline. DAPI images were used to identify nuclear boundaries, which were expanded isotropically by up to 15 μm or until they reached neighboring cell boundaries. This nuclear expansion method generated non-overlapping cell polygons approximating renal epithelial cell boundaries. Decoded transcripts located within each polygon were assigned to the corresponding cell, producing a cell-by-gene expression matrix for downstream single-cell spatial analysis [ 23 ].    2.4.3  Post-Xenium histology  After transcript profiling, the same tissue sections were re-stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) to correlate molecular data with tissue morphology. H&E images were acquired using a Leica Aperio AT2 slide scanner at 40× magnification and processed in QuPath 0.5.1 to generate OME-TIFF files. The H&E images were then aligned to DAPI images in Xenium Explorer, allowing transcript-defined cell types and spatial regions to be evaluated in relation to histological structures, such as glomeruli and renal tubules.     2.5  Bioinformatic analysis of spatial transcriptomics data   2.5.1  Data preprocessing and normalization  Xenium outputs (six rat kidney FFPE tissue samples: WT_CT, MUT_CT, WT_Fe1w, MUT_Fe1w, WT_Fe3w, MUT_Fe3w) were loaded into R (version 4.4.1) and converted to a Seurat object using Seurat v5.0.1. All data normalization was performed by SCTransform to stabilize variance transformation and to regress out sequencing-depth effects. This yielded log-normalized count data (stored in Seurat “SCT” assay) for each sample, mitigating technical variability while preserving biological variation. Low-quality cells (e.g. with extremely low transcript counts) were minimal due to Xenium's preprocessing and only cells with nCount_Xenium >0 were retained.    2.5.2  Data integration and clustering  Following normalization, the unified object containing data from six samples was processed for joint analysis. We re-ran SCTransform (merged), PCA (all genes; 30 PCs), FindNeighbors (dims 1–30), FindClusters (resolution 2.0), and UMAP (PCA), which yielded multiple clusters with distinct transcriptional signatures. Mixing across samples in PCA/UMAP was inspected to verify minimal batch effects. Clusters were manually annotated to kidney lineages (proximal tubule, stromal, endothelial, loop of Henle, collecting duct principal/intercalated, podocyte, inflammatory, proximal-like) based on canonical markers [ 21 ] and spatial context provided by Xenium Explorer. For focused analyses, we subset proximal_tubules and stromal_cells contents and re-ran the same pipeline on (i) the merged dataset to confirm lineage assignments and (ii) each compartment separately to resolve fine subclusters (pt_n; st_n) for downstream analyses.    2.5.3  Pathological score maps  Proximal-tubule clusters were defined into four pathology groups by expressional signatures and tubular morphology: normal_tubules (PT_1,2,5,6,10,11), acute_injured (PT_8), subacute_injured (PT_0,3,4,7), and dying_tubules (PT_9). Using Seurat v5.0.1 we set group identities and performed one-vs-rest DE per group with FindMarkers (two-sided Wilcoxon; min.pct = 0.2, logfc.threshold = 0.25, only.pos = TRUE). The top 10 genes by avg_log2FC per group were used for visualization (group-wise AverageExpression heatmap, z-scored by gene). For quantitative per-cell scores, we computed module scores with AddModuleScore on the available marker genes for each group (requiring ≥5 genes), using nbin = 3 and ctrl = 10 to ensure robust background control on the limited panel. Scores were then row-matched by cell_ID and merged into the Giotto (v4.2.0) object's cell_metadata for downstream spatial mapping. All plotting of score maps used fixed global min–max limits per score and unified diverging palettes to enable cross-sample comparison.    2.5.4  Morphological-transcriptomics analysis of nuclei  Nuclear polygons from Xenium segmentation (“nucleus_boundaries.csv.gz”) were imported into R (sf v1.0.19; tidyverse v2.0.0) to compute per-nucleus morphometrics: nuclear area, eccentricity (elongation, 0–1), circularity (4π·area/perimeter 2 ), compactness, convexity, solidity (area/convex hull area) and perimeter/area ratio (boundary irregularity). Polygons were linked to the same cell barcodes used in Seurat; analyses were restricted to proximal tubule cells with expression taken from the SCT assay.  For each gene–feature pair, we fit single-cell linear models per FOV (WT_Fe3w: FOV_3; MUT_Fe3w: FOV_6) with the morphology feature z-scored and technical covariates (library size, detected features) included; slopes (β) and two-sided  P  values were recorded and FDR-adjusted within FOV (Benjamini–Hochberg). As robustness checks, we computed Spearman correlations and ran elastic net models (glmnet) to assess whether multiple features jointly predict expression; a non-zero coefficient denoted feature selection.  To obtain genotype-robust effects, per-FOV slopes were combined by sample-size–weighted averaging (pooled β), and per-FOV  P  values were combined by Stouffer's method (weights ∝ √n), followed by FDR across all pairs. For each gene we derived a “consensus rank” integrating pooled β, pooled FDR, and elastic-net selection.  To identify coordinated programs, each gene was represented by its vector of pooled β across morphology features. Cosine similarity was computed between genes; pairs with similarity ≥0.6 were connected and clustered by Louvain community detection to define morphology-linked gene modules.    2.5.5  Quantification of nuclear phenotypes and integration with transcriptomics  For fields of view (FOVs) from WT_Fe3w (FOV3) and MUT_Fe3w (FOV6), nuclei were segmented using Cellpose (v2.3.2; pretrained nuclei model) [ 37 ]. Three per-cell nuclear morphological readouts were derived from the hematoxylin channel (skimage.color.rgb2hed) within each nuclear mask: (i) hematoxylin optical density (HOD), mean channel intensity following Gaussian smoothing (σ = 0.5 μm); (ii) nuclear substructure density (NSD), the count of intranuclear hematoxylin-dense foci, detected after within-nucleus 2nd-98th percentile normalization, Otsu thresholding, and filtration by area (0.3–6.0 μm 2 ) and circularity (4πA/P 2  ≥ 0.40), expressed per 100 μm 2  of nuclear area; and (iii) peripheral intensity index (PII), (mean        H  O  D   periphery      − mean        H  O  D   interior     )/section-median HOD, where peripheral (distance ≤ s) and interior (distance > s) zones were defined from a Euclidean distance transform of the nuclear boundary at shell thicknesses  s  ∈ (0.5, 1.0, 1.5) μm ( Fig. S4C ); section-median HOD was estimated once per FOV from a random sample of ∼2000 nuclei.  Cellpose-segmented nuclei were assigned Xenium cell identity via two-stage spatial registration. First, an existing QuPath-to-Xenium cell correspondence (established by manual landmark selection and iterative refinement) provided position anchors for an affine transform between the FOV image and Xenium coordinate spaces. Second, true nuclear centroids (QuPath nucleus geometry) were matched to the affine-registered Cellpose nuclei by reciprocal nearest-neighbor matching within the shared coordinate space, at the tightest tolerance (0.5–5 μm ladder) retaining ≥90% of the maximum achievable match count. PT filtering was performed after registration to avoid selection bias. Registration accuracy was confirmed by comparing QuPath's measurements (HOD;  Fig. S4A ) against Cellpose/scikit-image values.    2.5.6  Gene–morphometry association models (HOD/NSD/PII)  For each gene     g     and within a condition (WT_Fe3w; MUT_Fe3w) independently, a single-cell ordinary least-squares model was fitted:     Y  i   =  α  +   β  g   ·   X   i  g    +  γ   A  i   +   ϵ  i     where      Y  i      is the nuclear morphometric readout for cell     i     (HOD; NSD;       P  I  I   s     ),      X   i  g       is the log 1 p-normalized Xenium transcript count for gene     g     in cell     i    , and      A  i      is Cellpose-measured nuclear area (μm 2 ). Two-sided Wald p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons across 50 genes within each condition (Benjamini–Hochberg, FDR <0.05). Cross-condition concordance was assessed by Pearson correlation and sign agreement of per-gene      β  ˆ      between FOVs. Estimates were pooled by fixed-effects inverse-variance weighting:      β  ˆ    F  E    =     ∑  k    w  k     β  ˆ   k      ∑  k    w  k     ,   w  k   =  S   E  k   −  2      with pooled Wald z-statistics BH-FDR corrected across all 50 genes. Models were implemented in Python (statsmodels v0.14; scipy).    2.5.7  Karyomegaly sub-stratification and peri-karyomegaly analysis  PT cells from merged Xenium dataset were defined as karyomegalic (enlarged) if nuclear area > mean+2SD within the PT cell population, and elongated if major/minor axis ratio >2. SCTransform-normalized RNA counts from karyomegalic cells were stored as a SCTx assay. Morphological features processed from nuclear polygons were stored as a MORPH assay and reduced by PCA.  Karyomegalic PTs were then reclustered by a weighted nearest-neighbor (WNN) model that integrates RNA and morphology: SCTx PCA (dims 1–30) and a PCA of z-scored morphology (dims 1–6) were combined with FindMultiModalNeighbors (modality weights recorded as SCTx.weight/MORPH.weight), followed by UMAP on the weighted graph and Louvain communities on wsnn; we grid-searched morphology PCs (2-4, 6) × resolution (0.2, 0.3) and selected the setting with the highest mean silhouette in the WNN UMAP, followed by further resolution tuning, yielding the final result (K0–K5, resolution 0.15). Gene markers were computed using Seurat FindAllMarkers (logistic regression with covariates sample, fov_num, nCount_SCTx). Morphology tiles report per-feature means with significance from two-sided linear models (BH-FDR <0.05).  Spatial context was obtained by overlaying subcluster labels onto H&E in Xenium Explorer (Fe-NTA, 3-week). For peri-karyomegalic analyses, each karyomegalic PT served as a center; PT neighbors within 30 μm were compared with PTs >30 μm away, and hallmark expression visualized as z-scored heatmaps/dot plots (Wilcoxon, BH-FDR where indicated).    2.5.8  Neighborhood composition and microenvironment analysis  Cell centroids (centroid_x, centroid_y) and annotations from the Seurat metadata were filtered to proximal_tubules and stromal_cells, and used for point map plotting and neighbor-associated computations. Independently for each sample, the number of stromal neighbors within a 30 μm Euclidean radius was recorded for each PT cell, by a KD-tree constructed over stromal cell centroids (FNN v1.1.4.1, R; k ≤ 500). Group differences were assessed by Kruskal–Wallis test; pairwise post-hoc comparisons used Dunn's test with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction (rstatix v0.7.3, R). Beyond cell-intrinsic analysis, we modeled proximal-tubule/stromal spatial organization with Giotto (v4.2.0; Python backend) [ 25 ]. For each field, we constructed a radius-based neighbor graph (30 μm) to capture tubulointerstitial contacts in renal tissue [ 26 ]. Community detection on this neighborhood graph using the Leiden algorithm (findNetworkCommunities) yielded microenvironment (ME) clusters, i.e., spatially coherent neighborhoods that may contain mixed PT (pt_n) and stromal (st_n) subtypes. We quantified the cell-type composition and contact enrichment for each ME cluster (normalized by cell abundance). ME prevalences were compared across the six samples to assess genotype/treatment effects. ME labels were overlaid on tissue images in Xenium Explorer to verify anatomic plausibility.  To test whether ME states were independent of karyomegalic clusters, we constructed a WNN-karyomegalic × ME contingency table and applied a Pearson χ 2  test of independence (chisq.test) Tiles in the heatmap display standardized Pearson residuals (Haberman adjustment, chis$stdres): positive (green) indicates over-representation; negative (red) indicates under-representation. Significance stars denote: ∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  1.96    , ∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  2.58    , and ∗∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  3.00    . Global association was summarized by Cramér's     V  =     χ  2   /   (   N   [   min  ⁡   (   r  ,  c   )   −  1   ]    )       ; extremely small P values are reported as thresholds (e.g.,     p  <  2.2  ×   10   −  16      ).    2.5.9  Data visualization  All data visualization was performed in R (v4.4.1), using ggplot2 and plotters bundled with Seurat unless noted otherwise. Low-dimensional embeddings (UMAP) were rendered with DimPlot and annotated by cluster, sample, or FOV; single-gene summaries used VlnPlot or Seurat DotPlot. Heatmaps were produced with ComplexHeatmap for clustered expression/annotation panels and pheatmap for compact correlation/residual matrices. Panel assembly used patchwork/cowplot with harmonized color palettes, fixed aspect ratios for spatial panels, and consistent legends/scales. Multi-panel gene maps ( Fig. 2 C) and pathology-score maps ( Fig. 3 E) were generated in Giotto and exported in R. Xenium Explorer was used only to overlay labels on H&E/DAPI micrographs. Differential expression (DE) used Seurat FindMarkers/FindAllMarkers on SCT-normalized data with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Genes were eligible if detected in ≥5% of cells in either group; we report avg_log2FC (positive = higher in the first group), pct_in/pct_out, and adjusted P. Multiple testing was controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg; genes with FDR <0.05 and log 2 FC ≥ 0.25 were considered significant. Random subsampling (set.seed 42) was applied only to downsample points for visualization and was never applied in statistical testing. Box-and-violin plots display median and inter-quartile range; error bars represent 95% confidence intervals unless specified. Because the Xenium dataset included one representative specimen per genotype/treatment condition, cell-level statistics were interpreted as discovery-level measures of spatial association or enrichment rather than animal-level biological replication; key conclusions were supported by prior Fe-NTA data, mitochondrial TEM/REF analyses, and TCGA-based human validation.    2.5.11  Code availability No new algorithms were developed for this manuscript. All code created for analysis is available from the authors upon request.  Mitochondrial cristae morphometry analysis  Transmission electron microscopic images were acquired on a JEM-1400PLUS (JEOL; Tokyo, Japan). Images were analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ (v1.54p). After pixel calibration, individual mitochondria were manually outlined as ROIs with area (μm 2 ) recorded. Within each ROI, cristae ridges were segmented using Trainable Weka Segmentation (Fiji) to obtain a probability map for cristae vs. matrix. High-confidence pixels were thresholded and processed with Ridge Detection to obtain ridge centerlines, followed by Skeletonize (2D/3D) and Analyze Skeleton to quantify branch geometry. Derived per-mitochondrion metrics were: Total cristae length (μm) = Σ branch lengths;  Mean branch length (μm) = Σ branch lengths / number of branches;  Cristae length density (μm/μm 2 ) = total cristae length / mitochondrial area.   Metrics were exported as CVS files and plotted in R.    2.7  Immunoblotting  Kidney cortex lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer, resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred by standard methods. Primary antibodies included: anti-FTMT (ab124889, Abcam), anti-Mfrn1 (PA5-26720, Invitrogen), anti-Mfrn2 (PA5-42498, Invitrogen); anti-ACTB (AC-15, Sigma) served as loading control. Bands were quantified in ImageJ, normalized to ACTB, and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test; significance thresholds: ∗ P  < 0.05, ∗∗ P  < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P  < 0.001; n.s., not significant).    2.8  Primary rat embryonic fibroblasts (REFs) and treatments  REFs were derived from E13–15 embryos by standard protocols [ 28 ]. Genotypes and sex were determined by PCR [ 15 , 29 ]. Male-derived WT and Brca1-MUT REFs were maintained in DMEM (043-30085, Wako, Osaka, Japan) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Biowest; Nuaillé, France) and Mito + Serum Extender (355006, Corning, USA). REFs were immortalized via lentiviral transduction of SV40 (Addgene#22298) packaged with pspAX2 (#12260) and VSV-G (#14888). For oxidative stress, cells were treated with Fe-NTA (500 μM, 6 h) prior to fixation.    2.9  Immunofluorescence (confocal)  Cells were fixed, permeabilized and stained with anti-TOM20 (11802-1-AP, Proteintech) and anti-γ-H2AX (05-636, Sigma-Aldrich); nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. A Zeiss confocal microscope (LSM880, Carl Zeiss) was applied for image acquisition.    2.10  Mitochondrial respiration  Oxygen consumption (OCR) and extracellular acidification (ECAR) were measured on a Seahorse XFe24 Analyzer (Agilent) following manufacture's instructions. Briefly, REFs were seeded (6 × 10 4 /well) in Seahorse XF DMEM (103575-100) supplemented with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine (103577/8/9-100) on a Seahorse XFe24 plate and incubated overnight. The XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (103015-100) was run with sequential injections of oligomycin 1.5 μM, FCCP 1 μM, and rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 μM. Cell count was quantified using BioTek Cytation 5 and Keyence BZ-X800 for normalization. Data were processed per manufacturer's instructions and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test with significance shown in  Fig. 8 E ).    2.11  TCGA transcriptomic cohorts  To evaluate the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated transcriptional programs identified in our experimental model, we analyzed data obtained from the TCGA Pan-Cancer Clinical Data Resource, for TCGA-KIRC as the primary validation cohort, and additional tumor types for exploratory analyses, including TCGA-BRCA, TCGA-COAD, TCGA-LIHC, TCGA-LUAD, and TCGA-LUSC [ 30 ].  RNA-seq data were retrieved via TCGAbiolinks v2.32.0 [ 31 ] from the NCI GDC. Tumor-adjacent solid tissue normal (STN) samples were used for the primary analyses, whereas primary tumor samples were evaluated separately for independent validation. Raw counts were normalized by the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method using edgeR v4.2.2 [ 32 ] and converted to log 2 -counts per million (log 2 -CPM; prior count = 1). For duplicate gene entries, the isoform with the highest mean expression was retained.   2.11.1  Karyomegalic module definition and scoring  Four gene modules were evaluated (Fig. S7A). Three gene modules were defined based on findings from our Xenium spatial transcriptomics data. Module activity was quantified by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) using GSVA v1.52.3 [ 33 ], computed independently within each tissue compartment (STN or tumor). Only modules with at least three genes present in the expression matrix were retained. Patient-level scores were derived as mean across available samples.    2.11.2  Survival analysis  Clinical annotations, including progression-free interval (PFI) and overall survival (OS), were obtained from curated TCGA clinical datasets. For each module, patients were stratified into high- and low-score groups using the cohort-specific median module score as the cutoff. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated using the survival and survminer packages.  Associations between module activity and clinical outcome were evaluated using log-rank tests and univariable Cox proportional hazards models. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated from Cox models. Analyses were performed separately for PFI and OS endpoints. Cohorts with fewer than five outcome events or insufficient matched samples were excluded from survival testing.  A tiered strategy was used for Multiple-testing correction. We designated TCGA-KIRC as the confirmatory cohort and analyzed non-renal cancer cohorts in an exploratory manner. Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was therefore performed separately within confirmatory and exploratory tiers. Statistical significance was assessed primarily using the tier-specific FDR-adjusted results.    2.11.3  BRCA1 mutation carrier and control definition  BRCA1 germline carriers were defined as described [ 34 ]. Non-carrier controls were identified by a two-tiered exclusion strategy requiring availability of diagnostic WSIs and absence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, RAD51C, RAD51D, BARD1, and NBN. Controls were further selected by two-stage propensity score matching to control for clinical covariates [ 35 ] .  The final cohort comprised 20 BRCA1 germline carriers and 63 matched non-carrier controls (76.2% ductal, 4.8% lobular, 19.0% other histological subtypes).    2.11.4  Histopathological image analysis  Diagnostic whole slide images (WSIs) for TCGA-BRCA were obtained from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (GDC). Germline variant data were accessed from the TCGA PanCanAtlas Germline dataset [ 34 ] under controlled GDC access (dbGaP: phs000178), in compliance with the TCGA data use agreement.  Regions of interest (ROIs) containing well-formed ductal tubules were manually annotated in ductal carcinoma WSIs from both groups using QuPath v0.4 [ 36 ] (15 controls, 7 carriers; ROI count was limited by preserved adjacent normal portions). Nucleus segmentation was performed using Cellpose v2.3.2 [ 37 ], and morphological features were extracted using scikit-image. A post-hoc quality filter was applied to remove spurious detections. Nucleus-level analyses are presented as exploratory findings; patient-level analyses constitute the primary statistical inference.      3  Results   3.1  Xenium in situ on early stages of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis  To identify early alterations during iron-driven renal carcinogenesis, we analyzed kidneys from wild-type (WT) and  Brca1  mutant ( L63X/+ ; MUT) rats subjected to Fe-NTA administration, as previously described [ 15 ]. Because rat-compatible spatial transcriptomic panels remain limited, we designed a custom 50-gene Xenium panel covering renal structural markers from single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets [ 21 ], together with genes related to iron metabolism, mitochondrial function, and tumorigenesis based on our previous studies [ 5 , 38 ].  Six kidney samples representing control, 1-week, and 3-week Fe-NTA exposure in WT and MUT rats were analyzed across two Xenium slides. DAPI-based segmentation captured approximately 324,765–531,476 cells per sample, with median transcript detection of 62–104 transcripts per cell ( Fig. 1 A). Post-Xenium H&E staining preserved tissue morphology and enabled direct integration of spatial transcriptomics with histopathology ( Fig. 1 A–D). Seurat-based clustering identified 53 cellular clusters, which were annotated into 10 major renal cell categories based on marker expression and histological context ( Fig. 1 B and C;  Fig. S1A and B ). Molecular annotations closely matched H&E-defined structures, supporting robust cell-type assignment even with a focused gene panel ( Fig. 1 D). Cluster composition varied across genotype and treatment conditions, with prominent changes in proximal tubules and stromal cells ( Fig. S1C ), indicating early remodeling of epithelial and interstitial compartments during Fe-NTA-induced carcinogenesis.    3.2  Characterization of key-gene signatures in early renal carcinogenesis  We next focused on transcriptional remodeling of proximal tubular cells (PTs), the principal target of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis. Refined clustering of PT and stromal compartments improved resolution of treatment- and genotype-associated cell states ( Fig. S2A and B ). Single-cell expression analysis revealed reciprocal regulation of homeostatic and injury-associated genes in PTs ( Fig. 2 A). In control kidneys, PTs highly expressed renal function and mitochondrial metabolism genes, hereafter referred to as “friend key-genes,” including  Lrp2, Pink1,  and  Amacr . In contrast, Fe-NTA exposure induced “foe key-genes” associated with injury and tumorigenesis, including  Myc, Met, Lcn2 , and  Anxa2 , with concomitant reduction of homeostatic markers.  Several foe key-genes were induced as early as 1 week after Fe-NTA exposure in both genotypes ( Fig. 2 A). Although  Met, Anxa2, Lcn2, Sfxn3 , and  Klf4  showed partial reduction by 3 weeks,  Myc  and  Slc22a17  remained elevated or further increased. At 3 weeks, MUT PTs showed stronger expression of foe markers than WT, whereas  Lrp2  and  Amacr  were more strongly reduced, indicating genotype-dependent epithelial remodeling under oxidative stress. Spatial mapping with Giotto confirmed that friend key-genes were enriched in intact tubular segments, whereas foe key-genes localized to histologically abnormal regions with tubular dilation, disruption, or loss of recognizable tubular organization ( Fig. 2 C).  Because karyomegalic PTs are a characteristic lesion in Fe-NTA-treated kidneys [ 39 , 40 ], we quantified nuclear morphology using Xenium-derived nuclear polygons ( Fig. 2 B). Fe-NTA exposure was associated with nuclear enlargement, reduced compactness and circularity, and increased eccentricity. WT karyomegalic cells had larger nuclei than MUT cells under comparable treatment conditions ( Fig. S5A ). These data indicate that nuclear remodeling accompanies early Fe-NTA-induced epithelial injury and is modified by Brca1 haploinsufficiency.    3.3  Dynamics of diverse PT subtypes in early renal carcinogenesis  To resolve PT dynamics during early carcinogenesis, we reclustered PTs and identified 11 subtypes ( Fig. 3 A and B). Homeostatic PT clusters 1, 2, 5, 6, 10, and 12 predominated in control kidneys and expressed renal functional and mitochondrial genes. In contrast, clusters 0, 3, 4, 7, 8, and 9 emerged after Fe-NTA exposure and showed increased injury-, repair-, or foe key-gene expression with reduced homeostatic programs. Genotype-specific differences became evident after Fe-NTA exposure: WT kidneys showed transient loss of normal tubular states at 1 week with partial recovery by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed expansion of injured clusters, particularly clusters 4 and 7.  The PT subtypes represented distinct biological states ( Fig. 3 B). Oxidative Stress–Adaptive PTs (cluster 0; OA_PT) expressed antioxidant and metabolic genes such as  Cubn, Slc40a1, Lrp2, Slc27a2 , and  Gpx4 , together with moderate  Myc  and  Met  expression. DNA Damage–Response PTs (cluster 3; DR_PT) expressed repair and regenerative markers including  Mki67, Rad51, Bard1 , and  Bap1 . Maladaptive Repair PTs (clusters 4 and 7; MR_PT) expressed  Lcn2, Slc22a17 , and other foe key-genes, with cluster 4 retaining more friend key-gene expression than cluster 7. Transient Regenerative PTs (cluster 8; TR_PT) expressed proliferation and DNA repair markers, whereas Ferroptotic PTs (cluster 9; Fer_PT) were often isolated necrotic or pyknotic cells within otherwise preserved tubules, as confirmed by Xenium Explorer alignment with H&E images ( Fig. S3A ).  Spatially, DR_PT localized mainly near the cortex–medulla boundary in WT kidneys at 1 week but was less evident in MUT kidneys ( Fig. 3 C). MR_PT populations frequently co-localized within MUT tubules, whereas WT tubules showed greater admixture of homeostatic, oxidative stress–adaptive, and transient regenerative states. Stromal reclustering further identified 13 stromal subtypes with genotype- and treatment-dependent composition ( Fig. 3 D). After 3 weeks of Fe-NTA, MUT kidneys showed expansion of stromal states enriched for regenerative, injury-response, iron-handling, matrix-remodeling, and macrophage-recruiting signatures, including ST_1, ST_3, ST_5/8, ST_6, and ST_9.  To summarize PT status spatially, we generated pathology-informed module scores ( Fig. S3B–D ). Spatial score maps showed that normal tubular scores declined after 1 week of Fe-NTA exposure and partially recovered in WT kidneys by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed more persistent dysfunction ( Fig. 3 E). Interestingly, scores representing renal injury and cell death (acute/subacute injured score; dying tubules score) displayed inverse spatial patterns to normal tubules score at 1-week Fe-NTA treatment, with reduced acute injured score at 3-week Fe-NTA treatment, marking the progression of homeostatic PT clusters toward subacute injury and the initiation of cellular adaptations linked to ferroptosis resistance and potential oncogenic transformation.    3.4  Nuclear morphometrics reflect transcriptional behaviors in pathological/genotype-dependent patterns  We next asked whether nuclear morphology captures transcriptional states at single-cell resolution. Morphological features derived from Xenium polygons included nuclear area, eccentricity, circularity, compactness, convexity, and solidity ( Fig. 4 A). Gene–morphology associations were quantified using covariate-adjusted linear models with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction. In Fe-NTA 3-week samples, morphology-associated coefficients revealed coordinated relationships between nuclear shape and PT transcriptional state ( Fig. 4 B). Oncogenic and iron-associated genes, including  Lcn2, Anxa2, Met, Pcbp2, Myc , and  Sfxn3,  were positively associated with eccentricity and convexity, whereas circular and compact nuclei were associated with preserved PT markers such as S lc27a2, Lrp2, Pink1,  and  Tfrc . Although the overall direction of associations was similar between WT and MUT kidneys, MUT showed stronger coefficients, indicating amplified coupling between nuclear morphology and stress-associated transcription under Brca1 haploinsufficiency.  We then converted morphology–gene β profiles into gene–gene networks using cosine similarity. Under the pre-specified criteria of FDR ≤0.05, β ≥ 0.10, and cosine ≥0.70, robust modules were absent in control kidneys and WT Fe-NTA 3-week kidneys, whereas WT Fe-NTA 1-week kidneys showed compact Slc27a2–Lrp2–Pink1 and Mki67–Anxa2 modules ( Fig. 4 C). In contrast, MUT kidneys retained modules at both 1 and 3 weeks, including a recurrent Slc27a2–Lrp2 core and an Lcn2–Anxa2 injury-associated core, suggesting genotype-dependent persistence of morphology-linked transcriptional programs.  To identify transcriptional correlates of nuclear chromatin organization during early carcinogenic nuclear transformation, we derived three nuclear morphometric parameters: hematoxylin optical density (HOD), nuclear substructure density (NSD) [ 41 ], and peripheral intensity index (PII) [ 42 ], from H&E images of WT and MUT Fe-NTA 3w kidneys. HOD provided quantitative readout of bulk nuclear chromatin compaction. In WT, the genes most strongly associated with HOD (e.g.,  Gpx4 ,  Fth1 ,  Ncoa4 ,  Pcbp1 , Tfrc) were uniformly negative, indicating that more robust iron-homeostatic programs correspond to lower nuclear hematoxylin density, consistent with a more open chromatin state ( Fig. 4 D;  Table S2 ). In MUT, PT identity genes (e.g.,  Amacr ,  Slc27a2 ,  Lrp2 ) again showed strong negative associations, whereas top positive associations were observed for  Sfxn3 ,  Sting1 ,  Mcub ,  S100a9 ,  Anxa2 , and  Lcn2 , suggesting that chromatin compaction is associated with mitochondrial alteration and stress responses in Brca1 deficient carcinogenesis. Despite that majority of significant genes were genotype-specific, effect direction was replicated across genotypes for  Lrp2 ,  Slc27a2 , and  Amacr  (negative in both) and for  Lgals1 ,  Anxa2 ,  Pcbp2 , and  Bard1  (positive in both). Fixed-effects meta-analysis was consistent with an overall pattern during oxidative stress-based carcinogenesis, where homeostatic genes downregulate with chromatin compaction, while carcinogenetic pathways across injury/iron-overload/fibrosis are activated, especially more pronounced in  BRCA1  mutants.  NSD [ 41 ], which detected hematoxylin-dense intranuclear foci, showed no detectable gene-level association in either genotype ( Fig. S4B ), consistent with its proposed role as constitutive, transcriptionally silent chromatin compartment (e.g., chromocenters). PII captured the distribution of peripheral heterochromatin (lamina-associated domains (LADs)), providing a complementary readout of nuclear architectural organization. In WT, PT metabolic genes (e.g.,  Pink1 ,  Slc27a2 ,  Tfrc ,  Fth1 ,  Gpx4 ,  Ncoa4 ,  Pcbp2 ) were positively associated with PII, indicating that they correspond to greater peripheral enrichment of condensed chromatin, consistent with intact LAD organization ( Fig. 4 E;  Table S2 ). In MUT,  Slc27a2 ,  Amacr , and  Lrp2  retained similar positive associations, while  Mcub ,  Sting1 , and  Cdkn1/2a  showed significant negative associations not observed in WT, implying a distinct transcriptional signature related to peripheral heterochromatin loss [ 43 , 44 ]. As with HOD, cross concordance was low overall, although  Slc27a2 ,  Gpx4 , and  Pink1  replicated a consistent positive direction in both genotypes. Meta-analysis identified positive pooled effects for PT/iron/mitochondrial metabolic genes (e.g.,  Lrp2 ,  Slc27a2 ,  Amacr ), alongside negative effects including  Cdkn1/2a ,  Mcub ,  Lcn2 ,  Myc , and  Lgals1  ( Fig. 4 E).  Together, these results indicate that HOD and PII both capture a shared transcriptional axis linking proximal tubule homeostasis to chromatin reorganization, with this signature more extensive in MUT. These findings also demonstrate that nuclear chromatin morphometry can be systematically linked to spatial transcriptomic profiles, identifying candidate chromatin-state markers of early renal carcinogenesis.    3.5  Epithelial karyomegaly classified into subtypes with distinct biological signatures  We defined karyomegalic epithelial cells as PTs with nuclear area greater than mean + 2SD and elongated cells as those with axis ratio >2. Compared with other PTs, enlarged nuclei showed consistent  Cdkn1a  upregulation and  Pink1  downregulation, with heterogeneous induction of DNA damage repair and regenerative genes ( Fig. 5 A;  Fig. S5C and D ). Elongated cells showed impaired epithelial function with increased  Sfxn3  and modest  Rad51  and  Mki67  induction ( Fig. S5B ). Because karyomegalic cells showed clear transcriptional heterogeneity and group-dependent differences in incidence, we focused subsequent analyses on enlarged epithelial nuclei. We next investigated the morphological and transcriptional features of re-clustered karyomegalic subpopulations. Among all clusters, K1 displayed the most pronounced nuclear enlargement with irregular, rough nuclear contours, and thus most closely aligned with the canonical pathological definition of karyomegaly ( Fig. 5 B, D). Transcriptional profiling further revealed strong induction of  Cdkn1a , coordinated with elevated  Ncoa4  and reduced  Fth1 , indicative of stress-associated cell-cycle arrest with an active ferritinophagy-mediated iron-mobilization program ( Fig. 5 C, S5E). K4 was enriched for markers of proximal tubule homeostasis and metabolic competence (e.g.,  Lrp2, Slc27a2, Amacr, Pink1 ), suggesting maintenance of epithelial transport and mitochondrial quality control in WT ( Fig. 5 B, C). And in morphological perspectives, K4 showed relatively more solid and compact nucleus. Strikingly, K2 and K5 co-expressed  Met, Lcn2,  and  Myc , pointing to an adaptive stress program with oncogenic features, whereas significant nuclear morphology features included elongation yet smaller area than K1. We interpret these states as a potential early pro-tumorigenic niche in BRCA1-haploinsufficient kidneys that may represent an actionable window for intervention in carcinogenesis.  To determine whether karyomegaly represents not only an altered epithelial state but also a local epithelial microenvironment, we profiled PT neighbors located within 30 μm of either karyomegalic or non-karyomegalic PT cells. PTs adjacent to karyomegalic cells showed increased expression of iron-handling, oxidative stress–adaptive, and pro-survival genes, including  Lcn2, Anxa2, Mki67, Sfxn3, Cdkn1a,  and  Myc , together with reduced  Amacr, Aqp3,  and  Pink1  ( Fig. 5 E). These signatures partially mirrored those of karyomegalic cells themselves, indicating that surrounding epithelial cells acquire a stress-adapted, survival-biased state. This interpretation is supported by the induction of factors linked to ferroptotic vulnerability, including  Lcn2 , which can modulate labile iron availability and antioxidant defenses [ 45 ], and by reduced  Pink1 , suggesting impaired mitophagy [ 46 ].  Subtype-stratified analysis further showed that PTs surrounding K2 cells were enriched for  Myc, Lcn2, Slc40a1,  and  Met , with reduced  Amacr, Pink1,  and  Slc27a2,  whereas PTs surrounding K4 cells maintained metabolic and mitochondrial homeostasis genes ( Fig. 5 E). Thus, karyomegalic states appear to act as focal organizers of local epithelial programs, with BRCA1-haploinsufficient karyomegaly defining a stress-adaptive, iron-handling, proto-oncogenic niche permissive for iron-driven carcinogenesis.    3.6  Stromal neighbors contribute to distinct regulatory system in BRCA1-MUT kidneys  Because renal epithelial injury occurs within an integrated tubulointerstitial environment [ 47 , 48 ], we examined stromal proximity and microenvironmental organization. To characterize these changes, we performed Leiden-based microenvironmental (ME) clustering, using previously defined PT and stromal subclusters within a 30 μm radius. Twelve predominant MEs were retained for analysis ( Fig. 6 B;  Fig. S6B ). ME_2 and ME_5 showed marked differences between WT and MUT kidneys after 3 weeks of Fe-NTA exposure ( Fig. 6 C). Spatial projection revealed that ME_2 localized mainly to the cortex–medulla boundary, whereas ME_5 predominated in the upper cortex ( Fig. 6 D). ROIs containing well-formed ductal structures adjacent to ductal carcinoma were manually annotated, followed by nuclear segmentation and morphometric analysis in  BRCA1  germline mutation carriers and matched non-carrier controls. In  BRCA1 -mutant carriers, Karyo2 activity positively correlated with nuclear eccentricity (Spearman ρ = 0.82, p = 0.034), whereas KaryoCore activity correlated with nuclear solidity (ρ = 0.86, p = 0.024) ( Fig. 9 C). This stress-adaptive state was markedly expanded in Brca1 haploinsufficient rats, linking hereditary cancer susceptibility to impaired ferroptotic elimination under iron-catalyzed oxidative stress during tumor initiation. ( Fig. 7 ).  Spatial transcriptomics has transformed tissue biology by enabling molecular profiling while preserving histological architecture. Here, we further integrated spatial transcriptomic data with quantitative nuclear morphology derived from H&E sections. In diagnostic pathology, nuclear atypia remains one of the most fundamental indicators of cellular state, yet its quantitative integration with molecular programs has remained limited. By establishing digital metrics for nuclear size, contour smoothness, chromatin density, and nuclear substructure, we generated a framework that translates classical histopathological features into spatially resolved functional genomic states. This approach revealed that nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia closely track ferroptosis-resistant and stress-adaptive transcriptional programs during early carcinogenesis.  Our analysis identified a karyomegalic proximal tubular population enriched for oncogenic, iron-handling, and ferroptosis-resistance pathways. Importantly, neighboring non-karyomegalic epithelial cells displayed highly similar transcriptional profiles, suggesting that karyomegaly marks a broader pre-neoplastic field rather than an isolated cellular phenotype. Although karyomegalic cells themselves may represent a transient stress-adaptive state, they function as a histological beacon for the earliest detectable stages of tumor initiation under oxidative stress.  A central feature of this state was mitochondrial dysfunction. Electron microscopy previously demonstrated abundant small, interconnected mitochondria in  Brca1  mutant kidneys after Fe-NTA exposure [ 15 ], consistent with stress-induced mitochondrial remodeling. Concordantly, mitochondrial stress assays demonstrated impaired respiration and reduced metabolic flexibility, likely driven by a broad failure of mitochondrial quality control. Because mitochondria are major execution sites of ferroptosis [ 52 ], these alterations likely promote ferroptosis resistance and aberrant epithelial survival under iron-catalyzed oxidative stress. Reduced 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (HNE) production detected by HNEJ-1 staining may similarly reflect depletion of mitochondrial substrates for lipid peroxidation [ 15 , 53 ]. Further investigation into biogenesis and maintenance of the diminished functional mitochondrial pool will likely clarify how exposome-related iron stress establishes and sustains the ferroptosis-resistant niches. Moreover, Brca1 haploinsufficiency perturbs iron homeostasis even under physiological conditions [ 15 ], potentially increasing susceptibility to stress-adaptive transformation through heightened iron demand during DNA synthesis [ 54 ].  Importantly, integration with human cancer datasets suggested that this ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic state is conserved across multiple epithelial cancers beyond the experimental rat model ( Fig. 9 ). These findings support a broader model in which oxidative stress and hereditary susceptibility cooperate to generate stress-adaptive epithelial states that evade ferroptotic elimination during early tumorigenesis.  In conclusion, this study establishes a spatial and morphological framework for dissecting early tumor initiation by integrating single-cell spatial transcriptomics with digital pathology. We identify a ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic epithelial state associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and expanded under BRCA1 haploinsufficiency, linking nuclear morphology to stress-adaptive pre-neoplastic programs across experimental and human tissue contexts. These findings provide a framework for understanding how exposome-driven oxidative stress intersects with hereditary cancer susceptibility during the earliest stages of tumor initiation. Limitations include the use of a preclinical male rat model, a restricted Xenium gene panel, and representative rather than biologically replicated specimens for each Xenium condition. Accordingly, single-cell statistical significance should be interpreted as supporting spatial cell-state associations rather than animal-level biological replication, with biological relevance strengthened by independent mitochondrial analyses, prior Fe-NTA observations, and human TCGA validation. Future studies should determine whether targeting mitochondrial adaptation or ferroptosis resistance can prevent tumor initiation in genetically susceptible tissues exposed to carcinogenic oxidative stress. evidence_text:
Asynchronous Evolution of Epithelium and Stroma Differentiates Precursor Lesions from Pancreatic Cancer. Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) precedes pancreatic cancer, a deadly disease characterized by an extensive tumor microenvironment. How the microenvironment evolves during cancer progression is largely unknown, as PanINs are microscopic and nondiseased pancreas samples are exceedingly rare, while adjacent normal samples are disrupted by the presence of malignancy. Leveraging donor organs and spatial technologies, we mapped the evolution of PanIN to cancer. The PanIN epithelial component falls on a continuum with cancer, whereas the PanIN microenvironment is drastically distinct. Progression to cancer is accompanied by profound geographic reorganization of myeloid cells and lymphocytes and the formation of a cancer-specific fibroblast population characterized by high levels of smooth muscle actin, LRRC15, and the WNT signaling component LEF1. Together, our data show asynchronous evolution of epithelial and stromal components during pancreatic carcinogenesis. Lack of stromal reprogramming might explain why most PanINs do not progress to cancer. Compiled data available at https://www.pancreas-precancer-atlas.com/.

Significance

Pancreatic cancer precursor lesions are widely prevalent in the population, but progression to invasive cancer is uncommon. Identifying barriers to cancer progression is critical for cancer interception. Our findings describe unique features of the precancer microenvironment that are likely responsible for keeping precursor lesions from progressing to malignancy. Significance: Pancreatic cancer precursor lesions are widely prevalent in the population, but progression to invasive cancer is uncommon. Identifying barriers to cancer progression is critical for cancer interception. Introduction Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal cancers, often diagnosed at late stages because of the asymptomatic nature of early disease and the absence of routine screening and early detection tools [for review see ( 1 )]. Two main types of precursor lesions give rise to pancreatic cancer in humans. Cystic lesions, most often classified as intrapapillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN), can be visualized with abdominal imaging techniques; pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), the most common precursor to pancreatic cancer [for review see ( 2 )], is microscopic and cannot be detected noninvasively. At the genetic level, more than 90% of human pancreatic cancer samples are associated with oncogenic mutations in the KRAS gene; mutant KRAS is also a feature of nearly all human PanIN lesions ( 3 ). Most of our understanding of human PanIN lesions derives from the study of tumor-adjacent samples, which might harbor field defects caused by proximity to cancer and typically are collected from older individuals ( 4 ). Through our collaboration with Gift of Life Michigan, we procured healthy donor pancreata from more than 150 individuals across age ranges (20–70 years). In initial analysis of 30 pancreata, we discovered that more than 60% of the healthy population harbors PanIN lesions regardless of age ( 5 ), contrary to the long-held belief that PanINs are rare and accumulate with age ( 6 ). The observation that PanIN are extremely common implies that progression to malignancy is rare. Pancreatic cancer is associated with an extensive tumor microenvironment (TME) that constitutes up to 90% of the tumor mass [for review see ( 2 )]. Fibroblasts and immune cells are key components of the TME and play complex roles in the biology of pancreatic cancer. Although a large body of literature has dissected the nature and functional status of TME components in pancreatic cancer, our understanding of the early stages of carcinogenesis and TME formation relies on genetically engineered mice, due to the paucity of available human samples. Although mouse models are an essential tool for basic discovery and preclinical work, mouse PanINs differ in fundamental ways from their human counterpart. Mice very rarely develop spontaneous PanIN, even in old age; furthermore, in most available models, oncogenic KRAS —a hallmark mutation in pancreatic cancer—is activated during embryonic development of the pancreas ( 7 , 8 ). Even in models that allow adult activation of oncogenic KRAS ( 9 , 10 ), expression is driven simultaneously in every epithelial cell of the pancreas, which in turn might cause field effects that are not observed in human spontaneous PanIN. Finally, mice are genetically homogeneous and are maintained in a constant and highly controlled environment throughout their lifespan, in sharp contrast with the constant change that characterizes human life. To understand the nature of human PanIN and map the evolution of the microenvironment surrounding PanINs, it is essential to leverage human samples. Human PanIN lesions, like their mouse counterpart, are surrounded by an accumulation of fibroblasts, immune cells, and extracellular matrix (ECM). The nature of the cells composing the PanIN microenvironment and their specific characteristics remain unknown. A key challenge to studying PanIN lesions and their microenvironment is the microscopic nature of lesions, which cannot be dissected and studied in isolation from surrounding healthy tissue. Previous studies of human PanIN largely relied on “adjacent normal” ( 4 , 11 – 15 ). This poses a challenge as adjacent normal tissue is not, in fact, normal but is disrupted by cancer-driven field effects such as extensive inflammation ( 5 , 16 ). To obtain sporadic PanIN in otherwise healthy pancreata, we leveraged our unique collaboration with Gift of Life Michigan, which allowed us to accrue more than 150 donor pancreata; we also leveraged the pancreatic cancer biobank at the University of Michigan. Together, we accrued a comprehensive cohort of samples that enabled direct mapping of the epithelial and stromal components during the progression from indolent PanIN to cancer. Given that PanIN form a microscopic portion of otherwise healthy organs, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is not suitable for analyzing their evolution. To specifically analyze the transcriptional status of PanINs and their microenvironment, we employed spatial transcriptomics, together with histopathologic annotation of epithelial structures, followed by protein validation. Our samples encompassed nonneoplastic epithelial cell types, such as acinar and ductal cells, and partially dedifferentiated acinar clusters co-expressing acinar and ductal markers, which we refer to as acinar–ductal metaplasia (ADM), a response to tissue damage that is usually transient. Donor samples also contained sporadic PanIN, and tumor samples contained PanIN, areas of well-differentiated or glandular tumor (GLTumor), and areas of poorly differentiated tumor (PDTumor). In addition, though not the focus of the current study, our sections included endocrine islets. We discovered that PanIN epithelial domains are distinct from normal pancreas domains (both acini and ducts) and that they fall on a continuum with neoplastic samples and are closest to GLTumor, although clear differences exist. Key characteristics of malignancy, such as upregulation of signaling in RAS/MAPK, JAK/STAT3, and other inflammatory pathways were slightly upregulated in PanIN compared with normal pancreas structures, higher in GLTumor, and drastically higher in PDTumor. In contrast, the microenvironments of PanIN and invasive cancer differed markedly. The PanIN microenvironment was abundantly infiltrated by plasma cells, whereas macrophages tended to be located away from epithelial cells; this spatial organization was reversed in tumor samples, in which plasma cells were scattered and macrophages were near tumor epithelium. Furthermore, tumor samples were associated with the de novo appearance of a fibroblast population characterized by high expression of smooth muscle actin (SMA), LRRC15, and LEF1, a WNT signaling component and target gene. We utilized 3D cocultures and observed that cancer organoids drive LEF1 expression in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF), but not in fibroblasts from the normal pancreas, functionally validating our key findings. Together, our data show that the PanIN microenvironment lacks key characteristics of the TME, a finding that might in part explain the lack of progression of the vast majority of PanIN to cancer. Results Integration of Single-Cell RNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics Defines Tumor-Specific Domains To overcome the limitation posed by the scarcity of PanIN within a pancreas, we developed a spatial domain identification workflow that integrates scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics using spatially informed clustering and spot deconvolution along with histologic annotation ( Fig. 1A ). Utilizing this workflow, we compared the transcriptional status of epithelial and stromal compartments of PanIN and pancreatic cancer ( Fig. 1B ). To validate our findings, we utilized independent Visium datasets, publicly available Xenium datasets, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD) dataset, donor and PDAC tissue immunostaining, and tumor organoid/fibroblast cocultures ( Fig. 1C ). To compare transcriptional features of sporadic PanIN and pancreatic cancer, we performed spatial transcriptomics using the 10x Genomics Visium platform on 11 PanIN-containing donor samples, 7 pancreatic adenocarcinoma samples, and 2 adjacent normal pancreas samples from patients with cancer ( Fig. 1D and E ; Supplementary Fig. S1A; Supplementary Table S1). All samples were annotated by board-certified gastrointestinal pathologists (J. Shi, J.M. Szczepanski, and A. Maitra). Prior to analyzing spatial transcriptomics, we generated a reference scRNA-seq atlas of both previously published ( 12 , 17 ) and new samples of healthy donor pancreatic tissue ( n = 24), adjacent normal to cancer ( n = 3), and pancreatic adenocarcinoma ( n = 18; Supplementary Table S1). Together, the atlas contained more than 200k cells, representing a variety of epithelial and stromal populations ( Fig. 2A ). Different cell clusters were annotated according to published known lineage markers (Supplementary Fig. S2A; Supplementary Table S2) and were present at expected proportions (Supplementary Fig. S2B and S2C; ref. 5 ). As expected, we identified several epithelial cell populations of the exocrine pancreas, which we classified as acinar, ADM, acinar/ADM, and ductal. To identify cancer cells, we used the Numbat algorithm that allows prediction of copy-number variation (CNV; as a proxy of genomic aberrations) from scRNA-seq data ( 18 ). A cluster expressing markers including KRT17 , KRT19 , CLDN18 , and TFF1 exhibited the highest CNV probability, allowing us to identify it as tumor epithelial cells ( Fig. 2B ; Supplementary Fig. S3A). Interestingly, the CNV profile derived from transcriptomic data was consistent with that in the TCGA-PAAD dataset, including recurrent deletions in chromosomes 6, 17, and 18 (Supplementary Fig. S3B; ref. 19 ). Among components of the microenvironment, we identified immune cell types (macrophages, granulocytes, T cells, NK cells, B cells, plasma cells, and mast cells) and nonimmune stromal cell types (endothelial, lymphatic endothelial, endocrine, fibroblasts, pericytes, and neurons). The single-cell atlas included both normal pancreas and cancer samples; however, cells belonging to PanIN lesions cannot be readily identified in dissociated tissue because of the loss of histology, relative transcriptional similarity to neoplastic cells in the tumor, and their relative rarity.
